passages.title: From investment potential to shared prosperity.
passages.text:
A systems-led roadmap to turn the Bangsamoro’s natural assets, entrepreneurial energy, cultural strengths and strategic location into productive investment, decent work and resilient communities.
Executive decision brief IEDS-led strategy 2026–2035 Evidence-informed · adaptive
Explore the strategy ↓ Investment requirements

passages.title: Why BIRD, and why now?
passages.text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) has substantial economic potential: agricultural and marine resources, a young population, a distinctive halal economy opportunity, renewable-energy and nature-based assets, and access to the wider BIMP-EAGA market. Yet these advantages do not automatically become jobs, exports or sustained private investment. BIRD responds to a system-wide problem. Infrastructure, skills, public-service capacity, land and resource governance, standards, finance and market access depend on one another. When they are planned in isolation, strong performance in one area can be cancelled by a bottleneck elsewhere. The roadmap moves beyond a list of projects towards a sequenced investment system: prepare enabling conditions, build productive capacity, then connect competitive firms to larger markets. The report recommends the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS) . It brings together the strongest elements of halal-led growth, green-economy value creation and infrastructure-first enabling, sequencing them according to dependencies. The intended result is not investment volume alone, but investment that creates local value, broadens opportunity, protects natural capital and remains resilient through political, fiscal, climate and security shocks.

passages.title: Why BIRD, and why now?
passages.text:
BIRD is a strategic framework, not an approved appropriation or a guarantee that every target will be achieved. Its credibility depends on verified baselines, ready and safeguarded projects, transparent financing decisions and routine learning from implementation.
2025 GRDP of the five-province region (PSA, +5.0%). The ₱299.5B figure for 2024 included Sulu (Chapter 2, Table 2-3). Approvals reported for January–April 2026, not a full-year result. Consented survey responses in the latest linked snapshot; stakeholder evidence, not official statistics.
2026–2035, organised into three phases with review and readiness gates. The 2024 GRDP series predates Sulu’s exclusion. Chapter 7 calls for a reconciled five-province baseline and consistent territorial definitions before targets are formally calibrated.

passages.title: A region of strong assets—and binding constraints
passages.text: Chapter 2 treats BARMM as an interconnected economy. Opportunity is significant, but value creation depends on converting assets into productive capacity and market access.

passages.title: Opportunity
passages.text:
• Young people and human potential: a foundation for skills, entrepreneurship and a more productive workforce if education, health and training systems meet demand.
• Halal economy: cultural authenticity and standards-based production can open differentiated markets.
• Natural capital: agriculture, fisheries, forestry, marine resources and renewable energy can support value addition and carefully governed green revenue.
• Strategic location: BIMP-EAGA connections create potential for trade, tourism, logistics and cross-border value chains.
• Digital leapfrogging: connectivity and digital public services can lower transaction costs and widen access.

passages.title: Risks and constraints
passages.text:
• Poverty and skills gaps: weak purchasing power and human-capital constraints can limit productivity and market depth.
• Infrastructure deficits: power, logistics, cold chain and broadband constrain reliable production.
• Investment friction: project-preparation gaps, uncertain processing pathways, fragmented information and weak aftercare can impede conversion from interest to operating investment.
• Governance and delivery capacity: coordination problems, underspending, unclear data ownership and discontinuity can weaken execution.
• Climate and security exposure: shocks can affect livelihoods, assets, investor confidence and delivery continuity.

passages.title: What the evidence implies
passages.text:
• Enablers—especially infrastructure, human capital and implementation capacity—are a binding constraint in the diagnostic.
• High opportunity ratings do not prove that investment-ready supply, certification, finance or buyers already exist.
• Island and mainland contexts need differentiated territorial delivery, not one regional average alone.
• Climate, peace, inclusion and governance must be built into economic programmes.

passages.title: Strategic implication
passages.text:
• Prepare enabling systems before, or alongside, productive investments.
• Link infrastructure to credible production, processing, skills and offtake.
• Prioritise the weakest links and measure whether they improve.
• Make readiness, safeguards, financing and accountability prerequisites for scale-up.
Chapter 2 distinguishes official statistics, stakeholder evidence and analytical synthesis. Survey-based SWOT scores diagnose perceived conditions; they are not official baselines.

passages.title: Why Integrated Ecosystem Development was selected
passages.text:
Chapter 3 compared four options against seven weighted criteria. IEDS ranked first because it addresses interdependence and sequencing—not only one sector or constraint. Table 1. Strategic options: analytical baseline scores
Rank | Option | Score / 10 | Emphasis | Limitation if pursued alone
1 | IEDS Integrated Ecosystem Development | 8.83 | All clusters and operating systems, sequenced by dependency | Requires strong orchestration and readiness gates to avoid overloading delivery capacity.
2 | HEDS Halal Economy Dominance | 7.53 | Halal market access, certification and value addition | Can outrun power, logistics, skills and processing capacity if pursued alone.
3 | IFES Infrastructure-First Enabling | 7.46 | Infrastructure and human capital as prerequisites | Capacity may be built without sufficient processing, production or demand.
4 | GEMS Green Economy Monetisation | 7.16 | Natural-capital value, climate finance and green revenue | Requires credible safeguards, measurement, legal instruments and buyers. Stakeholder validation cross-check: the reported survey comparison also ranked IEDS first. Among all respondents with valid option ratings (n = 75), scores were IEDS 6.05, HEDS 5.90, IFES 5.77 and GEMS 5.73. Among slider movers (n = 50), scores were IEDS 6.57, HEDS 6.35, IFES 6.16 and GEMS 6.10. These are separate evidence streams, not a population-wide vote.

passages.title: Why Integrated Ecosystem Development was selected
passages.text: Analytical scores are structured expert judgements, using the seven criteria and weights shown above. They are a decision aid, not a forecast of realised economic performance.

passages.title: One connected strategy, five growth engines
passages.text: IEDS combines the strongest elements of halal-led growth, green-economy value creation and infrastructure-first enabling. Foundational capacity supports value addition; value addition supports market connections; finance and governance connect the system.

passages.title: Halal Economy
passages.text: Build credible assurance, capable firms, processing capacity and recognised standards so cultural authenticity becomes a market advantage.

passages.title: Agro-industrial Development
passages.text: Raise productivity and local value capture through aggregation, post-harvest systems, cold chain, processing and reliable market links.

passages.title: Green Economy
passages.text: Protect natural capital while developing viable renewable energy, ecosystem services and eligible nature-based revenue with safeguards.

passages.title: Infrastructure and Connectivity
passages.text: Address binding power, transport, logistics, broadband and human-capital constraints that limit the productivity of every other engine.

passages.title: Islamic Finance and Investment Promotion
passages.text:
Prepare investable projects, deepen Shariah-compliant financial access, mobilise blended capital and improve investor facilitation and aftercare.
How the engines connect: infrastructure and skills enable reliable supply; agro-industry and halal assurance convert supply into differentiated products; green practices protect the resource base; market connectors create demand; investment facilitation and Islamic finance help turn a credible pipeline into financed, operating enterprises.

passages.title: Targets to guide decisions—not promises detached from evidence
passages.text: These are strategic targets reported in the BIRD chapters. They must be calibrated against verified baselines, consistent territorial coverage, price basis and approved indicator definitions before being treated as formal commitments.

passages.title: Regional economy
passages.text: GRDP by 2035; reconcile the series and price basis with the five-province baseline.

passages.title: Employment
passages.text: At least 20,000 jobs; distinguish net additional jobs from jobs supported or sustained.

passages.title: Annual investment approvals
passages.text: Approvals are not the same as realised investment, disbursement, operating projects or jobs.

passages.title: Poverty incidence
passages.text: Strategic target. Chapter 7 notes differing reference periods and family/person measures; recalibrate against the authoritative full-year series.

passages.title: Total exports
passages.text: Chapter 4 headline trajectory; verify product/service coverage, origin and valuation with the data owner.

passages.title: Green economy
passages.text:
Verified green revenue target in Chapter 3, alongside an 85% renewable-energy mix target in Chapter 4.
Other indicators include 5,000+ halal-certified MSMEs and Islamic banking assets of ₱20 billion or more by 2035. Every target series requires a named data owner, source, refresh frequency, territorial definition and verification method.

passages.title: Build foundations. Scale value. Consolidate gains.
passages.text:
Chapter 6 converts strategy into a phased programme and project pipeline. The timeline below follows the canonical phase definitions used in Chapters 3–6.
Phase 1 · Activate

passages.title: Purpose
passages.text: Establish governance, data, project-preparation and enabling conditions required to move from concept to delivery.

passages.title: Strategic priorities
passages.text:
• Reconcile legal and institutional arrangements; define coordination roles.
• Establish verified baselines and a common project pipeline.
• Prepare infrastructure, energy, logistics, skills and digital enablers.
• Strengthen halal assurance, safeguards and investor aftercare.

passages.title: Expected outcomes
passages.text:
Prioritised projects, clear accountabilities, agreed indicator definitions and early enabling capacity.
₱35–45 billion Indicative planning envelope; not an approved appropriation.
Phase 2 · Scale

passages.title: Purpose
passages.text: Expand value addition and market formation where infrastructure, skills, standards, finance and offtake are sufficiently ready.

passages.title: Strategic priorities
passages.text:
• Scale halal and agro-industrial processing and cold chain.
• Develop viable renewable and nature-based projects with safeguards.
• Expand MSME capabilities, Islamic finance and industry-aligned skills.
• Strengthen market corridors, certification recognition and digital trade.

passages.title: Expected outcomes
passages.text:
More operating firms, stronger local sourcing, higher productivity and a broader investable pipeline.
₱50–65 billion Indicative envelope, subject to readiness and financing.
Phase 3 · Consolidate

passages.title: Purpose
passages.text: Consolidate competitive production systems and connect them to wider domestic, ASEAN, OIC and BIMP-EAGA markets.

passages.title: Strategic priorities
passages.text:
• Scale proven exporters, tourism offerings and cross-border supply chains.
• Deepen aftercare, retention, reinvestment and local supplier networks.
• Expand eligible green revenue and climate-resilient productive assets.
• Institutionalise learning and plan continuity beyond 2035.

passages.title: Expected outcomes
passages.text:
Stronger market recognition, resilient value chains and measurable productivity, inclusion and territorial gains.
₱35–50 billion Indicative envelope; later projects remain conditional.
Readiness gates matter: the start date of a phase does not automatically authorise later projects. Scale-up depends on verified delivery, project preparation, safeguards, financing, procurement readiness and annual budget decisions. The phase ranges sum to an indicative ₱120–160 billion envelope.

passages.title: Use public capital to unlock a broader investment system
passages.text: The capital stack combines public resources for enabling and public-good investments, national programmes and development finance where eligible, private capital for viable commercial activity, and PPP structures where value-for-money and risk allocation are demonstrated.

passages.title: Indicative public catalytic envelope
passages.text: Ten-year planning envelope across three phases. It is a scenario for prioritisation and capital planning—not an approved budget, confirmed funding commitment or consolidated list of fully costed projects.

passages.title: Wider capital mobilisation estimate
passages.text:
Total investment needed to reach ₱550B: a capital–output ratio of 3.5–4.0 applied to the ₱283 billion gap between the 2025 five-province base (₱266.59B) and the 2035 target, at constant 2018 prices. It is not a committed pipeline or a forecast of funds available.
Reconciled in this edition: earlier drafts gave ₱1.55–1.77T, which implied a larger output gain than the five-province series supports (Chapter 7, Table 7.6). The public envelope is therefore about one-sixth to one-ninth of the total; private, national and development capital must supply the rest.

passages.title: Public sector
passages.text: Core infrastructure, public services, project preparation, resilience, safeguards and catalytic investment through lawful appropriations.

passages.title: National programmes
passages.text: Sector programmes, national infrastructure and technical assistance, subject to eligibility, mandates and confirmed allocations.

passages.title: Development finance
passages.text: Concessional finance, ODA and climate finance where projects meet eligibility, safeguards and financial criteria.

passages.title: Private investment
passages.text: Commercial capital for viable production, processing, tourism, logistics, renewable energy and export enterprises.

passages.title: PPP and blended finance
passages.text: Potential structures for bankable infrastructure and services, subject to legal frameworks, value-for-money and transparent risk allocation.

passages.title: Islamic finance
passages.text:
Shariah-compliant finance, takaful, waqf and other instruments to widen appropriate access and support viable enterprises.
No definitive percentage split between funding sources is presented as approved. Shares must be based on appropriations, documented commitments, financing agreements and project-level models. Avoid double-counting public commitments, private investment and approvals.

passages.title: Measure what changes—not only what gets delivered
passages.text: Chapter 4 defines and calibrates KPIs; Chapter 5 connects them to the Balanced Scorecard; Chapter 6 links performance to projects, budgets and delivery reviews; Chapter 7 sets the policy, data and learning rules to sustain the system.

passages.title: Financial perspective
passages.text: Investment approvals and realisation, budget execution, capital mobilisation and economic outcomes—without treating approvals as realised investment.

passages.title: Stakeholder perspective
passages.text: Investor aftercare, MSME participation, jobs, inclusion and territorial access using defined populations and disaggregated results.

passages.title: Internal Process perspective
passages.text: Project readiness, service standards, procurement and licensing performance, safeguards and cross-agency dependencies.

passages.title: Learning and Growth perspective
passages.text: Skills, institutional capability, data quality, digital capacity and the ability to learn and improve across the system.

passages.title: Official baselines
passages.text: GRDP, poverty, exports, infrastructure access, employment, investment approvals and other official indicators must be confirmed by authoritative data owners. Record source, period, territorial coverage, unit and revision history.

passages.title: Stakeholder diagnostics
passages.text: The latest linked validation snapshot contains 76 consented responses and uses analyticsVersion 2 . SWOT formulas follow the canonical analytics contract; missing SWOT families remain missing observations, not zero scores. Survey diagnostics inform prioritisation and learning, not official baselines.

passages.title: Adaptive management
passages.text: Review linked indicators quarterly, distinguish data-quality issues from implementation and external-shock variance, and document corrective actions, owners and dates. Proposed alert thresholds require calibration and formal adoption.

passages.title: Transparent governance
passages.text:
Use a common project and investor pipeline, publish non-sensitive results and maintain a change log for target revisions. Protect personal data, commercially confidential information and security-sensitive records.
Canonical phase boundaries are Phase 1 (2026–2028), Phase 2 (2029–2031) and Phase 3 (2032–2035). The 2030 point may be an interim checkpoint. Dashboards, workplans and public reporting should use the same definitions unless an authorised revision is recorded.

passages.title: A Bangsamoro economy where opportunity becomes lasting public value
passages.text: Success in 2035 will mean more than higher headline figures. It will mean communities with stronger livelihoods; competitive enterprises that process and sell more of what the region produces; infrastructure and skills that allow firms to grow; credible institutions that make decisions transparently; and development that protects the natural systems on which future prosperity depends. It will mean island and mainland communities are connected to opportunity, women and young people can participate in productive work, investors can navigate clear and reliable processes, and public resources are directed towards projects that are ready, inclusive and resilient. Bangsamoro identity and values will be expressed not only in the story of growth, but in how growth is governed and who benefits. BIRD’s central proposition: investment becomes transformative when the whole system is prepared to turn it into productive, inclusive and resilient value. Prosperous communities More productive work, stronger local enterprises and better access to opportunity. Competitive industries Halal, agro-industrial, tourism and green value chains that meet standards and reach markets. Ethical and capable governance Clear accountabilities, transparent data, reliable service standards and learning that survives transitions.

passages.title: A Bangsamoro economy where opportunity becomes lasting public value
passages.text: A resilient economy Investments designed for climate, resource, fiscal and security risks. Inclusive development Territorial fairness and wider participation for MSMEs, women, youth and underserved communities. Investment leadership A credible pipeline, effective aftercare and partnerships grounded in evidence and delivery.

passages.title: Evidence and interpretation
passages.text:
• Source basis: BIRD 2026–2035 Chapters 2–7 in the project repository, including the strategic-options matrix and updated implementation and policy architecture.
• Planning figures: ₱120–160 billion public catalytic envelope and ₱0.99–1.13 trillion wider investment estimate are planning parameters, not approved appropriations or committed capital.
• Targets: headline targets remain strategic directions until baselines, territorial series, price basis, indicator definitions and data ownership are reconciled and approved.
• Validation evidence: survey results are reported separately from official administrative data. Missing observations are not interpreted as zero.

passages.title: Acknowledgements
passages.text: The Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035 has been shaped by analytical work, institutional knowledge, technical exchange and the perspectives of people and organisations working across the Bangsamoro economy. The roadmap is offered as a shared planning resource: its value depends on the continued stewardship, validation and implementation of the institutions and communities it is intended to serve. Appreciation is extended to the leadership of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) and the Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism (MTIT) for providing the institutional setting for investment strategy and coordination. Particular recognition is due to the Bureau of Investments team for its investment-facilitation mandate, working knowledge of the investor environment and continued engagement with the roadmap’s strategic and operational questions. The work also acknowledges the contributions of officials, technical personnel and practitioners across BARMM ministries, offices and agencies; provincial, city and municipal local government executives and teams; national government agencies; statistical and planning institutions; chambers of commerce, business associations, investors and entrepreneurs;

passages.title: Acknowledgements
passages.text: MSMEs and producer organisations; development agencies and financing partners; universities, researchers and training institutions; civil society organisations; and community representatives. Their respective perspectives help connect regional ambition with the practical realities of service delivery, enterprise development, infrastructure, finance, market access, environmental stewardship and inclusive growth. Gratitude is extended to participants in the structured workshops and consultations convened at regional, provincial, local and sectoral levels. Their discussions and critical reflections have helped test assumptions, surface implementation barriers and highlight the interdependencies that a systems-led roadmap must address. The contribution of the BIRD Validation Survey participants is also acknowledged. The survey provides diagnostic and validation evidence; it is not treated as a population-representative vote or a replacement for authoritative administrative and statistical baselines. Engr. Addie T. Unsi is recognised for contributing as a facilitator and technical contributor to the roadmap process, helping structure dialogue and support the integration of stakeholder perspectives. The report’s preparation and systems architecture were led by Alvin M. Silva, MDM , consultant and systems architect.

passages.title: Acknowledgements
passages.text: These acknowledgements recognise meaningful participation without implying that every individual or institution endorses each finding, target or recommendation. Institutional and evidence note. The inclusion of an organisation or stakeholder group acknowledges its role in the wider planning and validation environment; it does not imply endorsement of the report by that organisation. Findings, targets and implementation proposals remain subject to verification, formal review and decisions by the competent authorities. The roadmap is strongest when regional leadership, local knowledge, responsible investment and community aspirations are brought together through transparent decisions, shared learning and sustained implementation.

passages.title: Messages
passages.text: Editorial status. The messages below are draft institutional texts for review and approval by the offices concerned. They do not represent any officeholder until formally adopted. The first Bangsamoro Parliament convenes and elects the Chief Minister on 30 October 2026.

passages.title: Message from Chief Minister of BARMM
passages.text:
Office of the Chief Minister
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
Bismillāhir-Raḥmānir-Raḥīm. The Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035 presents a shared direction for translating the gains of peace and autonomy into dignified livelihoods and lasting economic opportunity. Guided by the values of amanah (trust), adl (justice) and stewardship, development must be judged not only by the capital attracted, but by the lives strengthened and the opportunities opened to our people.
Our provinces, island communities and cities possess young talent, productive land and seas, cultural knowledge and a strategic position within wider regional markets. These strengths can generate broader prosperity when linked to reliable infrastructure, capable institutions, responsible investment, access to finance and fair opportunities for local enterprises.
Such a task calls for cooperation across government, local communities, national institutions, the private sector and development partners. The roadmap offers a common framework, while the choices and priorities of the Bangsamoro people must remain central to implementation. May our collective effort serve the public good, protect the trust placed in our institutions and contribute to a peaceful, resilient and prosperous Bangsamoro.
Abdulraof “Sammy Gambar” Macacua Chief Minister, BARMM

passages.title: Message from the Minister, MTIT
passages.text:
Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism (MTIT)
Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao
The BIRD 2026–2035 positions trade, investment promotion and tourism as connected drivers of enterprise growth and regional competitiveness. For MTIT, the practical challenge is to convert the region’s comparative strengths into credible opportunities that investors can assess, enterprises can join and communities can benefit from.
This calls for more than promotion alone. Investor services, standards, business development, halal value chains, tourism readiness, market intelligence, aftercare and coordination with infrastructure and finance must work as one facilitation system. MSMEs should be able to enter value chains, improve quality and reach markets, while investors receive clear information and predictable, lawful processes.
MTIT’s contribution is to help connect policy direction with business realities: build the investment pipeline, work with partners to resolve barriers, support responsible enterprise and measure results transparently. The roadmap provides a basis for coordination; specific programmes and commitments remain subject to institutional review, financing and approval.
Farsernina A. Mohammad Minister, Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism

passages.title: Message from the Director General, MTIT
passages.text:
Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism
Directorate and operational coordination
The value of BIRD lies in turning a strategic direction into a practical system of responsibilities, work plans and review. The Balanced Scorecard links staff capability and institutional processes with investor and community outcomes and, ultimately, economic performance. For the directorate, this means clarifying who owns each action, which office provides the evidence, where a decision is required and how performance will be reviewed.
Sound execution also requires honesty about what is known. Baselines need source-owner verification; targets must be defined and approved; project readiness, budget execution and physical progress must be distinguished; and material variances require diagnosis before corrective action. The proposed BIF-Net can support shared visibility and coordination, but it must respect legal mandates, data-governance rules and the authority of each participating institution.
Institutional discipline is not administrative overhead. It is part of investor confidence and public accountability. A reliable management system can help the region learn from implementation, direct resources towards binding constraints and connect investment activity with demonstrable development value.
Rosslaini Alonto-Sinarimbo Director General, MTIT

passages.title: Message from the Director, Bureau of Investments, MTIT
passages.text:
Bureau of Investments
Ministry of Trade, Investments and Tourism
Investment promotion succeeds when investors can identify opportunities, receive dependable information, navigate lawful processes and resolve implementation barriers. The BIRD gives the Bureau of Investments a common framework for improving that journey while connecting promotion with enterprise capacity, infrastructure readiness, standards, finance and access to markets.
The objective is not approvals alone. A strong pipeline must distinguish expressions of interest from prepared projects, approvals from realised investment, and projected employment from jobs actually created and sustained. Aftercare, provincial outreach, investment intelligence and coordination with responsible agencies are essential to building trust and retaining viable projects.
The Bureau’s role is to facilitate, connect and monitor within its mandate, working with investors, MSMEs, local governments and development partners. With clear service standards and transparent evidence, investment promotion can support productive local value creation and broader opportunity across the Bangsamoro.
Shameera Abobakar Director, Bureau of Investments, MTIT

passages.title: Glossary of Terms
passages.text: Adaptive management Using monitoring, feedback, learning and governed recalibration to respond to changing implementation conditions. Bankable project A project supported by a credible business or public-service case, feasibility work, financing pathway, safeguards, legal approvals, implementation capacity and evidence of demand. BIMP-EAGA The Brunei Darussalam–Indonesia–Malaysia–Philippines East ASEAN Growth Area, a regional cooperation initiative for connectivity and economic links. Balanced Scorecard (BSC) The management architecture that translates the strategy map into four linked perspectives: Financial, Stakeholder, Internal Process, and Learning and Growth. Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) The BIRD framework that organises economic activity into five interdependent clusters (Foundations, Transformers, Enablers, Connectors and Financiers) governed by cross-cutting operating systems. BIF-Net The proposed Bangsamoro Investment Facilitation Network: a coordination layer for investment information, investor support, action tracking and performance visibility. It does not replace statutory agency mandates. Catalytic capital Public funds deployed to enable or attract additional investment. The BIRD ₱120–160 billion envelope is indicative; the leverage ratio is a planning objective, not a secured commitment.

passages.title: Glossary of Terms
passages.text: Evidence provenance The documented source, owner, reference period, geography, definition, calculation, revision history and validation status of a reported value. Critical Leverage Point (CLP) A high-impact intervention point identified through systems analysis. BIRD uses five: halal certification integrity; the infrastructure, energy and connectivity nexus; governance and investor confidence; the Islamic finance ecosystem; and green economy revenue. Green Lane status Priority facilitation for qualified strategic investments, granted by the investment council under the proposed BIF-Net Executive Order. Implementation framework The three-phase sequence for delivery: Phase 1 Foundation Building (2026–2028), Phase 2 Acceleration (2029–2031) and Phase 3 Consolidation and Global Integration (2032–2035). Incremental capital-output ratio (ICOR) The investment needed to add one unit of output. BIRD applies 3.5 to 4.0 to estimate the total investment the growth path requires.

passages.title: Glossary of Terms
passages.text: Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS) The recommended strategy, aligning investment, production, infrastructure, finance, market access and governance across the BEIE rather than optimising one sector. Investment approval A formal approval recorded by the relevant authority; it is not equivalent to cash disbursed, capital realised, a project completed or jobs sustained. Key performance indicator (KPI) A defined measure used to track progress against an approved objective, with a stated owner, formula, unit, period, source and validation method. Monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL) A systematic process for tracking delivery and outcomes, assessing what explains results, and using evidence to improve decisions and implementation. Investment roadmap A decision and coordination framework that links strategy, facilitation, programmes, financing, implementation and performance management. It does not replace feasibility studies, appropriations or statutory approvals. Moral governance A cross-cutting operating principle emphasising transparency, accountability, ethical conduct and institutional integrity in investment and public administration, aligned with Bangsamoro governance values. MSME Micro, small and medium enterprise; size classification should follow the relevant official standard and dataset.

passages.title: Glossary of Terms
passages.text: Public–private partnership (PPP) A contractual arrangement between the public sector and a private party for eligible infrastructure or services, subject to legal approval, risk analysis and procurement requirements. Pareto-style headline KPI One of six high-signal indicators chosen for executive monitoring. The term is a management designation; it does not claim that six indicators cause a fixed share of impact. Special Geographic Area (SGA) The 63 barangays in North Cotabato that voted to join BARMM, organised into eight municipalities. Strategy map A causal diagram showing how Learning and Growth capabilities enable internal processes, which create stakeholder value and contribute to financial outcomes. Links are hypotheses to test, not proof of causation. Value chain The linked activities through which inputs are transformed into products or services and delivered to markets or end users. Systems archetype A recurring pattern of system behaviour, such as Limits to Growth, Fixes that Fail, Tragedy of the Commons, Growth and Underinvestment, or Shifting the Burden. TOWS matrix A tool that pairs strengths and weaknesses with opportunities and threats to generate SO, WO, ST and WT strategies.

passages.title: From investment potential to shared prosperity
passages.text: The Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035 sets out a coordinated strategy to help BARMM turn its human, cultural, natural and geographic strengths into productive investment, decent work and resilient communities. It matters now because the region must convert the gains of peace and autonomy into durable economic opportunity while addressing poverty, weak connectivity, infrastructure gaps, limited market access and fragmented investment-enabling systems. BARMM is uniquely positioned to build value across halal products and services, agro-industrial production, the green economy, tourism, trade and Islamic finance. Its location within the Brunei Darussalam–Indonesia–Malaysia–Philippines East ASEAN Growth Area (BIMP-EAGA) provides a platform for wider regional connections—provided that logistics, skills, standards, finance and institutions develop together. BIRD therefore recommends an ecosystem approach rather than isolated sector initiatives. The roadmap is a strategic and coordination framework, not an approved budget or a guarantee of results. It links the diagnosis in Chapter 2, the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS) selected in Chapter 3, the calibrated measures in Chapter 4, the Balanced Scorecard (BSC) in Chapter 5, implementation in Chapter 6 and policy recommendations in Chapter 7.

passages.title: From investment potential to shared prosperity
passages.text:
Its promise depends on accountable leadership, responsible investment, community participation and transparent, evidence-led execution. ₱120–160B Indicative public catalytic envelope, 2026–2035
₱0.99–1.13T Estimated total investment requirement; scenario, not committed pipeline
₱550B+ Proposed BARMM GRDP ambition by 2035; verify price basis and territorial series
76 Consented BIRD Validation Survey responses, August 2026
Decision message. Adopt the integrated direction as a basis for coordinated planning; verify all baseline definitions and target series with authoritative data owners; prepare bankable, safeguarded projects; and release public catalytic resources through phase gates tied to readiness, delivery and measurable outcomes.

passages.title: At a glance
passages.text:
BIRD decision architecture
Decision area | What the report establishes | What leaders and institutions need to do
Strategy | IEDS provides the strongest integrated response to the system-wide constraints. | Align sector, infrastructure, finance, market-access and governance actions to common priorities.
Performance | Four BSC perspectives and a calibrated KPI architecture connect capability, process, stakeholder value and economic results. | Assign KPI owners; validate baselines, targets, methods and data sources.
Investment | ₱120–160 billion in public catalytic capital is an indicative planning envelope. | Confirm fiscal space, financing sources, safeguards, feasibility and approvals project by project.
Delivery | Three phases sequence enabling conditions, scale-up and consolidation. | Gate later-phase investment on readiness, evidence of demand and performance reviews.
Governance | BIF-Net is proposed as a coordination and facilitation network, not a replacement for statutory mandates. | Harmonise the legal and institutional model and publish clear decision rights.

passages.title: Opportunities and constraints must be addressed together
passages.text: Chapter 2 frames BARMM’s investment economy as five connected clusters: Foundations, Transformers, Enablers, Connectors and Financiers. The system has real assets—young people, agriculture and fisheries, halal enterprise potential, renewable and natural resources, tourism and strategic regional location—but benefits are constrained when infrastructure, standards, market access, finance, skills and public-sector coordination do not develop in step.

passages.title: People and enterprise
passages.text:
Opportunity: a youthful population, entrepreneurs, MSMEs and producer communities can deepen local value chains.
Risk: skills, productivity, access to finance and decent-work pathways may not keep pace with labour-force growth.

passages.title: Halal economy
passages.text:
Opportunity: build trusted halal value chains, services, certification and market access rooted in Bangsamoro identity and enterprise.
Risk: fragmented standards, limited conformity-assessment capacity and weak traceability could constrain market recognition.

passages.title: Location and connectivity
passages.text:
Opportunity: deepen trade, logistics, tourism and business links through BIMP-EAGA and wider regional corridors.
Risk: ports, roads, inter-island links, energy reliability and digital connectivity raise costs and limit dependable access.

passages.title: Natural assets and green value
passages.text:
Opportunity: raise value in agriculture, fisheries, forestry, renewable energy and eligible ecosystem services.
Risk: climate hazards, ecosystem degradation, weak project preparation and uncertain revenue pathways threaten returns.

passages.title: Investment climate
passages.text:
Opportunity: clearer facilitation, aftercare, investment intelligence and ethical governance can improve confidence.
Risk: fragmented responsibilities, administrative barriers, uncertain readiness and limited coordination slow conversion from interest to operating investment.

passages.title: Poverty and inclusion
passages.text:
Opportunity: value-chain investment can expand jobs, household income and market participation across provinces and communities.
Risk: poverty, market-access limitations and territorial disparities can prevent growth from becoming broad-based.

passages.title: What the diagnostics imply
passages.text:
Chapter 2’s systems diagnostics caution against treating each constraint in isolation. Enablers—including infrastructure, energy, digital systems, skills and service delivery—are critical because they influence the performance of the other clusters. The report’s survey analysis found institutional readiness to be the lowest of three assessed dimensions in each of the six survey clusters. This is diagnostic survey evidence, not a substitute for formal agency capacity assessments.
Implication for decisions. Pair productive investments with their dependencies: project preparation, infrastructure and energy, standards and certification, trained people, finance, logistics, buyer demand, climate and conflict-sensitive safeguards, and clear institutional accountability. Where a prerequisite is missing, mark the project accordingly rather than treating it as investment-ready.
Evidence basis: Chapter 2 diagnostics and the BIRD Validation Survey (3–20 August 2026; 76 consented responses). Survey results should be read in light of the sample’s composition and geographic coverage; they are not population-representative estimates.

passages.title: Four choices were assessed; an integrated approach ranked first
passages.text:
Chapter 3 assessed four strategic options. Each offers a useful emphasis, but the decision was which approach could address the connected constraints of BARMM’s investment ecosystem rather than improve one sector while leaving binding dependencies unresolved. Strategic options and analytical ranking
Rank | Option | Analytical score | Strategic contribution | Main limitation if used alone
1 | IEDS Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy | 8.83 / 10 | Synchronises production, infrastructure, finance, standards, market access, governance and institutional capability. | Requires strong coordination, sequencing and performance discipline.
2 | HEDS Halal Economy Dominance Strategy | 7.53 / 10 | Builds distinctive halal value chains, standards, certification and market positioning. | Needs wider enabling infrastructure, finance, skills and market systems.
3 | IFES Infrastructure-First Enabling Strategy | 7.46 / 10 | Addresses connectivity, energy and core enabling infrastructure. | Infrastructure alone does not guarantee productive use, enterprise growth or market demand.
4 | GEMS Green Economy Monetisation Strategy | 7.16 / 10 | Develops eligible green-economy and ecosystem-service revenue opportunities. | Depends on legal, technical, environmental, financing and buyer/registry conditions. Scores reproduce the analytical comparison in the BIRD planning materials.

passages.title: Four choices were assessed; an integrated approach ranked first
passages.text: They are decision-support assessments, not measured economic outcomes. HEDS, IFES and GEMS remain strategic engines within the integrated approach.

passages.title: Why IEDS was selected
passages.text:
Evaluation logic The weighted assessment considered economic impact (20%), feasibility (18%), risk–return (16%), identity alignment (15%), systems leverage (15%), inclusivity (10%) and sustainability (6%). The criteria assess complementary aspects of strategic fit and implementation prospects.
Systems leverage IEDS links the five BEIE clusters and addresses cross-cutting operating conditions: moral governance, resilience, inclusivity, and peace and security. It sequences interventions around dependencies rather than assuming sector growth will occur independently.
Stakeholder validation Survey respondents’ mean ratings also placed IEDS first: 6.05, compared with 5.90 for HEDS, 5.77 for IFES and 5.73 for GEMS among respondents with valid ratings for all options (n=75).
Interpretation discipline The separate survey comparison supports further consideration of IEDS; it does not convert the sample into a public referendum or prove that the strategy will cause the projected results.

passages.title: Critical leverage points
passages.text:
• Halal certification integrity: build credible standards, conformity assessment and traceability.
• Infrastructure, energy and connectivity: reduce the costs and uncertainty that constrain productive activity.
• Governance and investor confidence: clarify decision rights, publish service standards and improve aftercare.
• Islamic finance ecosystem: connect Shariah-compliant financing and risk-sharing to viable enterprise and investment needs.
• Green-economy revenue: pursue lawful and technically credible mechanisms with environmental safeguards and fair benefit-sharing.
Recommended decision. Use IEDS as the integrating strategy, while retaining the specific contributions of HEDS, IFES and GEMS as mutually reinforcing growth engines. Implement through readiness-based phases and test causal assumptions through MEL.

passages.title: BSC: Strategy and Investment Roadmap
passages.text:
The Balanced Scorecard translates IEDS into linked objectives, measures, initiatives and review routines. The causal logic runs from Learning and Growth to Internal Process , then to Stakeholder outcomes and Financial results. The four perspectives are interdependent; weights shown in Chapter 5 are proposed management weights and do not replace the definitions and validation rules in Chapter 4. Selected high-impact objectives, measures and 2035 ambitions
Perspective | Strategic objective | Strategic measure / KPI | 2035 ambition in the report
Financial (30%) | Increase investment; grow the regional economy; expand exports; activate green revenue; mobilise Islamic finance | Annual investment approvals; GRDP; exports; verified green-economy revenue; Islamic banking assets | ₱15B+ annual approvals; ₱550B+ GRDP; ₱40B+ exports; ₱500M annual green revenue; ₱20B+ Islamic banking assets
Stakeholder (25%) | Strengthen investor experience; empower MSMEs; reduce poverty; widen access and quality employment | Investor satisfaction; valid halal certificates; poverty incidence; jobs from investment-approved firms; financial inclusion | 8.0+/10 satisfaction; 5,000+ halal-certified MSMEs; poverty below 20%; 20,000+ jobs as a roadmap-level aspiration

passages.title: BSC: Strategy and Investment Roadmap
passages.text:
Internal Process (25%) | Streamline facilitation; strengthen certification; improve infrastructure delivery; coordinate investment readiness | Business registration time; verified certification/recognition milestones; budget execution; PAP readiness and delivery | Digital, one-day registration ambition; recognised standards pathway; budget execution above 90%; project-specific readiness gates
Learning and Growth (20%) | Build sector expertise; strengthen staff capability; foster digital services and institutional learning | Trained/certified staff; digital services deployed; data quality and review-cycle compliance | 100+ halal certification officers; 80% of relevant staff trained or certified; 20+ digital services, all subject to target and baseline verification
Performance discipline. Distinguish investment approvals from realised investment, announced jobs from sustained jobs, certificate counts from active valid certificates, and budget execution from physical completion. Assign every KPI an owner, definition, unit, baseline year, territorial coverage, reporting cycle, validation source and a record of revisions.

passages.title: From objectives to portfolio execution
passages.text: Each strategic measure should connect to an identifiable programme, activity or project (PAP), with a responsible owner, dependencies, financing status, safeguards, timetable and verifiable milestones. The scorecard is a management tool: it supports decisions and learning but does not prove causal effects merely because indicators move together.

passages.title: The BIRD Growth Strategy
passages.text:
The growth strategy connects the BEIE clusters and five strategic growth engines through a common investment logic: build enabling conditions, strengthen productive value chains, connect firms to finance and markets, and govern delivery through evidence and accountability. The engines reinforce one another; they are not competing standalone strategies.
1. Halal Economy Strengthen certification integrity, standards, traceability, compliant processing, skills and access to regional and international markets. Link MSME support to buyer requirements and verified demand.
2. Agro-Industrial Development Increase value addition in agriculture, fisheries and other eligible local products through storage, cold chain, processing, quality systems, producer organisation and resilient supply chains.
3. Green Economy Develop renewable energy, sustainable production and lawful ecosystem-service opportunities where technical integrity, environmental safeguards, community participation and benefit-sharing are demonstrable.
4. Infrastructure and Connectivity Prioritise enabling investments in energy, transport, logistics, digital connectivity and climate-resilient infrastructure that remove binding constraints on productive activity.
5.

passages.title: The BIRD Growth Strategy
passages.text: Islamic Finance and Investment Promotion Improve access to Shariah-compliant finance, risk-sharing and capital mobilisation through regulated institutions; strengthen investor intelligence, facilitation, aftercare and project readiness. One integrated system All five engines depend on ethical governance, skills, market demand, reliable data and coordinated implementation. Their contribution should be measured by real outcomes, not activity counts alone. Delivery principle. Prioritise projects by readiness, developmental contribution, risk, climate and conflict sensitivity, local value capture, market potential and public affordability. No sector label alone makes a project bankable or eligible for public support.

passages.title: The 2035 vision: prosperity that is productive, inclusive and resilient
passages.text:
₱550B+ GRDP ambition by 2035; price basis and series require verification
20,000+ Jobs associated with investment-led growth; define direct/indirect and sustained jobs
₱15B+/year Annual investment approvals; approvals are not realised investment
20% Poverty incidence ambition: below 20%; confirm consistent measure and official series
₱40B+ Total exports ambition; source, scope and valuation basis to be confirmed
₱500M/year Verified green-economy revenue ambition, net of applicable costs and safeguards
These figures are strategic ambitions in the current report , not independently verified forecasts or adopted statutory targets. Chapter 4’s calibrated headline indicators additionally include 5,000+ halal-certified MSMEs, a household electrification ambition of 90% by 2035 and broadband connectivity of 85%, with indicator definitions and baselines subject to source-owner verification. Renewable-energy share, access to electricity and investment approvals are different measures and must not be conflated.

passages.title: Three-phase implementation roadmap
passages.text: Purpose: remove binding constraints and establish credible delivery conditions. Priorities: institutional and legal coordination; verified baselines; project preparation; investor service and aftercare; halal standards readiness; priority energy, transport and digital dependencies; capability and safeguards. Expected outcome: a validated PAP pipeline, clear ownership, reliable reporting and projects that meet documented readiness gates. Purpose: scale investment only when enabling conditions, demand and project viability are verified. Priorities: agro-industrial processing, halal value chains, cold chain and logistics, green-economy pilots that meet requirements, Islamic finance, export readiness and market links. Expected outcome: more productive enterprises, better market access and measurable value addition from projects that demonstrate performance. Purpose: deepen proven capability and embed institutional continuity. Priorities: higher-value exports, reliable cross-border market links, institutionalised facilitation, sound green revenue pathways, financial inclusion and independent outcome review. Expected outcome: stronger economic resilience, a more competitive investment ecosystem and a successor agenda shaped by evaluation findings. Phase-date consistency. This document uses the canonical Chapter 6 sequencing: 2026–2028, 2029–2031 and 2032–2035.

passages.title: Three-phase implementation roadmap
passages.text: Phase boundaries should be changed only through a controlled cross-chapter revision.

passages.title: Investment requirements: catalyse, do not overstate
passages.text:
₱120–160B Indicative public catalytic envelope across 2026–2035
₱0.99–1.13T Estimated total investment needed under the report’s capital-output scenario
6–9× Indicative leverage objective for each peso of public catalytic capital
3.5–4.0 Assumed incremental capital-output ratio (ICOR); a planning assumption
The report’s ₱120–160 billion public catalytic envelope is indicative and phased at ₱35–45 billion, ₱50–65 billion and ₱35–50 billion. The wider ₱0.99–1.13 trillion requirement is derived from an assumed capital-output ratio of 3.5–4.0 and the five-province path to ₱550B (Table 7.6); it is not a list of committed projects, a forecast with guaranteed returns or an approved financing package. The report’s indicative financing scenario allocates potential sources across BARMM public resources, national programmes, development and climate finance, and private, PPP and Islamic finance. Shares must only be reported as financing secured when supported by appropriations, signed agreements or documented commitments. Financing pathways and controls
Pathway | Potential contribution | Required control before counting
Public sector | Foundational infrastructure, institutional capability, project preparation and public goods. | Approved appropriations, fiscal-space assessment, procurement and implementation authority.

passages.title: Investment requirements: catalyse, do not overstate
passages.text: Private sector | Productive assets, processing, logistics, services, tourism and enterprise investment. | Documented investor commitments, feasibility, market demand and safeguards; separate approvals from realised capital. Development financing | Technical assistance, concessional finance, climate and resilience funding where eligible. | Formal programme eligibility, signed financing instruments, agreed co-financing and reporting arrangements. Public–private partnerships (PPPs) | Risk allocation and delivery for eligible infrastructure and service investments. | Legal authority, value-for-money and fiscal-risk assessment, procurement and contract approval. Islamic finance | Shariah-compliant financing and risk-sharing for eligible enterprises and investments. | Regulatory compliance, licensed providers, commercial viability and transparent risk allocation.

passages.title: Monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL)
passages.text:
MEL links strategy to implementation and institutional learning. It should report not only money spent and activities completed, but also whether the programme is removing constraints, changing service quality, increasing productive capacity and delivering outcomes. The BSC gives decision-makers a causal structure; Chapter 4 defines indicators and calibration; Chapter 6 specifies reviews and controls; Chapter 7 addresses policy and institutional continuity. Measure → Learn → Adapt → Improve → Scale
Core MEL discipline
Step | Management question | Evidence and response
Measure | What has changed against the approved baseline and target? | Verified KPI and PAP records, provenance, date, territory and definition. Learn | What explains the change or variance? | Root-cause analysis of delivery, finance, dependency, data quality and external shocks. Adapt | Which response is justified and by whom? | Options appraisal, impact on other perspectives, legal authority and stakeholder considerations. Improve | Was the corrective action implemented and effective? | Named owner, due date, decision log and follow-up verification. Scale | Is the intervention effective, affordable, lawful and replicable? | Evidence of outcomes, costs, safeguards and readiness before scale-up decisions.

passages.title: Monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL)
passages.text: Illustrative review cadence in Chapter 6: monthly operational pipeline review where data allow; quarterly KPI and delivery review; twice-yearly cross-cluster and territorial review; annual performance and investment programming; a 2030 mid-term review; and a 2035 terminal evaluation. Data integrity rule. Keep official statistics, administrative records, stakeholder survey findings and management targets distinguishable. Correlation is not proof of causation. Where evidence is unavailable, publish the gap and assign responsibility for closing it.

passages.title: What success should look like in 2035
passages.text:
Success is not a single headline number. It is a Bangsamoro investment ecosystem in which enterprises can grow, public institutions can deliver, communities participate in the gains of development, and the economy becomes more diversified and resilient.
Prosperous communities More decent and sustained work, higher local value capture, stronger MSMEs and wider access to productive opportunity across provinces, islands and municipalities.
Competitive industries Halal and agro-industrial enterprises that meet standards, add value locally, connect to reliable logistics and win repeat business in domestic and international markets.
Ethical and accountable governance Transparent facilitation, clear decision rights, lawful public spending, credible data and effective routes to resolve investor and community concerns.
A resilient economy Infrastructure and production systems better able to absorb climate and market shocks, with natural assets managed for long-term public and community benefit.
Inclusive development Women, young people, Indigenous Peoples, conflict-affected communities and underserved localities have fairer routes into skills, finance, enterprise and decent employment.
Investment leadership A reputation built on dependable information, project readiness, responsible investors, effective aftercare and measurable results—not promotional claims alone.

passages.title: The decisions that matter now
passages.text:
• Confirm institutional ownership. Agree decision rights, coordination arrangements and roles for MTIT–Bureau of Investments, participating agencies and local government partners.
• Validate the evidence base. Reconcile territorial and price bases; confirm baselines, definitions, source owners and target approval status.
• Prepare bankable investments. Prioritise feasibility, demand, finance, safeguards, resilience, local value creation and implementation capacity.
• Sequence public catalytic support. Make later releases contingent on readiness and verified performance, with transparent records of funding status.
• Review and learn publicly. Publish progress, limitations, corrective action and evaluation findings to sustain trust and improve the next decisions.
The ambition for 2035 is a Bangsamoro where ethical leadership, responsible investment and local ingenuity reinforce one another—where growth is not only larger, but more inclusive, more resilient and more widely shared.
Read the full report Continue with Chapter 1, then Chapters 2–7 for the full analytical and implementation basis.

passages.title: A. Background and Rationale: From Post-Conflict Recovery to Investment Destination
passages.text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) was formally established on 26 February 2019, following the ratification of the Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act No. 11054, 2018) in the plebiscite held earlier that year. The region is more than an administrative reorganisation. It is a political settlement that seeks to turn decades of armed conflict into a durable framework for self-governance, cultural affirmation and economic self-determination. The region enters the roadmap period with clear evidence of progress and of continuing constraints. On the first-semester measure, poverty incidence among families fell from 55.9 percent in 2018 to 34.8 percent in 2023 (PSA, 2023). On the full-year measure, it fell from 28.0 percent in 2021 to 23.5 percent in 2023, still among the highest of all regions (PSA, 2024). The improvement is substantial, but poverty remains a central development constraint. The economy is growing again after a slow 2024. Gross Regional Domestic Product (GRDP) grew 2.7 percent in 2024, after 4.3 percent in 2023. In 2024, services accounted for 42.0 percent of GRDP; agriculture, forestry and fishing for 32.4 percent; and industry for 25.6 percent (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025). Growth then accelerated to 5.0 percent in 2025, the sixth fastest of the country's 18 regions (MindaNews, 2026).

passages.title: A. Background and Rationale: From Post-Conflict Recovery to Investment Destination
passages.text: This structure means that value addition, infrastructure, market access, human capital and finance have to be considered together rather than as separate sector programmes. Investment activity is also rising. Investment approvals reached ₱5.1 billion in the first four months of 2026 (BBOI, 2026). Approvals, however, are not the same as realised capital formation or broad investor confidence. BIRD therefore treats investor confidence as an outcome to be measured through administrative and market indicators, not inferred from a single approval figure. Provincial trajectories differ. Lanao del Sur was the fastest-growing province in 2023, at 5.02 percent, and grew 4.0 percent in 2024, supported by the SPDA Agro-Industrial Development Program and anchor investments such as DoleFil's ₱306 million pineapple facility. Maguindanao del Norte grew fastest in 2024, at 4.1 percent, on the strength of a services-led economy and growing industrial capacity (MFBM, 2025). Basilan was declared free of the Abu Sayyaf Group on 9 June 2025, a milestone that improves the conditions for normal investment activity (PIA, 2025).

passages.title: B. Scope, Coverage and Temporal Horizon
passages.text: The Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035 is MTIT's ten-year strategic framework for investment-led, inclusive and sustainable economic transformation. It builds on the region's productive assets and institutional context: agriculture and fisheries, halal identity and enterprise, a strategic position in BIMP-EAGA, renewable-energy resources, cultural assets, human capital and emerging Islamic finance. The roadmap does not assume that comparative advantage automatically becomes investment advantage. It focuses on the enabling conditions, linkages and execution capabilities needed to turn assets into investable opportunities and broad-based economic outcomes.

passages.title: B.1 Geographic Scope
passages.text:
The roadmap covers BARMM as now constituted: five provinces (Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, Basilan excluding Isabela City, and Tawi-Tawi), the Special Geographic Area (SGA) and Cotabato City. Sulu has been outside BARMM since the Supreme Court decision of 9 September 2024 (Supreme Court of the Philippines, 2024). Cotabato City, the regional seat of government and the main commercial centre, is treated as a distinct urban node. Each province is profiled through the Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework to analyse sectoral linkages and identify priority investment corridors.
Note on official series. Some official statistics, including those for 2023 and earlier, describe the region before Sulu's exclusion. Chapter 4 sets out how baselines are verified and rebased to the current territory before targets are tracked.

passages.title: B.2 Sectoral Coverage
passages.text:
The roadmap addresses six priority investment sectors, the same six used in the stakeholder workshops, together with the green economy as an emerging cross-cutting pillar. Each is mapped to the BEIE Framework's five functional clusters.
Table 1-1. Sectoral coverage and BEIE cluster mapping
Priority sector | BEIE cluster | Key investment areas
Agro-industry | Foundations → Transformers | Rice, corn, coconut, rubber and seaweed processing; cold chain; farm-to-market linkages
Halal economy | Transformers | Halal processing, certification and testing; halal parks; export market linkages
Tourism and cultural economy | Connectors | Halal tourism, cultural heritage, eco-tourism, Lake Lanao
Energy and utilities | Foundations / Enablers | Renewable generation, Zamboanga–Basilan interconnection, island mini-grids, household electrification
Infrastructure, logistics and connectivity | Enablers | Farm-to-market roads, ports, digital broadband, BIMP-EAGA corridors
Services (health, education, finance, digital) | Enablers / Financiers | Human capital, Islamic finance, e-governance, digital literacy
Green economy (cross-cutting pillar) | Foundations / cross-cutting | Carbon credits, payments for ecosystem services, REDD+, sustainable forestry, eco-tourism fees

passages.title: B.3 Temporal Scope and Three-Phase Architecture
passages.text:
The roadmap spans 2026–2035 in three implementation phases, sequenced by investment readiness and system dependencies. The indicative public catalytic envelope is ₱120–160 billion across the decade. The Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS) connects the strategic options and sets the implementation sequence. All amounts remain subject to project readiness, financing, safeguards, feasibility and annual budget decisions. Table 1-2. Three-phase implementation architecture
Phase | Period | Envelope | Strategic focus | Key deliverables
Phase 1: Foundation Building | 2026–2028 | ₱35–45B | Governance and enablers | Enact the Forestry Code and sign JMC No. 2026-01; operationalise the halal certification authority with OIC/SMIIC-aligned processes; launch one-day digital business registration; advance the Zamboanga–Basilan interconnection; fund farm-to-market roads; establish BIF-Net and its coordination protocols
Phase 2: Acceleration | 2029–2031 | ₱50–65B | Transformers and green economy | Operationalise the Bangsamoro Halal Park; register REDD+ and activate payments for ecosystem services; extend Islamic banking to all provincial capitals; deploy cold-chain and logistics hubs; scale TVET–industry alignment; raise functional literacy towards 70 percent
Phase 3:

passages.title: B.3 Temporal Scope and Three-Phase Architecture
passages.text: Consolidation and Global Integration | 2032–2035 | ₱35–50B | Connectors and ecosystem maturity | Secure OIC endorsement and an SMIIC mutual recognition arrangement; reach ₱500M+ annual green revenue; deepen BIMP-EAGA integration; reach ₱550B+ GRDP and poverty below 20 percent; 90 percent household electrification (100 percent by 2040) and 85 percent broadband coverage

passages.title: C. Purpose of the Investment Roadmap Development
passages.text:
The BIRD 2026–2035 translates the Bangsamoro Government's investment-promotion mandate into a coherent, evidence-informed roadmap. It connects policy, investment facilitation, sector development, infrastructure, finance, market access and implementation governance, so that individual projects contribute to a functioning investment ecosystem. The roadmap is a decision and coordination framework. It does not replace project feasibility studies, statutory approvals, annual appropriations or agency mandates. The roadmap serves five related purposes:
1. Integrated analytical framework. Provide a research-based, policy-oriented framework that combines provincial insight, global trends, workshop outputs and multi-sector analysis, kept ecosystem-based by the BEIE Framework and Strat Planner Pro.
2. Evidence-based strategic guidance. Guide policymakers, planners and investors over the decade with strategies grounded in verified PSA-BARMM data, stakeholder evidence and international benchmarks (OIC/SMIIC, ESG, PDP 2023–2028).
3. High-leverage opportunity identification. Identify the investment opportunities and interventions where a small change at the right point produces a large, system-wide effect (Meadows, 1999).
4. Measurable target architecture.

passages.title: C. Purpose of the Investment Roadmap Development
passages.text:
Set measurable targets and monitoring mechanisms aligned with international standards, national priorities and Bangsamoro objectives, operated through the Balanced Scorecard and the MEL Dashboard.
5. Synchronised ecosystem development. Replace scattered, siloed interventions with synchronised development, using TOWS and systems archetypes so that strategies reinforce one another across clusters.

passages.title: D. Guiding Principles
passages.text: Six guiding principles shape analysis, strategy, implementation and learning. They work as operating rules for investment facilitation and public decision-making. Where they carry measurable indicators, targets remain subject to baseline verification and periodic calibration.

passages.title: D. Guiding Principles (continued)
passages.text:
Table 1-3. Guiding principles: operational definitions and applications
Principle | Operational definition | Application in BIRD | KPI target (2035)
Moral Governance | Transparency, accountability and Islamic ethics as the operating system | Public disclosure; investor ombudsman; anti-corruption safeguards | 100% procurement disclosure
Ecosystem Thinking | Interconnected clusters, not isolated silos | BEIE Framework; inter-cluster linkage mapping | All projects cluster-tagged
Cultural Authenticity | Halal, Islamic finance and heritage as competitive advantages | Halal certification; Islamic finance; cultural tourism | 5,000+ halal-certified MSMEs
Environmental Stewardship | Green economy as opportunity, not compliance cost | Forestry Code; REDD+; PES; carbon markets | ₱500M+ green revenue
Inclusivity | Equitable benefit-sharing across all segments | MSME programmes; focus on IDPs, women and youth; anchor linkages | <20% poverty; 60% MSME participation
Data-Driven Decision-Making | Verified data and stakeholder evidence | PSA integration; workshop synthesis; KPI benchmarking | Quarterly dashboard updates

passages.title: E. Regulatory and Policy Anchors
passages.text: The BIRD 2026–2035 operates within a legal and policy framework that spans three tiers: national legislation, BARMM-specific instruments, and regional and international frameworks. These anchors align the roadmap with national priorities, international standards and the region's autonomous governance structure.

passages.title: E.1 National Legislation and Issuances
passages.text:
Bangsamoro Organic Law (Republic Act No. 11054, 2018). The BOL establishes BARMM's autonomous government and directs it to promote investment and create a favourable climate for business in the region (Article XIII, Section 24). It provides the legal basis for region-specific policies on investment facilitation, halal development and economic zones, within the Constitution and applicable national laws. CREATE MORE Act (Republic Act No. 12066, 2024). CREATE MORE sets the national fiscal incentive framework that applies to registered enterprises in BARMM: income tax holidays, the special corporate income tax, the enhanced deductions regime, duty and VAT incentives, and the RBE local tax. Its enhanced deductions for research and development, training, power and domestic inputs directly support the Enablers and Transformers clusters.
2026 Strategic Investment Priority Plan (Memorandum Order No. 47). The SIPP defines the activities eligible for incentives nationwide. It includes area-specific priority activities for BARMM, namely halal tourism and investment operations of Islamic banks under RA 11439 (Office of the President, 2026). Widening this BARMM list is a policy objective of the roadmap (Chapter 7). Islamic Banking Law (Republic Act No. 11439, 2019). The law provides the framework for Islamic banks and Shariah-compliant financial services.

passages.title: E.1 National Legislation and Issuances
passages.text: The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas licenses and supervises Islamic banks; the Bangsamoro Government's role is to build demand, project pipelines, Shariah-governance capacity and public-sector use of Islamic instruments. Republic Act No. 11550 (2021). The law divided the former Maguindanao province into Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur, enabling province-specific investment strategies.

passages.title: E.2 BARMM-Specific Legal and Policy Instruments
passages.text:
2nd Bangsamoro Development Plan (BDP) 2023–2028. The BDP sets medium-term development priorities and sectoral targets. It is the primary planning document that the BIRD operationalises through investment facilitation strategies (BPDA, 2023).
Bangsamoro Investment Code (draft). The draft Code, as of 22 April 2026, sets out the regional framework for investment incentives, the roles of investment promotion agencies, an investment development council and non-fiscal support (MTIT, 2026a). Its harmonisation with CREATE MORE and with BIF-Net is addressed in Chapter 7.
Proposed Executive Order on the Bangsamoro Investment Facilitation Network (BIF-Net). The proposed order establishes BIF-Net as the inter-agency investment facilitation framework and creates a Regional Green Lane for Strategic Investments, with MTIT-BoI as permanent secretariat (Office of the Chief Minister, 2026).

passages.title: E. Regulatory and Policy Anchors (continued)
passages.text:
Bangsamoro Halal Industry Development Plan (BHIDP) 2025–2030. The BHIDP sets the strategy for the halal ecosystem, certification infrastructure and export market linkages (MTIT-BARMM, 2025). It is the primary operational plan for halal investment in the Transformers cluster.
Bangsamoro Sustainable Energy Master Plan (BSEMP). The BSEMP reports a renewable share of generation of 75.86 percent and sets the pathways for renewable development, grid connection and electrification (MENRE-BARMM, 2024). It anchors energy investments in the Foundations and Enablers clusters.
Bangsamoro Forestry Code (pending). The Code was pending before the interim Parliament's Committee on Environment, Natural Resources and Energy; its enactment now rests with the first elected Parliament. It will set the legal basis for sustainable resource use, value-added forest products and access to environmental markets, including REDD+ and payments for ecosystem services.
Draft MENRE–MILG Joint Memorandum Circular No. 2026-01. The draft circular, for signature, sets frameworks for carbon credit programmes, payments for ecosystem services and eco-tourism user fees as revenue mechanisms for local governments and communities. Its adoption is a Chapter 7 recommendation.

passages.title: E.3 Regional and International Frameworks
passages.text:
BIMP-EAGA EGL Sub-Committee Strategic Plan 2025–2028. The Brunei Darussalam–Indonesia–Malaysia–Philippines East ASEAN Growth Area (BIMP-EAGA) Environment, Green Economy and Land Use plan provides a regional framework for green economy integration and cross-border trade (BIMP-EAGA, 2024). Tawi-Tawi's proximity to Sabah and the SGA's position on the central Mindanao corridor give BARMM natural trade advantages within the growth area.
Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023–2028. The PDP sets national priorities and indicators against which BARMM's contribution is aligned and monitored (NEDA, 2023).
OIC/SMIIC standards. The Standards and Metrology Institute for Islamic Countries (SMIIC) provides the main international framework for halal standards and for the accreditation of halal certification bodies, guiding BARMM's certification infrastructure and market-access strategy (SMIIC, 2021).
ASEAN Economic Community Strategic Plan 2026–2030. Adopted in May 2025 under the ASEAN Community Vision 2045, the plan succeeds the AEC Blueprint 2025 as the regional integration framework that BARMM engages through BIMP-EAGA (ASEAN, 2025).
UN Sustainable Development Goals. The SDGs inform the roadmap's inclusive growth strategies, particularly Goals 1 (no poverty), 8 (decent work and economic growth), 9 (industry, innovation and infrastructure) and 13 (climate action).
