passages.title: F. Analytical Frameworks and Methodology
passages.text: The BIRD 2026–2035 uses two complementary analytical frameworks, the Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework and the Strat Planner Pro Architecture, to provide methodological rigour, systems-level analysis and actionable outputs. This section introduces both frameworks, the five-step methodology that integrates them, and the stakeholder process that supplied much of the evidence.

passages.title: F.1 The Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework
passages.text:
The BEIE Framework moves investment analysis away from isolated sectoral silos towards an integrated view of how economic clusters interact and reinforce one another. Grounded in systems-based economic theory, it organises BARMM's economy into five functional clusters, anchored by moral governance and supported by four cross-cutting enablers: tourism and culture, peace and security, human capital, and environmental sustainability (Silva, 2026a).
The framework's core insight, that BARMM's sectors are deeply interconnected and that treating them in isolation wastes effort and opportunity, is a governance imperative as much as an analytical finding. The five clusters are set out in Figure 1-3 and Table 1-5.

passages.title: F.1 BEIE Functional Clusters
passages.text:
Table 1-5. Five BEIE functional clusters: components, actors and strategic functions
Cluster | Key components | Key actors | Strategic function
Cross-cutting operating systems | Moral governance, resilience, inclusivity, peace | Bangsamoro Parliament, OCM, MILG, MPOS, civil society, development partners | Determine whether all clusters function effectively, equitably and sustainably
C1: Foundations | Agriculture, fisheries, forestry, energy, environment | MAFAR, MENRE, SPDA, LGUs, producer organisations | Resource base supplying inputs to all other clusters
C2: Transformers | Industry, manufacturing, logistics, halal processing | MTIT, BBOI, BEZA, halal certification authority, anchor investors | Value-adding transformation of Foundation resources
C3: Enablers | Infrastructure, health, education, human capital | MPW, MOTC, MBHTE, MOH, MICT | Physical, digital and human infrastructure that makes value creation viable
C4: Connectors | Tourism, digital connectivity, trade, BIMP-EAGA | MTIT, BEZA, MOTC, MICT, BIMP-EAGA partners | Market access and regional and global integration
C5: Financiers | Islamic banking, takaful, waqf, microfinance | MFBM, Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank, BSP (regulator), IsDB, cooperatives | Capital access aligned with Shariah principles

passages.title: F.2 The Strat Planner Pro Architecture
passages.text:
The Strat Planner Pro Architecture (Silva, 2026b) provides the planning and roadmapping architecture for the BIRD 2026–2035. It integrates five analytical layers, namely SWOT analysis, systems thinking and mapping, the strategy matrix, metrics and KPI benchmarking, and the Balanced Scorecard, so that diagnosis becomes measurable, time-bound implementation.
1. Diagnostics BEIE context and quantified SWOT
2. Systems CLDs, archetypes and leverage points
4. Measurement KPI benchmarking and calibration
5. Execution BSC, implementation and learning
Tool 1: SWOT analysis with quantified indices. Strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats are identified with stakeholder attribution and variable classification, then scored with a distinct formula for each quadrant (see Chapter 2 for the full diagnostic). SWOT formulas • RI Strengths = (Impact × Likelihood) / 5 — scale 0.2–5, resilience capacity • RI Opportunities = √(Impact × Likelihood) — scale 1–5, resilience through exploitation • Risk Weaknesses = Impact × Likelihood — scale 1–25, internal risk exposure • VI Threats = (Impact² × Likelihood) / 25 — scale 0.04–5, external vulnerability
Tool 2: Systems thinking and systems mapping. Causal loop diagrams map reinforcing and balancing feedback loops.

passages.title: F.2 The Strat Planner Pro Architecture
passages.text: Systems archetype analysis identifies recurring patterns such as Limits to Growth , Fixes that Fail , Shifting the Burden and Tragedy of the Commons that determine where intervention has the most leverage (Senge, 1990; see Chapter 2). Tool 3: Strategy matrix (TOWS). The TOWS matrix matches internal strengths and weaknesses with external opportunities and threats to generate SO, WO, ST and WT strategies. Each strategic option is evaluated with a seven-criteria weighted scoring matrix (see Chapter 3).

passages.title: F.2 Strategic Options and Evidence Contract
passages.text: Tool 4: Metrics benchmarking and KPI calibration. Strategic objectives are translated into KPIs with baselines, targets and data sources, benchmarked against international standards (OIC/SMIIC, ESG, SDGs), national targets (PDP 2023–2028) and Bangsamoro objectives (see Chapter 4). Tool 5: Balanced Scorecard (BSC). The BSC translates strategy into measurable outcomes across four perspectives (Financial, Stakeholder, Internal Process, and Learning and Growth), linking capability investments to economic and inclusion outcomes. The scorecard is developed in Chapter 5; implementation, annual programming and MEL in Chapter 6; and policy and institutional recommendations in Chapter 7. Evidence, measurement and governance contract. The roadmap distinguishes three evidence layers: (1) official administrative and statistical baselines; (2) stakeholder-validation evidence; and (3) analytical assumptions used for scenario development. The BIRD validation snapshot contains 76 consented survey responses , analysed under analyticsVersion 2 . Survey-derived SWOT diagnostics use the canonical formulas above, as implemented in the validation-survey analytics service. Missing SWOT answers are reported as missing observations, not zeros. Survey diagnostics support prioritisation and learning; they do not establish official baselines or targets. Chapter 4 governs KPI calibration;

passages.title: F.2 Strategic Options and Evidence Contract
passages.text: Chapters 5 and 6 translate calibrated measures into scorecard and implementation systems; Chapter 7 sets the policy and institutional conditions for sustained execution.

passages.text:
The BIRD 2026–2035 applies a five-step methodology that integrates the BEIE Framework and the Strat Planner Pro Architecture. Each step builds on the previous one, so that the analysis is rigorous, stakeholder-informed and systems-aware. Table 1-6. Five-step strategy formulation methodology and chapter outputs
Step | Analytical activity | Core tools | Primary output | Chapter
1. Context and ecosystem diagnosis | Establish the economic, institutional, demographic, environmental and spatial context; map the five BEIE clusters. | BEIE Framework; PEDSET context analysis; provincial profiles; stakeholder evidence | Context diagnosis and BEIE cluster architecture | 2
2. Quantified SWOT and systems mapping | Quantify strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats; test causal relationships and recurring patterns; identify leverage points. | Canonical SWOT formulas; CLDs; systems archetypes; Meadows leverage points | Cluster diagnostics, systems maps and leverage-point implications | 2
3. Strategy formulation and sequencing | Translate diagnostics into TOWS strategies, strategic options and a phased investment sequence using a documented decision aid. | TOWS; seven-criteria decision aid; BEIE dependencies; phasing logic | Strategic options, leverage architecture and roadmap sequencing | 3
4.

passages.text:
Metrics and KPI calibration | Define indicators, baselines, targets, data owners and variance rules; separate verified baselines from analytical or stakeholder-derived assumptions. | KPI framework; benchmark alignment; calibration governance; MEL logic | Calibrated KPI architecture and monitoring rules | 4
5. Execution, implementation and policy feedback | Translate strategy into causal objectives, implementation actions, annual investment programming and policy recommendations, with feedback into planning cycles. | BSC; causal pathways; PAPs; MEL; BIF-Net coordination; policy review | Scorecard, implementation system, annual action plan and policy agenda | 5–7

passages.title: F.4 Stakeholder Engagement and Workshop Process
passages.text:
The BIRD 2026–2035 was built from the ground up. It started with regional working sessions, moved through the provinces, and was then checked through a region-wide validation survey. At each stage the Strat Planner Pro Framework's participatory data-collection method guided the work. Participants did not only comment on a draft: they wrote the problem statements, opportunities, priorities and pathways that the roadmap analyses. The process ran in five stages (Figure 1-6).
Stage 1 Regional workshops January–February 2026 Two rounds; five Strat Planner Pro tools across six sectors
Stage 2 Mainland provincial workshop 24 March 2026 · Cotabato City Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, SGA
Stage 3 Provincial workshops 12 May · Marawi City 20 June 2026 · Isabela City Lanao del Sur and Basilan; BEIE cluster conversations
Stage 4 Validation survey 3–20 August 2026 76 consented responses
Stage 5 Tawi-Tawi provincial validation 28 October 2026 · Bongao Validated the Tawi-Tawi Economic and Investment Outlook

passages.title: Stage 1: Regional workshops (January–February 2026)
passages.text:
Two rounds of regional workshops brought together representatives of Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies (BMOAs), the private sector (small and medium enterprises and major businesses) and development partners. Working in sector groups, participants applied five Strat Planner Pro tools in sequence to six investment sectors: agro-industry, halal, tourism, energy and utilities, infrastructure, and services. Each tool took the previous tool's output as its input (Table 1-7). Table 1-7. Workshop tools and outputs
Workshop | Guiding question | What participants produced
1. Sectoral challenges | What holds investment back in each sector, and why? | Problem statements (what, where, who), effects on the sector, root causes and supporting evidence
2. Sectoral opportunities | How can each challenge become an opportunity for joint action? | Opportunity and investment areas, possible programmes, partner institutions and time horizons
3. Opportunity prioritisation | Which opportunities should come first? | Opportunities placed on an impact-and-feasibility matrix ( Do first , Plan and advocate , Nice to have , Park ), with the top three to five presented in plenary and justified by impact and feasibility
4. Industry SWOT | What are each industry's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats? | A structured SWOT for each sector
5.

passages.title: Stage 1: Regional workshops (January–February 2026)
passages.text: Industry strategy | What is the pathway from today's situation to the desired outcome? | A description of the current situation, three sequenced milestones and expected outcomes for each sector

passages.title: Stage 2: Mainland provincial workshop, Cotabato City (24 March 2026)
passages.text: The process then moved to the provinces. On 24 March 2026, a workshop in Cotabato City brought together BMOAs, local government units (LGUs) and private-sector participants from Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur and the Special Geographic Area (SGA). It used the same participatory method to test the regional findings against provincial conditions.

passages.title: Stage 3: Provincial workshops with BEIE cluster conversations (May–June 2026)
passages.text:
On 12 May 2026, a provincial workshop for Lanao del Sur was held in Marawi City. On 20 June 2026, a workshop for Basilan followed the same design. It was held in Isabela City, which lies outside BARMM, and the discussion covered the BARMM part of the province. Both sessions strengthened the method in two ways:
• discussion was organised around the clusters of the Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE), so participants looked at how sectors depend on one another rather than treating each in isolation;
• each workshop started from a prepared Provincial Economic and Investment Outlook, which gave participants a shared base of data and context before they began (MTIT, 2026b).
Both workshops drew a wide range of government, LGU and private-sector stakeholders.
Every province consulted in person. All five provinces and the SGA took part in a provincial workshop: Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur and the SGA in Cotabato City (24 March 2026), Lanao del Sur in Marawi City (12 May 2026), Basilan in Isabela City (20 June 2026), where participants validated the Basilan Economic and Investment Outlook, and Tawi-Tawi in Bongao (28 October 2026), where participants validated the Tawi-Tawi Economic and Investment Outlook ( results ).

passages.title: Stage 4: Validation survey (3–20 August 2026)
passages.text: The BIRD Validation Survey tested the workshop findings and the roadmap's draft logic with a wider audience. All 76 responses carry final consent under the Data Privacy Act of 2012. The online survey drew no responses from Basilan or Tawi-Tawi; the two island provinces were validated in person, Basilan at its June workshop and Tawi-Tawi at its October validation (BIRD Validation Survey, 2026).

passages.title: From Environmental Scanning to Systems Sensing
passages.text:
A conventional environmental scan lists political, economic, social, environmental and technological factors one after another. That is useful but incomplete, because in BARMM these factors do not act separately. A drought in Maguindanao del Sur is an environmental event, but it becomes an economic shock to processors, a fiscal pressure on local governments and a social strain on farming households within one season. This chapter therefore uses the Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework as a living systems lens: it asks not only what is happening in each domain, but where each force acts within the economy and how it travels between clusters (Silva, 2026).
Deep presencing means sensing both the visible and the emergent: the data and trends, and also the relationships, feedback loops, institutional habits and cultural currents that produce them (Senge, 1990; Meadows, 2008). The chapter moves from context (Sections 2.1 and 2.2), through a quantified diagnosis of the cross-cutting operating systems and the five clusters (Sections A to F), to a synthesis of how the clusters behave as one system (Section G).

passages.title: The PEDSET–BEIE lens
passages.text: How evidence is used in this chapter. Three kinds of evidence are kept distinct: official statistics (PSA and other data owners), stakeholder evidence (the workshops and the BIRD Validation Survey, n = 76 consented responses) and analytical synthesis. Survey scores show how stakeholders judge conditions; they are not official baselines. Where a figure is an estimate from the BIRD KPI register, it is labelled as such.

passages.title: The PEDSET–BEIE lens
passages.text:
The six PEDSET domains (political, economic, demographic, social, environmental and technological) are mapped to the clusters where they actually operate. Table 2-1 is the reading key for the rest of the chapter: each cluster section begins with the PEDSET signals that matter most for that cluster, and Section G traces how those signals cross cluster boundaries. Table 2-1. Where PEDSET forces act within the BEIE clusters
PEDSET domain | Primary point of action | How the force travels across clusters
Political | Cross-cutting operating systems (moral governance, peace) | Governance credibility and security set the risk premium for every cluster; policy continuity decides whether incentives in Transformers and Financiers are believed. Economic | All five clusters | Prices, demand and capital flow from Foundations through Transformers to Connectors; Financiers determine how fast the cycle turns. Demographic | Enablers (human capital) | A young, fast-growing population is a labour supply for Transformers and a consumer market for Connectors only if Enablers convert it into skills. Social | Enablers; Connectors; operating systems (inclusivity) | Poverty, literacy and trust shape productivity, market depth and the social licence for investment.

passages.title: The PEDSET–BEIE lens
passages.text: Environmental | Foundations; operating systems (resilience) | Climate shocks and resource degradation start in Foundations and pass into processing, logistics and credit risk. Technological | Enablers (digital, infrastructure); Connectors | Connectivity and digital public services lower transaction costs everywhere; their absence caps the scale of every other cluster. The systems question. For each force, the chapter asks three things: where it lands first, which cluster it reaches next, and whether the resulting loop reinforces investment or holds it back. The answers, taken together, identify the binding constraint on the whole system (Section G).

passages.title: 2.1 Global Economic Trends: Implications for BARMM
passages.text:
The global outlook is steady but fragile. The International Monetary Fund projects world growth of 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027 (IMF, 2026). For BARMM, the external environment matters less through headline growth than through specific channels: the price of food, fuel and fertiliser; the direction of regional supply chains; the availability of climate and Islamic finance; and the pace of digital change. Table 2-2 sets out each trend and the cluster through which it enters the regional economy. Table 2-2. Global trends and their entry points into the BEIE clusters
Trend | Global context | Implication for BARMM (entry cluster)
Moderate global growth | World growth of about 3 percent, with downside risks from trade tensions and geopolitical uncertainty (IMF, 2026). | Export demand for agricultural, fisheries and halal products may soften; domestic consumption and public investment must carry more of the growth (Connectors). Supply-chain realignment | Trade is shifting towards regional supply chains, including within ASEAN. | BIMP-EAGA corridors and ecozones become more valuable as alternative routes and production sites (Connectors, Transformers). Commodity price volatility | Food, fuel and fertiliser prices remain exposed to climate and geopolitical shocks. | Higher input costs hit farm margins and diesel-dependent island power (Foundations, Enablers).

passages.title: 2.1 Global Economic Trends: Implications for BARMM
passages.text: Digital transformation and AI | Investment in digital infrastructure, e-government and AI-driven productivity is accelerating. | Without broadband and digital skills, BARMM risks a widening productivity gap; the Bangsamoro e-Governance Master Plan is the main response (Enablers). Climate adaptation finance | Multilateral and climate funds are expanding finance for resilience and green infrastructure. | Renewable energy, coastal protection and climate-smart agriculture can attract concessional finance if projects are prepared (Foundations, Financiers). Islamic finance growth | Islamic banking, sukuk and takaful continue to grow globally. | A culturally aligned source of capital for infrastructure and MSMEs, if domestic institutions and pipelines are ready (Financiers). Changing labour markets | Automation and AI are changing the skills that employers need. | Skills systems must move faster to match investor demand (Enablers). These trends reinforce one message. BARMM's exposure to the global economy runs mostly through its Foundations and Connectors clusters, while its capacity to respond sits in Enablers and Financiers. Resilience to external shocks is therefore an outcome of cluster coordination, not of any single sector policy.

passages.title: 2.2 Regional Economic Trajectory: Indicators and Inflection Points
passages.text:
BARMM's trajectory shows real progress on three fronts: output, investment and poverty (Figure 2-2). Growth slowed to 2.7 percent in 2024, after 4.3 percent in 2023 and 6.6 percent in 2022 (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2024, 2025a), then recovered to 5.0 percent in 2025, the sixth fastest of the country's 18 regions (MindaNews, 2026). Investment approvals have accelerated, and poverty has fallen sharply since 2018.
Approvals are a signal of intent, not of capital on the ground. They have also been volatile: ₱6.97 billion was approved in 2021, followed by lower totals before the recent rise (MTIT, 2026a). The roadmap therefore tracks realised investment, jobs and retention alongside approvals (Chapter 4).

passages.title: Economic structure
passages.text: The structure of the economy explains why value is lost between clusters. Agriculture, forestry and fishing (AFF) generate about a third of regional output, roughly four times their share nationally (about 8 percent), yet most of that output leaves the region unprocessed (Figure 2-3). The gap between a large Foundations cluster and a small Transformers cluster is the clearest structural signal in the regional accounts.

passages.title: 2.2 Regional Economic Trajectory: Indicators and Inflection Points (continued)
passages.text:
Table 2-3. Key regional indicators: verified values and 2035 targets
Indicator | Latest verified values | 2035 target | Source
GRDP growth | 6.6% (2022); 4.3% (2023); 2.7% (2024); 5.0% (2025) | — | PSA-RSSO BARMM; MindaNews (2026)

Series published before or shortly after the Supreme Court decision of 9 September 2024 may still include it; Chapter 4 sets out how baselines are rebased to the five-province region. The electrification figures use different denominators and are not directly comparable.

passages.title: Within and across contexts: the provincial snapshot
passages.text:
The regional average hides very different economies. Maguindanao del Norte is the largest and most services-led; Lanao del Sur grew fastest in 2023; Maguindanao del Sur and Basilan depend most on agriculture; and Tawi-Tawi, the smallest by output, holds the region's maritime gateway and most of the country's seaweed production (Table 2-4). Table 2-4. Provincial economic snapshot, 2023 (constant 2018 prices)
Province | GDP | Structure (share of GDP) | Distinctive endowment | Poverty, 2023
Maguindanao del Norte | ₱81.91B | Services 53%; industry 29%; AFF 18% | Polloc port; Bangsamoro Halal Park (Matanog); manufacturing up 27% since 2018 | —
Lanao del Sur | ₱75.38B (+5.02%) | Services 38%; industry 33%; AFF 29% | Lake Lanao and Agus hydropower; SPDA agro-industrial zones | —
Maguindanao del Sur | ₱39.54B | AFF 53%; services 36%; industry 11% | Rice and corn basin | 32.1%
Tawi-Tawi | ₱25.79B (+3.8%) | Services 35%; AFF and industry the balance | About 40% of national seaweed output; about 20 km from Sabah | 39.5%
Basilan (excluding Isabela City) | ₱23.15B | AFF 41%; services 36%; industry about 23% | About 48,366 ha of rubber; aquaculture | 33.7%
Sources: MTIT (2026b), Provincial Economic and Investment Outlooks, drawing on PSA-BARMM and MFBM data. "—" means the outlook does not report a provincial figure.

passages.title: Within and across contexts: the provincial snapshot
passages.text: No outlook has yet been prepared for the Special Geographic Area or Cotabato City.

passages.title: Inflection points
passages.text:
Governance transition. The first regular Bangsamoro Parliament was elected on 14 September 2026, with turnout of about 80 percent. No party won a majority, so the Chief Minister will be chosen through coalition when members take office after 30 October 2026 (Reuters, 2026). A peaceful election strengthens governance credibility; a contested coalition process would test it. The campaign also saw an ambush on the interim Chief Minister on 15 August 2026, who survived the attack (Daily Tribune, 2026), a reminder that political stability still needs active protection.
Security normalisation. Basilan was declared free of the Abu Sayyaf Group on 9 June 2025 (PIA, 2025). For investors, this lowers the risk premium in a province with large rubber and aquaculture endowments and a ₱6.67 billion power interconnection project under way (MTIT, 2026b).

passages.title: Quantified SWOT and Systems Mapping Within the BEIE Clusters
passages.text:
Sections A to F diagnose the cross-cutting operating systems and the five clusters in the same way: (1) the PEDSET signals that act on the cluster; (2) stakeholder-scored SWOT evidence from the validation survey; (3) the systems archetype that best describes the cluster's behaviour; and (4) the investment and institutional response. Table 2-5 brings the quantified evidence together on one page. Scoring method. Each SWOT item was rated for Impact (1–5) and Likelihood (1–5) and scored with the canonical BIRD formulas: Strength RI = (I × L) / 5; Opportunity RI = √(I × L); Weakness Risk = I × L (scale 1–25); Threat VI = (I² × L) / 25. Cluster values are the means across all valid item ratings. Where the survey asked no questions for a SWOT family in a cluster, the value is shown as n/a and is not treated as zero. Readiness and urgency are separate 1–5 ratings of each cluster as a whole. Table 2-5. Integrated diagnostic dashboard: quantified SWOT, readiness and dominant archetype
Cluster | Strength RI | Opportunity RI | Weakness Risk | Threat VI | Readiness | Urgency | Dominant archetype (rated accurate*)
Operating systems | 3.48 | 3.97 | 16.16 | 2.95 | 3.58 | 3.93 | Fixes that Fail (96%)
C1 Foundations | 3.45 | 3.93 | 15.92 | 2.69 | 3.45 | 3.70 | Tragedy of the Commons (99%)
C2 Transformers | 3.41 | n/a | 16.15 | 2.77 | 3.40 | 3.69 | Growth and Underinvestment (95%)

passages.title: Quantified SWOT and Systems Mapping Within the BEIE Clusters
passages.text:
C3 Enablers | 3.26 | 4.01 | 17.13 | 2.94 | 3.33 | 4.04 | Limits to Growth (99%)
C4 Connectors | 3.50 | 4.04 | n/a | 2.97 | 3.61 | 3.94 | Success to the Successful (99%)
C5 Financiers | 3.29 | 3.99 | 15.66 | n/a | 3.55 | 3.88 | Shifting the Burden (96%)
* Share of respondents rating the archetype "very" or "somewhat" accurate for the cluster. Source: BIRD Validation Survey (2026), n = 76 consented responses; 62–76 valid answers per item. Three readings stand out. First, Enablers carries the heaviest internal risk and the widest gap between urgency and readiness (0.71 points), which marks it as the binding cluster. Second, opportunity scores are consistently high (3.93–4.04 out of 5): stakeholders do not doubt that opportunities exist. Third, readiness is the lowest of the three cluster ratings everywhere ; the constraint is institutional throughput, not a shortage of assets. Section G shows how these readings combine.

passages.title: A.1 Functional Descriptions and Deep Presencing Indicators
passages.text:
The BEIE Framework treats moral governance, resilience, inclusivity and peace as the operating systems of the economy, not as aspirations. As an operating system manages how hardware and software interact, these four systems govern the trust, incentives and accountability through which value is created in every cluster (Silva, 2026). The political domain of PEDSET acts mainly here, together with the social and environmental domains through inclusivity and resilience. The workshops repeatedly identified three bottlenecks: fragmented programme delivery across Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies (BMOAs); weak inter-agency coordination that produces duplication and gaps; and investor hesitation rooted in perceptions of governance and security risk. These are not sectoral failures. They are operating-system failures, and they call for changes in rules, information flows and institutional design rather than more sector programmes (Meadows, 1999; BoI-MTIT, 2026). Table 2-6. Cross-cutting operating systems: functions, indicators and imperatives
Operating system | Function | Deep presencing indicators | Investment and policy imperative

passages.title: A.1 Functional Descriptions and Deep Presencing Indicators
passages.text:
Moral governance | Transparency, accountability, stability, Islamic ethics and the rule of law as the basis of investment facilitation | Budget execution; public disclosure of incentives; investor-protection mechanisms; integrity of halal certification | Institutionalise an investor ombudsman; publish procurement data; pair incentives with institutional milestones
Resilience | Absorbing climate and economic shocks; food, water and infrastructure security | Drought and flood losses; pest and disease early warning; value-chain diversification; contingency finance | Screen all infrastructure and agro-investments for climate risk; adopt continuity and adaptive-management protocols
Inclusivity | Fair sharing of benefits; MSME integration; opportunity for women, youth and internally displaced persons | MSME participation in value chains; sex-disaggregated employment; financial inclusion by municipality | Link anchor investments to local sourcing; scale Islamic microfinance and waqf; target skills programmes at excluded groups
Peace | Security, conflict prevention, normalisation and narrative management | Security incidents; investor perception; reconciliation coverage; return of displaced persons | Sustain normalisation; publish security and investment data; fund community-led peacebuilding

passages.title: A.2 Policy Architecture Supporting the Operating Systems
passages.text: A set of regional plans and instruments in the BIRD evidence base gives the operating systems an institutional backbone. Several are still drafts or pending, which is itself a governance signal: the rules that would let the operating systems work are not yet all in place (Table 2-7).

passages.title: A.3 Political Domain: Governance Credibility and Security Stability
passages.text:

Bangsamoro Forestry Code; MENRE–MILG JMC No. 2026-01 | MENRE; MILG | Pending; draft | Resilience and inclusivity: forest stewardship, carbon and PES revenue for communities
Bangsamoro MSME Development Plan 2026–2032 | MTIT | Plan (salient features) | Inclusivity: MSME integration into value chains (MTIT, 2026d)

passages.text:
Shariah-compliant financial inclusion
Status reflects the documents in the BIRD evidence base as at October 2026.

passages.title: A.3 Political Domain: Governance Credibility and Security Stability
passages.text:
The political domain shapes the investment climate through three channels: governance credibility, policy continuity and security. The validation survey shows that stakeholders see these channels as the region's most serious external threats (Table 2-8). Security incidents carry the highest vulnerability index of any threat in the survey, ahead of climate change.
Table 2-8. Political and governance threats as rated by stakeholders
Threat | Threat VI (0–5) | Clusters most exposed | What it signals
Security incidents | 3.20 | All; especially Connectors and Transformers | Peace gains need active maintenance; risk premium remains
Drifting goals | 3.03 | Operating systems | Targets may be quietly lowered unless they are governed
Weak national–regional coordination | 2.91 | Enablers; Financiers | National permits and regulators sit outside regional control
Political transition | 2.85 | All | Continuity of policy through the change of government
Fragmented mandates | 2.57 | Operating systems | Overlapping agency roles slow facilitation
Source: BIRD Validation Survey (2026); 70–73 valid ratings per item. Threat VI = (Impact² × Likelihood) / 25.

passages.title: A.4 Environmental and Geophysical Hazards
passages.text:
Security risk is uneven across the region. Clan feuds ( rido ), residual armed groups and disputes over land and resources are the main drivers on the mainland; maritime insecurity and smuggling are concerns in the island provinces. These patterns are monitored by the security sector and independent conflict monitors, and the roadmap uses them as risk signals rather than as fixed ratings. The most effective response is to keep normalisation programmes funded, invest in community-led peacebuilding and publish security and investment data together, so that improvements reach investors as evidence rather than as assertion.
Basilan illustrates the peace–investment link. Its declaration as free of the Abu Sayyaf Group on 9 June 2025 came as the ₱6.67 billion Zamboanga–Basilan Interconnection Project and major public works were advancing in the province (PIA, 2025; MTIT, 2026b). Security, power and logistics improvements reinforce one another; none of them alone would attract processing investment.

passages.title: A.4 Environmental and Geophysical Hazards
passages.text:
The provinces, the Special Geographic Area and Cotabato City face earthquakes, flooding, landslides, storm surges and drought. Climate change is the second-highest-rated threat in the survey (VI 3.14), and the evidence shows it is already a present cost: El Niño-induced drought led Maguindanao del Sur to declare a state of calamity in 2024, with ₱346 million in crop losses across 1,370 hectares, and Pestalotiopsis leaf disease has infested at least 800 hectares of Basilan's rubber (MTIT, 2026b). Table 2-9. Principal hazards by province and city
Area | Major hazards | Investment relevance
Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur | Flooding, drought, landslides, earthquakes | Flood-prone river basins put rice and corn production, roads and storage at risk
Lanao del Sur | Landslides, earthquakes, flooding | Upland erosion affects the Lake Lanao watershed and hydropower
Basilan | Flooding, storm surge, drought, crop disease | Coastal exposure for fisheries; disease risk for rubber
Tawi-Tawi | Storm surge, tsunami, sea-level rise, marine heatwaves | Heat stress on seaweed farms; vulnerable island infrastructure
Special Geographic Area | Flooding, drought | Low-lying agricultural land; new LGUs with limited response capacity
Cotabato City | Flooding, earthquakes | Regional administrative and commercial hub; port and urban services at risk

passages.title: A.4 Environmental and Geophysical Hazards
passages.text: The policy implication runs across clusters. Climate-resilient agriculture (drought-tolerant varieties, water management and diversified cropping) belongs in Foundations; climate-risk screening and resilient design belong in Enablers; and takaful and contingency finance belong in Financiers. Treating these as separate programmes would leave the shock free to pass between them.

passages.title: A.5 Deep Presencing Insight: Applying the Iceberg Model
passages.text:
The operating systems must be strengthened first. Incentives offered without parallel governance reform can produce short-term approvals but not lasting transformation. The Iceberg Model explains why: visible events are produced by deeper patterns, structures and mental models (Senge, 1990; Meadows, 1999). Stakeholders strongly endorsed this reading: 85 percent agreed that the Iceberg Model describes BARMM's investment system, with a mean rating of 4.26 out of 5 (BIRD Validation Survey, 2026).
Level 2: Patterns (what keeps recurring?)

passages.title: A.5 Deep Presencing Insight: Applying the Iceberg Model (continued)
passages.text:
Level 3: Structures (what produces the patterns?)
Level 4: Mental models (what beliefs hold the system in place?)
Table 2-10. Iceberg monitoring framework for the operating systems
Iceberg level | Indicator | Target | What it reveals
Events | Investment approvals (quarterly) | ₱15B a year by 2035 | Short-term momentum
Patterns | Investment retention rate | 85%+ | Whether capital stays after incentive periods end
Structures | Budget execution rate | >90% | Administrative capacity and fiscal discipline
Structures | Procurement disclosure | 100% public disclosure | Accountability in practice
Structures | Inter-agency coordination score | 8/10 | Whether silos are being dismantled
Mental models | Investor aftercare satisfaction | 8.0/10 | Whether facilitation matches promotion
Mental models | Community reconciliation coverage | 80%+ | Whether peacebuilding is built into economic planning
The lesson is that strengthening the operating systems first is an investment imperative, not a governance preference. Working only on events (approvals and incentives) without changing structures and mental models will keep reproducing the boom-and-bust cycle. Stakeholders were divided on how realistic this is: 36 percent rated moral governance "very realistic" as an operating system, but the largest group (39 percent) said it "needs stronger institutional support".

passages.title: Systems archetype and leverage response
passages.text:
Archetype: Fixes that Fail. Quick fixes such as incentives without capacity milestones relieve pressure briefly, then produce side-effects (dependency, capital flight, eroded trust) that recreate the original problem. 96 percent of respondents judged this an accurate description (37 percent "very accurately").
Leverage response. Change the rules and information flows: tie incentives to performance, publish delivery data and protect institutional reforms from in-year budget cuts (Chapter 7).

passages.title: B. Cluster 1: Foundations — Agriculture, Fisheries, Forestry, Energy and Environment
passages.text:
The Foundations cluster is the resource base on which the rest of the economy depends. It feeds raw materials to Transformers and commodities to Connectors, so it sits upstream of almost all value creation. AFF accounts for 32.4 percent of regional output, and the region's energy mix is predominantly renewable, led by the Agus hydropower cascade in Lanao del Sur (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025a; MENRE-BARMM, 2024).
PEDSET signals in this cluster. Environmental: drought, floods and crop disease. Economic: volatile commodity and input prices. Political: land tenure and resource governance. Technological: low farm mechanisation and post-harvest technology.

passages.title: B.1 Policy and Master Plan Alignment
passages.text:
Table 2-11. Foundations cluster: plan alignment
Plan or instrument | Lead | Strategic focus | BIRD-linked targets
2nd Bangsamoro Development Plan 2023–2028 | BPDA | AFF productivity, natural resource management and energy access | Poverty below 20% by 2035
Agro-industrial development programmes | MAFAR; SPDA | Value chains for rice, corn, coconut, rubber and seaweed; lower post-harvest losses | Post-harvest loss reduction (Chapter 4)
Bangsamoro Sustainable Energy Master Plan | MENRE | Energy security, renewable expansion, grid reliability and last-mile distribution | 90% household electrification by 2035; 100% by 2040
Ecozone development | BEZA | Industrial and agro-processing land with environmental safeguards | Polloc Freeport operational (Chapter 6)
Bangsamoro Forestry Code (pending) | MENRE | Sustainable forest management, carbon markets, PES and non-timber forest products | ₱500M+ annual green revenue by 2035

passages.title: B.2 Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry: The Living Resource Base
passages.text:
Agro-industry is the region's most strategic and most under-performing sector. Production remains concentrated in low-value primary goods, with limited processing, weak market links and high post-harvest losses. Anchor investments show what is possible: DoleFil's ₱306 million pineapple packing plant in Wao began commercial operation in 2022 and employs more than 1,200 people, and Green Arrow Agri-Ventures' foreign-owned project in Amai Manabilang, under the SPDA programme, is projected to create 499 jobs (MTIT, 2026b).
Climate and disease are already testing the base. AFF output contracted 4.2 percent in 2024 (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025a), as El Niño drought hit Maguindanao del Sur and Pestalotiopsis spread through Basilan's rubber. The provinces' endowments differ sharply (Figures 2-6 and 2-7; Table 2-12), so a single regional programme would fit none of them well.

passages.title: B.3 Energy and Environmental Systems: Powering and Protecting the Base
passages.text:
Table 2-12. Foundations cluster: provincial resource sensing matrix
Province | AFF share | Key endowment | Vulnerability signal | Emerging opportunity
Lanao del Sur | 29% | Lake Lanao watershed; SPDA agro-ecological zones; upland coffee | Upland erosion; lake-level fluctuation; processing skills gaps | Climate-smart crops; lake aquaculture; halal-certified high-value crops
Maguindanao del Sur | 53% | Rice and corn basin | Drought (₱346M crop losses, 2024); flooding | Irrigation modernisation; drought-tolerant varieties; solar drying
Maguindanao del Norte | 18% | Fertile plains near Cotabato City; coastal fisheries | AFF share falling as services grow; input-cost volatility | Agro-industrial corridors linked to the Halal Park and Polloc
Basilan | 41% | About 48,366 ha of rubber; coconut | Pestalotiopsis (≥800 ha infested); ageing trees | Rubber rehabilitation; rubber-wood biomass; processing
Tawi-Tawi | n.s. | About 40% of national seaweed output; marine biodiversity | Heat stress on seaweed; island power costs | Resilient seaweed varieties; marine protected areas; hybrid mini-grids
Special Geographic Area | n.s. | Agricultural land in the Rio Grande basin | Unresolved land tenure; new LGU capacity | Tenure-secure agro-processing
Source: MTIT (2026b), Provincial Economic and Investment Outlooks, 2023 data. n.s. = not stated in available outlooks.

passages.title: B.3 Energy and Environmental Systems: Powering and Protecting the Base
passages.text: Reliable, affordable power is the single most important enabling condition for industrial investment. The generation mix is predominantly renewable, but access is not: about 40 percent of potential household connections in BARMM electric cooperative areas were energised in 2023 (NEA, 2023), and region-wide household electrification stood at 67.52 percent at the end of 2025 (Context.ph, 2026). Island provinces rely heavily on diesel, which raises costs for processors. Workshop 1 identified three core energy problems: an unreliable power industry with ailing electric cooperatives; insufficient electrification in island and remote barangays; and unused renewable and non-renewable potential (BoI-MTIT, 2026). The devolution of power-sector functions from the DOE to MENRE, agreed in 2026, gives the region new tools and new responsibilities (Context.ph, 2026).

passages.title: Threat VI
passages.text:
Pestalotiopsis rubber disease is the registered threat.
Diagnostic | Validated reading | Investment implication
Strengths | AFF base; renewable endowments; Lake Lanao; Tawi-Tawi seaweed | Move from raw extraction to processing, resilient infrastructure and ecosystem-service revenue
Weakness | Complex land tenure, notably in the SGA | Land due diligence and tenure formalisation before large agro-industrial commitments
Opportunities | Renewables, carbon and REDD+, PES, the Forestry Code | Bankable green projects with community benefit-sharing and safeguards
Threat | Rubber Pestalotiopsis disease | Pair plantation investment with biosecurity, surveillance and diversification

passages.title: Systems archetype and leverage response
passages.text:
System structure. Resource gains attract more users; rising extraction meets ecological limits; delayed environmental feedback lets degradation build up before output falls.
Leverage response. Co-manage watersheds and fisheries, adopt sustainable rubber standards, use carbon and PES revenue, and price ecological risk into project screening. The shift is from managing projects to managing the resource system that many projects share.

passages.title: C. Cluster 2: Transformers — Industry, Manufacturing, Logistics and Halal Processing
passages.text:
The Transformers cluster is the value-adding engine: the processing and manufacturing capacity that turns Foundation materials into market-ready products. It decides whether BARMM captures value within its borders or exports it as unprocessed commodities. Industry accounts for 25.6 percent of regional output (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025a), and manufacturing in Maguindanao del Norte grew 27 percent between 2018 and 2023 (MTIT, 2026b).
PEDSET signals in this cluster. Economic: scale, input costs and access to buyers. Political: halal certification governance and standards recognition. Technological: cold chain, quality laboratories and traceability. Social: cultural legitimacy of Bangsamoro halal products.

passages.title: Cluster 2 – Transformers: Quantified SWOT and Systems Diagnostic: Halal, Manufacturing, Processing and Value Addition
passages.text:
Priority investment corridors. (1) Halal food processing: the Bangsamoro Halal Park in Matanog, Maguindanao del Norte, and Lake Lanao fisheries processing; (2) agro-industrial corridors: the SPDA Wao–Amai Manabilang zone and the SGA's Rio Grande basin; (3) marine products: seaweed processing in Tawi-Tawi; and (4) rubber and coconut processing: rubber processing in Basilan and coconut products in Maguindanao del Norte.
Table 2-13. Transformers cluster: provincial processing gaps and opportunities
Province | Primary raw material | Processing gap | Investment opportunity
Maguindanao del Norte | Rice, corn, coconut | Limited integrated processing | Bangsamoro Halal Park (Matanog); coconut products
Lanao del Sur | Pineapple, coffee, fish | Limited cold chain; little canning | Expansion around the Wao anchor; Lake Lanao fisheries processing
Basilan | Rubber, coconut | Limited local rubber processing | Integrated rubber processing; biomass energy
Tawi-Tawi | Seaweed | Mostly raw export | Seaweed processing linked to managed harvest
Special Geographic Area | Rice, corn, banana | Little agro-processing | Agro-industrial corridor; cold-chain hub

passages.title: Weakness Risk
passages.text: Cold chain (16.42), market links (16.41), certification (15.65).

passages.title: Systems archetype and leverage response
passages.text: Leverage response. Invest ahead of demand in certification capacity, quality laboratories, shared processing and cold-chain nodes, and digital facilitation, so that a successful pipeline does not become its own bottleneck.

passages.title: D. Cluster 3: Enablers — Infrastructure, Social Services and Protection, Health and Human Capital
passages.text:
The Enablers cluster is the physical, digital and human infrastructure that makes value creation possible. Without reliable power, transport, connectivity and skills, Foundations cannot reach Transformers and Transformers cannot reach Connectors. The quantified evidence identifies Enablers as the binding constraint : it has the highest weakness risk (17.13 out of 25), the lowest readiness (3.33) and the highest urgency (4.04) of all clusters (Table 2-5).
PEDSET signals in this cluster. Demographic: a young, fast-growing population. Social: poverty, literacy and malnutrition. Technological: broadband gaps and digital public services. Economic: infrastructure cost overruns and budget execution.
The human-capital gap is acute. In 2024, 81.0 percent of residents had basic literacy, the lowest of any region (national: 90.0 percent), and 64.7 percent were functionally literate (national: 70.8 percent) (PSA, 2025; PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025b). The population is growing about 3.43 percent a year (MTIT, 2026a). That growth becomes a demographic dividend only if education and skills keep pace with what employers need. Workshop 1 identified the skills mismatch, with technical and vocational programmes concentrated in a few oversubscribed qualifications, as a direct barrier to investment (BoI-MTIT, 2026).

passages.title: Cluster 3 – Enablers: Quantified SWOT and Systems Diagnostic: Infrastructure, Digital Systems, Health and Human Capital
passages.text:
Table 2-14. Enablers cluster: the five highest-rated weaknesses
Weakness | Risk (I × L, 1–25) | Supporting evidence
Low literacy | 18.19 | Basic literacy 81.0%, lowest region; functional literacy 64.7% (2024)
Infrastructure deficits | 17.41 | Household electrification 67.52% (end-2025); broadband below 30% (KPI register estimate)
Poverty | 17.15 | 23.5% of families poor (full-year 2023), against 10.9% nationally

passages.title: Systems archetype and leverage response
passages.text: Leverage response. Sequence infrastructure, connectivity and workforce capability ahead of productive scale-up. The test for any project is not only whether it is bankable, but whether the enabling system can absorb and sustain the extra load.

passages.title: E. Cluster 4: Connectors — Tourism, Digital Connectivity, Trade, Exports and BIMP-EAGA Integration
passages.text:
The Connectors cluster is how BARMM's products, services and cultural assets reach markets beyond the region. It determines whether value creation stays local or earns external revenue and multiplier effects. BARMM has a dual gateway: BIMP-EAGA to the south and west, through Tawi-Tawi, about 20 km from Sabah, and the Philippine domestic market to the north, through the mainland and the central Mindanao corridor (MTIT, 2026b). Ports, customs facilitation and digital trade platforms remain underdeveloped.
PEDSET signals in this cluster. Economic: halal market growth and competition from established hubs. Political: cross-border trade rules and security. Technological: logistics and digital trade. Social: cultural heritage as a tourism asset.

passages.title: Systems archetype and leverage response
passages.text: Leverage response. Design corridors as an inclusion mechanism: prioritise missing links, island logistics and trade facilitation where they unlock stranded assets, and track corridor performance by province.

passages.title: F. Cluster 5: Financiers — Islamic Banking, Waqf, Takaful and Microfinance
passages.text:
The Financiers cluster is the capital circulation system for all other clusters. In BARMM it has a distinctive dimension: Shariah-compliant finance fits the values of a predominantly Muslim population of about 4.5 million people, and offers a recognised route to global Islamic capital. Yet formal financial penetration is low, and Islamic banking assets in the region are estimated at below ₱2 billion (BIRD KPI register).
PEDSET signals in this cluster. Economic: MSME credit demand and project bankability. Political: national regulation and regional coordination. Social: religious values and financial literacy. Technological: digital financial services for island and rural users.
Republic Act No. 11439 provides the national framework for Islamic banking. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas licenses and supervises Islamic banks; the region's role is to build demand, project pipelines, Shariah-governance capacity and public-sector use of Islamic instruments. The government-owned Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank of the Philippines operates in the region, and CARD Islamic Bank has established operations in Marawi City under RA 11439 (MTIT, 2026b). Stakeholders favour macro-capital instruments such as sukuk and infrastructure finance as the first priority (56 percent), and 72 percent consider a coordinating Islamic finance authority essential.

passages.title: Cluster 5 – Financiers: Quantified SWOT and Systems Diagnostic: Islamic Finance, MSME Capital and Investment Mobilisation
passages.text:
Table 2-15. Financiers cluster: Islamic finance development pathway, aligned with the BIRD phases
Phase | Focus | Key actions | 2035-linked target
Phase 1 (2026–2028) | Institutions and capacity | Islamic finance coordination council; financial literacy; Shariah-governance talent; sukuk-ready pipeline | Islamic banking assets ₱20B+ by 2035 (BIRD KPI register)
Phase 2 (2029–2031) | Products and depth | Islamic banking in all provincial capitals; takaful for climate and farm risk; waqf development; digital Islamic finance
Phase 3 (2032–2035) | Regional integration | Cross-border Shariah-compliant trade finance within BIMP-EAGA

passages.title: Threat VI
passages.text:
A coverage gap, not a low-threat finding.
Diagnostic | Validated reading | Investment implication
Strength | Islamic finance legal framework under RA 11439 | Turn enabling law into products, institutions, talent and transaction infrastructure
Weakness | Minimal formal financial penetration | Expand MSME and island access through Islamic microfinance, cooperatives and digital channels
Opportunity | Growing Islamic finance ecosystem | Position projects for Shariah-compliant capital with commercial discipline
Threat | Not surveyed in this section | Treat as a data-coverage gap for the next validation wave

passages.title: Systems archetype and leverage response
passages.text:
System structure. Conventional or ad hoc capital meets immediate liquidity needs, but weak institutional development keeps the region dependent on symptomatic fixes, which in turn reduces demand for purpose-built Islamic products.
Leverage response. Build the fundamental solution: Islamic finance institutions, products, literacy, MSME readiness, Shariah governance and investable pipelines. Use blended finance to build market capacity, not permanent subsidy.

passages.title: G. Cross-Cluster Systems Synthesis: From Five Diagnostics to One Investment System
passages.text: The BEIE Framework's value lies less in describing each cluster than in showing how the clusters interact through reinforcing and balancing loops. These interactions decide whether the ecosystem compounds value or loses it through fragmentation and bottlenecks (Silva, 2026; Senge, 1990).

passages.title: Two Engines of Ecosystem Growth
passages.text:
System sequencing. Foundations supply the productive and ecological base; Enablers lift capacity ceilings; Transformers convert resources into higher-value products; Connectors move them into domestic, ASEAN and global markets; Financiers mobilise capital across the system. The operating systems decide whether these flows are trusted, inclusive, resilient and peaceful.
Integrated investment logic. The evidence supports a sequencing principle rather than five separate sector programmes: secure the resource base → build enabling capacity → scale transformation → connect markets → deepen finance , with governance, resilience, inclusion and peace working at every step.

passages.title: The throughput reality
passages.text:
Because value passes through the clusters in sequence, readiness gaps multiply rather than average. Table 2-16 makes the arithmetic explicit. Averaged, the clusters look about 69 percent ready; multiplied through the chain, the system converts only about 16 percent of its potential, and about 11.5 percent once the operating systems are applied. The weakest link, Enablers, caps the whole chain.
Table 2-16. From cluster readiness to system throughput
Stage in the value chain | Readiness (1–5) | As share of 5 | Cumulative throughput
C1 Foundations | 3.45 | 69.0% | 69.0%
C3 Enablers | 3.33 | 66.6% | 46.0%
C2 Transformers | 3.40 | 68.0% | 31.2%
C4 Connectors | 3.61 | 72.2% | 22.6%
C5 Financiers | 3.55 | 71.0% | 16.0%
Operating systems (applied to the chain) | 3.58 | 71.6% | 11.5%
Source: BIRD Validation Survey (2026), cluster readiness ratings (63–73 valid answers each). The multiplicative model is an illustrative systems heuristic: it assumes each stage passes on only the share of value it is ready to handle. It is not an econometric estimate.

passages.title: Provincial diagnostics and island–mainland dynamics
passages.text:
The cluster analysis shows an island–mainland divergence. In the island provinces, Basilan and Tawi-Tawi, strong Foundation endowments (rubber, seaweed and fisheries) hit hard Enabler ceilings in power, shipping, connectivity and skills, the Limits to Growth pattern. On the mainland, the main constraint is institutional: interventions produce uneven results because of coordination and capacity gaps, the Fixes that Fail and Shifting the Burden patterns. The Special Geographic Area, with new local governments and unresolved land tenure, needs institutional and infrastructure investment at the same time. Table 2-17. BEIE cluster profile by province (indicative synthesis)
Province | Foundations | Transformers | Enablers | Connectors | Priority archetype
Lanao del Sur | Strong (Lake Lanao, SPDA) | Growing (Wao anchor) | Moderate | Moderate | Growth and Underinvestment
Maguindanao del Norte | Moderate (AFF 18%) | Strong (Halal Park; manufacturing +27%) | Moderate | Strong (Polloc) | Fixes that Fail
Maguindanao del Sur | Strong (AFF 53%) | Weak | Weak | Weak | Limits to Growth
Basilan | Strong (rubber) | Weak | Improving (interconnection) | Weak (cross-boundary) | Limits to Growth
Tawi-Tawi | Strong (seaweed) | Weak (raw export) | Very weak | Moderate (Sabah) | Limits to Growth

passages.text:
Special Geographic Area | Strong (Rio Grande basin) | Weak | Weak (new LGUs) | Moderate (central corridor) | Shifting the Burden

passages.title: Introduction: From Diagnosis to Strategy
passages.text: Chapter 2 diagnosed the Bangsamoro economy as one connected system. It quantified 55 strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats across the cross-cutting operating systems and the five clusters of the Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework; it identified the systems archetypes that keep the region's investment performance below its potential; and it showed that readiness gaps compound along the value chain, so that clusters that look about 69 percent ready on average deliver only about 11.5 percent of their potential as a system. This chapter turns that diagnosis into a strategic choice. It does so through three analytical layers, each building on the one before: • SWOT-to-strategy conversion (Section A, A.1–A.4). The quantified SWOT register is converted into SO, WO, ST and WT strategies using the TOWS matrix (Weihrich, 1982). Every strategy is traced to scored survey items, the BEIE cluster that owns it and the archetype it addresses. • Systems-archetype-informed leverage points (Section B). Each archetype is mapped to the levels of Donella Meadows' hierarchy of places to intervene in a system (Meadows, 1999), and the results are consolidated into the five Critical Leverage Points (LP1–LP5) used in Chapters 4 to 7. • Multi-criteria evaluation of four strategic options (Section A, A.5–A.7).

passages.title: Introduction: From Diagnosis to Strategy
passages.text: Halal Economy Dominance (HEDS), Green Economy Monetisation (GEMS), Infrastructure-First Enabling (IFES) and Integrated Ecosystem Development (IEDS) are scored against seven weighted criteria, tested for sensitivity and then compared with stakeholder validation results.

passages.title: What Chapter 2 hands to Chapter 3
passages.text: Baseline scores and validation results are reported separately. The option matrix in Section A.6 is an analytical decision aid: its baseline scores are structured expert judgements made with the Strat Planner Pro method. Stakeholder validation results from the BIRD Validation Survey are a second, independent evidence stream and are reported beside the baseline, never blended into it. Where the two agree, confidence rises; where they differ, the difference is reported as a finding.

passages.title: What Chapter 2 hands to Chapter 3
passages.text:
Table 3-1 lists the diagnostic findings that shape the strategy, and the design requirement each one places on any option the region adopts. These requirements become the tests that the four options must pass in Section A.6. Table 3-1. Diagnostic findings carried forward and the strategic requirement each creates
Chapter 2 finding (evidence) | Requirement for the strategy
Enablers is the binding cluster. Lowest readiness (3.33 of 5) and the highest weakness risk (17.13), led by low literacy (18.19), malnutrition (17.84) and infrastructure deficits (17.41). | Infrastructure, energy and human capital must be financed ahead of, or alongside, productive scale-up; no option may assume them. Readiness gaps compound. Mean cluster readiness is about 69 percent, but serial throughput falls to 16.0 percent across the chain and about 11.5 percent once the operating systems are applied. | Clusters must be developed in a synchronised sequence; improving one cluster in isolation yields little system output. Opportunities are not the constraint. Opportunity ratings are uniformly high (cluster means 3.93–4.04); the global halal market (4.13), renewable investment (4.12) and digital leapfrogging (4.10) lead. | The strategy should concentrate on converting opportunity into investable projects, rather than on identifying new opportunities. Structural archetypes are recognised.

passages.title: What Chapter 2 hands to Chapter 3
passages.text: Between 95 and 99 percent of respondents rated each cluster archetype accurate; the governance archetypes (Big Man, Escalation, Drifting Goals) were rated accurate by 96–99 percent. | Interventions must work at the level of rules, information flows, goals and mindsets, not only at the level of projects and budgets. Security and climate are the leading threats. Security incidents (VI 3.20) and climate change (3.14) carry the highest vulnerability indices, followed by price volatility (3.19) and infrastructure cost overruns (3.07). | Every option needs explicit risk buffers: peace-conditioned delivery, climate screening and cost-control gates. Territorial divergence. Maguindanao del Norte is the largest economy (₱81.91 billion, 2023); Tawi-Tawi, the smallest, holds the region's maritime gateway and about 40 percent of national seaweed output, and was named by 44 of 72 respondents as the province with the most trapped value. | The strategy must counter "Success to the Successful" with explicit island and lagging-area priorities. Sources: BIRD Validation Survey (2026), n = 76 consented responses, 60–74 valid ratings per item; MTIT (2026); Chapter 2, Tables 2-4, 2-5 and 2-16.

passages.title: Systems-Based Strategy Matrix and Strategic Options
passages.text:
The TOWS matrix (Weihrich, 1982) pairs internal factors (strengths and weaknesses) with external factors (opportunities and threats) to generate four families of strategy. BIRD applies it with three disciplines borrowed from systems thinking. First, only scored items enter the matrix: each pairing uses factors from the BIRD Validation Survey register rather than descriptive lists. Second, each strategy is assigned to the BEIE cluster that owns its delivery, so that the matrix can be read as a map of the ecosystem. Third, each strategy is tagged with the archetype it is designed to weaken and the Meadows level at which it intervenes, which links Section A to Section B. Table 3-2. The scored SWOT register: top-ranked items in each family
Strengths (RI, 0–5) | Weaknesses (Risk, 1–25) | Opportunities (RI, 0–5) | Threats (VI, 0–5)
Seaweed dominance 3.71 (F) | Low literacy 18.19 (E) | Global halal market 4.13 (C) | Security incidents 3.20 (OS)
Agriculture, fisheries and forestry base 3.69 (F) | Malnutrition 17.84 (E) | Renewable energy investment 4.12 (F) | Commodity price volatility 3.19 (C)
Cultural heritage 3.59 (T) | Infrastructure deficits 17.41 (E) | Digital leapfrogging 4.10 (E) | Climate change 3.14 (OS)
Peace dividend 3.50 (OS) | Poverty 17.15 (E) | BIMP-EAGA integration 4.08 (C) | Infrastructure cost overruns 3.07 (E)

passages.text:

Polloc Freeport 3.43 (T) | Low technology adoption 16.62 (E) | Mindanao–Sabah landbridge 4.02 (C) | Halal hub competition 2.88 (C)
