The remaining items are halal legitimacy 3.26, Lake Lanao 3.24, renewable endowments 3.15 and Lanao del Sur growth 3.15 (strengths); fragmented data 15.75, financial penetration 15.66, halal certification 15.65 and fragmented policy 15.46 (weaknesses); post-conflict reconstruction 3.90, UAE corridor 3.92, tourism recovery 3.91 and carbon markets 3.66 (opportunities); standards recognition 2.77, Pestalotiopsis rubber disease 2.69 and fragmented mandates 2.57 (threats). Cluster codes: OS operating systems; F Foundations; T Transformers; E Enablers;

passages.title: Systems-Based Strategy Matrix and Strategic Options
passages.text: C Connectors; Fi Financiers. Source: BIRD Validation Survey (2026); 60–74 valid ratings per item. Scoring conventions. SWOT items use the canonical Strat Planner Pro formulas applied in Chapter 2: Strength Resilience Index (RI) = (I × L) / 5; Opportunity RI = √(I × L); Weakness Risk = I × L on a 1–25 scale; Threat Vulnerability Index (VI) = (I² × L) / 25, where I is impact and L is likelihood, each rated 1–5. The four families therefore sit on different scales and are compared within, not across, families.

passages.title: The strategy matrix at a glance
passages.text:
Figure 3-2 summarises the fourteen strategies derived in Sections A.1 to A.4. Read as a portfolio, the matrix is lopsided in a revealing way: the weaknesses are concentrated in one cluster (Enablers holds six of the ten highest-rated weaknesses and seven of the fourteen in the register), whereas strengths and opportunities are spread across Foundations, Transformers and Connectors. The binding constraint is therefore internal and structural, which is why the WO and WT quadrants, rather than the SO quadrant alone, carry the heaviest weight in the option evaluation that follows. SO · Maxi–maxi (use strengths to capture opportunities)
SO-1 Halal and agro-industrial value chains (T) SO-2 Renewable energy and natural-capital monetisation (F) SO-3 BIMP-EAGA gateway and Muslim-friendly tourism (C)
WO · Mini–maxi (use opportunities to overcome weaknesses)
WO-1 Infrastructure and energy enabling (E) WO-2 Human-capital transformation (E) WO-3 Cold chain, market linkage and certification capacity (T) WO-4 Islamic financial inclusion for MSMEs (Fi)
ST · Maxi–mini (use strengths to absorb threats)
ST-1 Standards recognition and halal quality assurance (T) ST-2 Climate-resilient Foundations (F) ST-3 Peace-conditioned investment confidence (OS)
WT · Mini–mini (reduce weaknesses and avoid threats)

passages.title: The strategy matrix at a glance
passages.text:
WT-1 Delivery, budget execution and data reform (OS) WT-2 Infrastructure cost and delivery assurance (E) WT-3 Land tenure and shared-resource governance (F) WT-4 Investment continuity through political transition (OS)
Figure 3-2. The BIRD TOWS strategy matrix: fourteen strategies, each assigned to the BEIE cluster that owns its delivery. Source: BIRD analysis of the BIRD Validation Survey (2026) SWOT register, using Weihrich (1982). How to read Sections A.1 to A.4. Each table gives the paired SWOT items with their scores, the archetype the strategy is designed to weaken, the Meadows level at which it intervenes (L-numbers follow Meadows, 1999, from L12 parameters to L1 transcending paradigms) and the Critical Leverage Point (LP1–LP5) it serves. Expected results are directional; quantified targets are set and calibrated in Chapter 4.

passages.title: A.1 SO Strategies: Using Strengths to Capture Opportunities
passages.text:
SO strategies are the growth pathway. They connect the region's strongest scored assets (a large resource base, seaweed and agricultural specialisation, cultural credibility and location) with its highest-rated external opportunities (halal markets, renewable investment and regional integration). They are attractive but conditional: each depends on Enablers that Chapter 2 found to be the weakest cluster. Table 3-3. SO strategies with leverage-point integration
Strategy | Strengths (RI) | Opportunities (RI) | Archetype addressed | Meadows level | CLP
SO-1 Halal and agro-industrial value chains | Seaweed dominance 3.71; AFF base 3.69; Polloc Freeport 3.43; domestic halal demand 3.36; halal legitimacy 3.26 | Global halal market 4.13; ASEAN halal economy 4.05; UAE corridor 3.92 | Growth and Underinvestment | L10 stock-and-flow; L5 rules | LP1
SO-2 Renewable energy and natural-capital monetisation | Lake Lanao 3.24; renewable endowments 3.15 | Renewable investment 4.12; PES 3.99; Forestry Code 3.97; carbon markets 3.66 | Tragedy of the Commons | L5 rules; L4 self-organisation; L6 information | LP5, LP2
SO-3 BIMP-EAGA gateway and Muslim-friendly tourism | Cultural heritage 3.59; BIMP-EAGA location 3.50 | BIMP-EAGA integration 4.08; landbridge 4.02; tourism recovery 3.91 | Success to the Successful | L10 stock-and-flow; L5 rules | LP2, LP3
SO-1 is the core of the halal pathway.

passages.title: A.1 SO Strategies: Using Strengths to Capture Opportunities
passages.text: Its strongest pairing is not halal legitimacy itself, which scores in the middle of the strength register (3.26), but the resource base that halal products are made from: seaweed (3.71) and agriculture, fisheries and forestry (3.69), matched with the highest-rated opportunity in the register, the global halal market (4.13). The constraint is conversion, not supply: Tawi-Tawi exports most of its seaweed raw, and cold chain (16.42) and market linkage (16.41) are among the highest-rated weaknesses. SO-1 therefore intervenes at L10 (processing, testing and cold-chain capacity built ahead of demand) and at L5 (accreditation rules that open export markets), anchored by the Bangsamoro Halal Park in Matanog and agro-industrial corridors in Lanao del Sur and the SGA (MTIT, 2025; MTIT, 2026). SO-2 converts environmental endowments into revenue through renewable energy, payment for ecosystem services (PES) and, where eligible, carbon markets. Its legal precondition is the Bangsamoro Forestry Code and the joint MENRE–MILG issuance on benefit sharing, both still pending. Without these rules, SO-2 would accelerate the Tragedy of the Commons rather than resolve it.

passages.title: A.1 SO Strategies: Using Strengths to Capture Opportunities
passages.text: SO-3 uses location and culture to reach BIMP-EAGA and Muslim-friendly tourism markets; it intervenes in physical links (ports, the Mindanao–Sabah landbridge concept, island logistics) and in rules that spread benefits beyond the already-connected mainland.

passages.title: A.2 WO Strategies: Using Opportunities to Overcome Weaknesses
passages.text:
WO strategies are turnaround initiatives. They matter most in BARMM because the register's highest-risk items are internal: six of the ten highest-rated weaknesses sit in the Enablers cluster. External opportunities, such as concessional climate finance, digital technology and Islamic finance, supply the capital and capability that internal resources alone cannot. Table 3-4. WO strategies with leverage-point integration
Strategy | Weaknesses (Risk) | Opportunities (RI) | Archetype addressed | Meadows level | CLP
WO-1 Infrastructure and energy enabling | Infrastructure deficits 17.41; low technology adoption 16.62 | Renewable investment 4.12; climate-adaptation finance 4.03; digital leapfrogging 4.10 | Limits to Growth | L10 stock-and-flow; L9 delays; L11 buffers | LP2
WO-2 Human-capital transformation | Low literacy 18.19; malnutrition 17.84; poverty 17.15; skills mismatch 16.96 | Digital leapfrogging 4.10; post-conflict reconstruction 3.90 | Limits to Growth; Fixes that Fail | L10 stock-and-flow; L3 goals | LP2
WO-3 Cold chain, market linkage and certification capacity | Cold chain 16.42; market linkages 16.41; halal certification 15.65 | Global halal market 4.13; ASEAN halal economy 4.05 | Growth and Underinvestment | L10 stock-and-flow; L9 delays; L6 information | LP1

passages.title: A.2 WO Strategies: Using Opportunities to Overcome Weaknesses
passages.text:
WO-4 Islamic financial inclusion for MSMEs | Financial penetration 15.66 | Islamic finance ecosystem 3.99 | Shifting the Burden | L4 self-organisation; L5 rules | LP4
WO-1 addresses the physical ceiling on growth. Household electrification reached 67.52 percent region-wide at the end of 2025, against a Bangsamoro Sustainable Energy Master Plan target of 90 percent by 2035 and 100 percent by 2040; broadband coverage is estimated in the BIRD KPI register at below 30 percent (MENRE-BARMM, 2024; Context.ph, 2026). The ₱6.67 billion Zamboanga–Basilan Interconnection Project is the clearest example of a single enabling asset that changes what Basilan can process (MTIT, 2026). WO-1 intervenes mainly at L10 (building the stock of roads, power and connectivity), L9 (shortening project preparation and delivery delays) and L11 (reserve capacity so that new investment does not immediately saturate the grid). WO-2 addresses the highest-rated risk in the entire register. In 2024 only 64.7 percent of BARMM residents were functionally literate, against 70.8 percent nationally, and basic literacy (81.0 percent) was the lowest of any region (PSA, 2025). Because human capital accumulates slowly, WO-2 must start in Phase 1 even though its returns arrive mainly in Phases 2 and 3; this is the classic delay that makes capacity investment easy to postpone.

passages.title: A.2 WO Strategies: Using Opportunities to Overcome Weaknesses
passages.text: WO-3 builds the conversion capacity that SO-1 depends on, and WO-4 builds Islamic financial capability (products, providers and financial literacy) rather than relying on one-off conventional or grant financing, the pattern that Chapter 2 identified as Shifting the Burden.

passages.title: A.3 ST Strategies: Using Strengths to Absorb Threats
passages.text:
ST strategies are protective. They deploy the region's strengths against the threats that could reverse investment gains. The threat register is led by security incidents (VI 3.20), commodity price volatility (3.19) and climate change (3.14), all external pressures that BARMM cannot remove but can buffer. Table 3-5. ST strategies with leverage-point integration
Strategy | Strengths (RI) | Threats (VI) | Archetype addressed | Meadows level | CLP
ST-1 Standards recognition and halal quality assurance | Halal legitimacy 3.26; cultural heritage 3.59 | Halal hub competition 2.88; standards recognition 2.77 | Success to the Successful (at international scale) | L5 rules; L6 information | LP1
ST-2 Climate-resilient Foundations | AFF base 3.69; renewable endowments 3.15 | Climate change 3.14; price volatility 3.19; Pestalotiopsis 2.69 | Fixes that Fail | L11 buffers; L6 information; L5 rules | LP5, LP2
ST-3 Peace-conditioned investment confidence | Peace dividend 3.50; policy recognition 3.45; young population 3.37 | Security incidents 3.20; political transition 2.85 | Escalation | L8 balancing loops; L6 information | LP3
ST-1 rests on a realistic reading of competition. Established halal hubs in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand have deeper supply chains and recognised certification systems.

passages.title: A.3 ST Strategies: Using Strengths to Absorb Threats
passages.text: BARMM's route to premium markets is therefore not price but trust: certification that importing authorities accept, backed by laboratory testing and traceability. This makes accreditation and mutual recognition under OIC/SMIIC standards a critical-path item for the halal pathway rather than a compliance formality (SMIIC, 2021; MTIT, 2025). ST-2 treats climate risk as a present cost. El Niño-related drought led Maguindanao del Sur to declare a state of calamity in 2024, and Pestalotiopsis leaf disease has affected at least 800 hectares of rubber in Basilan (Chapter 2). The strategy combines buffers (irrigation, crop diversification, climate-resilient varieties), information (early warning and climate-risk screening of projects) and rules (adaptation conditions on subsidies), avoiding relief-only responses that recreate the problem. ST-3 uses the peace dividend, including Basilan's declaration as free of the Abu Sayyaf Group on 9 June 2025 (PIA, 2025), to strengthen the balancing loops that keep isolated incidents from becoming investor-wide risk premiums: rapid incident response, verified security information for investors and protection of project sites.

passages.title: A.4 WT Strategies: Reducing Weaknesses and Avoiding Threats
passages.text:
WT strategies address the points where internal weakness meets external threat, and where the region is most exposed. They are defensive in form but preventive in purpose: they protect the roadmap itself from the failure modes Chapter 7 identifies, namely being ignored after a change of government, executed in silos or allowed to drift. Table 3-6. WT strategies with leverage-point integration
Strategy | Weaknesses (Risk) | Threats (VI) | Archetype addressed | Meadows level | CLP
WT-1 Delivery, budget execution and data reform | Underspending 16.85; fragmented data 15.75; fragmented policy 15.46 | Drifting goals 3.03; national coordination 2.91; fragmented mandates 2.57 | Drifting Goals; Fixes that Fail | L6 information; L5 rules; L3 goals | LP3
WT-2 Infrastructure cost and delivery assurance | Infrastructure deficits 17.41 | Cost overruns 3.07; cyber insecurity 2.80 | Limits to Growth | L9 delays; L8 balancing loops | LP2
WT-3 Land tenure and shared-resource governance | Land tenure 15.92 | Security incidents 3.20; Pestalotiopsis 2.69 | Tragedy of the Commons | L5 rules; L4 self-organisation | LP5
WT-4 Investment continuity through political transition | Fragmented policy 15.46 | Political transition 2.85; drifting goals 3.03 | Big Man; Drifting Goals | L3 goals; L5 rules; L2 paradigm | LP3
WT-1 is the cheapest source of additional capital in the roadmap.

passages.title: A.4 WT Strategies: Reducing Weaknesses and Avoiding Threats
passages.text: Underspending is rated a high risk (16.85), and every percentage point of budget execution recovered is capital that does not have to be raised. The strategy works through information (one version-controlled baseline and project register, as recommended in Chapter 7, B1), rules (readiness gates and published service standards) and goals (protecting targets from being lowered quietly when performance lags). Respondents rated the Drifting Goals archetype accurate at 98.6 percent, and 30 of 45 who answered the follow-up said both of its loops are equally observable (BIRD Validation Survey, 2026). WT-2 introduces cost and schedule assurance, because infrastructure cost overruns carry the highest impact rating of any threat (I = 4.28). WT-3 resolves the land-tenure overlaps (ancestral domain claims, private titles and public land) that block agro-industrial siting, with free, prior and informed consent where indigenous peoples' rights apply. WT-4 responds to the first elected Bangsamoro Parliament: the roadmap must be anchored in law, budget rules and published targets so that it outlasts any single administration (Chapter 7, D1).

passages.title: A.5 Strategic Options Formulation
passages.text:
The fourteen TOWS strategies can be bundled in different ways, and each bundle expresses a different theory of how BARMM's economy should grow. Four coherent options were formulated during the BIRD workshops and tested in the validation survey. The options are not mutually exclusive in content; they differ in emphasis, sequencing and the constraint they treat as binding. Table 3-7. How the TOWS strategies combine into the four options
Option | TOWS strategies bundled | Constraint treated as binding | Failure mode if pursued alone
HEDS Halal Economy Dominance | SO-1, WO-3, ST-1 | Market access and certification | Processing and export capacity outrun power, logistics and skills; growth stalls at the Enablers ceiling (Growth and Underinvestment becomes Limits to Growth). GEMS Green Economy Monetisation | SO-2, ST-2, WT-3 | Unpriced natural capital | Revenue depends on legal instruments, measurement systems and buyers not yet in place; green revenue currently stands near zero. IFES Infrastructure-First Enabling | WO-1, WO-2, WT-2 | Infrastructure and human capital | Capacity is built ahead of conversion; value accumulates upstream with no processing or market link to release it, and political support erodes before returns appear.

passages.title: A.5 Strategic Options Formulation
passages.text: IEDS Integrated Ecosystem Development | All fourteen, sequenced in three phases | The weakest link in a serial chain, wherever it lies | Coordination overload: too many fronts for the available institutional capacity unless a single orchestration function and readiness gates are in place.

passages.title: Option profiles
passages.text:
Option 1 · Halal Economy Dominance Strategy (HEDS)
Option 2 · Green Economy Monetisation Strategy (GEMS)
Option 3 · Infrastructure-First Enabling Strategy (IFES)
Option 4 · Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS)
Why serial throughput favours synchronisation. When value must pass through several clusters in sequence, system output is the product of their readiness levels, not the average. In a product, a one percent improvement in any cluster raises total throughput by about one percent, so no cluster can be safely deferred; and because the absolute gain is largest where readiness is lowest, the weakest link (Enablers) must be raised first. A single-sector option improves one factor of the product and leaves the others unchanged.

passages.title: A.6 Strategic Options Evaluation and Ranking
passages.text:
The options are evaluated with the seven-criterion weighted scoring matrix of the Strat Planner Pro architecture. Each option is scored from 1 to 10 against each criterion, and the composite is the weighted sum. The weights below are the canonical values coded in the BIRD analytical engine ( formulas.ts ), and are the only weights used in this chapter. Table 3-8. Evaluation criteria, weights and evidence basis
Criterion | Weight | What is assessed | Principal evidence
Economic impact | 20% | Contribution to GRDP, jobs, exports and poverty reduction | PSA-RSSO BARMM (2025) regional accounts; provincial outlooks (MTIT, 2026)
Feasibility | 18% | Technical, financial and institutional readiness to deliver | Cluster readiness ratings; workshop findings (BoI-MTIT, 2026)
Risk–return | 16% | Expected return relative to exposure to scored threats | Threat VI register (Table 3-2)
Identity alignment | 15% | Fit with Islamic values, moral governance and cultural authenticity | Moral governance principles; Bangsamoro Halal Industry Development Plan
Systems leverage | 15% | Depth of intervention and number of archetypes addressed | Archetype map (Section B); Meadows (1999)
Inclusivity | 10% | Reach to island and lagging areas, MSMEs, women, youth and indigenous peoples | Provincial diagnostics; poverty and literacy data

passages.title: A.6 Strategic Options Evaluation and Ranking
passages.text:
Sustainability | 6% | Environmental, fiscal and institutional durability beyond 2035 | Climate and resource diagnostics; fiscal analysis
Source: BIRD analytical engine, calculateStrategyOverallScore (Silva, 2026). Earlier circulating drafts used a superseded weight set (economic impact 25%, feasibility 20%, risk–return 10%, sustainability 5%); results under both sets are shown in Table 3-10.

passages.title: Sensitivity of the ranking
passages.text: Three readings follow. First, IEDS leads on five of the seven criteria and is never ranked below second. Second, each single-sector option leads where its thesis predicts: HEDS on identity alignment, GEMS on sustainability (tied with IEDS) and IFES on systems leverage among the standalone options. Third, the decisive gap is in systems leverage and economic impact, the two criteria that capture whether an option changes the structure of the system, which is precisely what Chapter 2's throughput analysis says is required. The lowest score for IEDS is risk–return (7.5): integration spreads exposure across more fronts, a cost that the phase gates in Section A.7 are designed to manage.

passages.title: Sensitivity of the ranking
passages.text:
A ranking that changes when the weights change slightly is not a robust basis for a ten-year roadmap (Belton and Stewart, 2002). Table 3-10 re-scores the baseline under alternative weightings and under a stress test that penalises IEDS for its coordination burden. Table 3-10. Sensitivity of the analytical baseline to weights and to an IEDS stress test
Scenario | HEDS | GEMS | IFES | IEDS
Canonical weights (Table 3-8) | 7.53 | 7.16 | 7.46 | 8.83
Equal weights (each criterion 1/7) | 7.50 | 7.43 | 7.50 | 8.86
Feasibility-led (feasibility raised to 30%, others rescaled) | 7.47 | 7.03 | 7.36 | 8.74
Risk-averse (risk–return raised to 30%, others rescaled) | 7.40 | 7.01 | 7.40 | 8.67
Superseded draft weights (25/20/15/15/10/10/5) | 7.60 | 7.15 | 7.48 | 8.93
Stress test: IEDS feasibility and risk–return each cut to 6.0 | 7.53 | 7.16 | 7.46 | 8.23
IEDS ranks first in every scenario, and remains first even when its feasibility and risk–return scores are cut below those of HEDS. The order of the three single-sector options is less stable: HEDS and IFES tie under equal and risk-averse weights. The practical conclusion is that the choice of IEDS is robust, whereas the relative priority of the halal and infrastructure components within it should be decided by sequencing logic (Section A.7) rather than by the scores alone. Correction to earlier drafts.

passages.title: Sensitivity of the ranking
passages.text: The composite of 8.93 for IEDS that appeared in earlier drafts and graphics was computed with the superseded weight set. Under the canonical weights the IEDS baseline composite is 8.83. The ranking is unchanged.

passages.title: Stakeholder validation results (reported separately)
passages.text:
The BIRD Validation Survey asked respondents to score the same four options against the same seven criteria. These results are a separate evidence stream: they test whether the people who will finance, regulate and deliver the roadmap read the options as the analytical baseline does.
Weighted stakeholder score, all respondents (n = 75)
Weighted stakeholder score, respondents who moved at least one slider (n = 50)
Figure 3-4. Stakeholder validation of the four options, weighted with the canonical criteria weights (scale 1–10). Source: BIRD Validation Survey (2026), Section 10 option matrix; computed by BoI-MTIT from consented responses.
Table 3-11. Baseline and validation compared
Evidence stream | HEDS | GEMS | IFES | IEDS | Order
Analytical baseline (Table 3-9) | 7.53 | 7.16 | 7.46 | 8.83 | IEDS › HEDS › IFES › GEMS
Survey, all respondents (n = 75) | 5.90 | 5.73 | 5.77 | 6.05 | IEDS › HEDS › IFES › GEMS

passages.title: Reading the validation evidence
passages.text:
The order is fully reproduced; the conviction is not. Stakeholders reproduced the baseline order exactly, in the full sample and in the subset who moved at least one slider. However, their scores are lower and closer together: the IEDS lead over HEDS is 0.15 points in the full sample and 0.22 among slider movers, against 1.30 points in the baseline. At the level of individual respondents, IEDS was the strict first choice of 22 percent of slider movers (32 percent including ties). The baseline should therefore be read as a well-supported direction, not as a decisive margin of stakeholder preference.
Default responses compress the spread. Twenty-five of the 75 respondents who reached the matrix left all 28 cells at the default value of 5. Their answers pull every option towards the midpoint, which is why the slider-mover subset is reported alongside the full sample.
Where stakeholders see it differently. Among slider movers, HEDS outscored IEDS on identity alignment (6.74 against 6.58), and inclusivity was IEDS's strongest criterion (7.06). Stakeholders thus see the integrated strategy as the more inclusive choice and the halal strategy as the more authentic expression of Bangsamoro identity. IEDS should carry the halal agenda visibly, rather than subsume it.

passages.title: Stakeholder validation results (reported separately) (continued)
passages.text:
Direct endorsement. Asked whether IEDS should be the overarching strategy, 44 of 65 respondents (67.7 percent) answered yes, 20 (30.8 percent) agreed partially and one asked for more evidence; none rejected it. Respondents agreed that the expected outcomes are achievable (mean 4.00 of 5; 80.3 percent agree) and that the sequencing logic is sound (59 of 66 agree or strongly agree).
Survey frame. The survey is a non-probability sample of 76 consented respondents, collected 3–20 August 2026. Of the 72 who named a location, 27 were from Cotabato City, 22 from Maguindanao del Norte, 11 region-wide, 7 from the SGA, 3 from Maguindanao del Sur and 2 from Lanao del Sur; none were from Basilan or Tawi-Tawi. Results are validation signals, not population estimates, and island perspectives must be gathered through the scheduled Tawi-Tawi workshop and follow-up consultations before the island-specific elements of the roadmap are finalised.

passages.title: A.7 Recommended Strategy: The Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS)
passages.text:
The Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy is recommended as the overarching strategy for BIRD 2026–2035. Three arguments support the recommendation, each independent of the others:
• Structural fit. The economy behaves as a serial chain whose output is capped by its weakest cluster. Only an option that raises all clusters in dependency order can lift system throughput materially (Chapter 2, Section G).
• Archetype coverage. IEDS is the only option that responds to all six cluster archetypes and the three governance archetypes diagnosed in Chapter 2 (Section B.2).
• Robustness. IEDS ranks first under every weighting tested and in both stakeholder samples, and was endorsed outright or partially by 64 of 65 respondents.
IEDS does not mean doing everything at once. It means testing each project against the upstream conditions it needs (reliable power and logistics, lawful land access, capable workers, accepted standards, finance, safeguards and credible offtake) and funding those conditions alongside the project where justified. The sequence is implemented through the three phases that Chapter 6 operationalises.

passages.title: IEDS sequencing with cluster synchronisation
passages.text:
Table 3-12. IEDS phases, cluster emphasis and stakeholder support
Phase (survey label) | Cluster emphasis | Representative capital deployments | Indicative envelope | Priority rating (1–5)
Phase 1 · Foundation Building Foundations and enabling conditions, 2026–2028 (Sequence A) | Enablers, Foundations, operating systems | Energy interconnection and mini-grids; farm-to-market roads; digital public services; halal assurance capacity; Forestry Code and safeguards; baseline register and project pipeline | ₱35–45 billion | 4.20 (80.0% rate 4+; n = 65)
Phase 2 · Acceleration Value addition and market formation, 2029–2031 (Sequence B) | Transformers, Foundations, Financiers | Halal and agro-industrial processing, including the Halal Park where feasible; cold chain; PES and eligible carbon projects; Islamic finance products; industry-aligned skills | ₱50–65 billion | 4.09 (80.6%; n = 67)
Phase 3 · Consolidation and Global Integration 2032–2035 (Sequence C) | Connectors, operating systems | BIMP-EAGA and GCC export logistics; standards recognition; eco-tourism; applied research; mature green and Islamic finance revenue streams | ₱35–50 billion | 4.00 (75.8%; n = 66)
Sources: Chapter 6, Sections 6.3.1–6.3.3; BIRD Validation Survey (2026), Section 10.

passages.title: IEDS sequencing with cluster synchronisation
passages.text: Phase 3 concerns island and maritime corridors; the online survey drew no respondents from Basilan or Tawi-Tawi, so its island evidence comes from the Basilan (20 June 2026) and Tawi-Tawi (28 October 2026) provincial workshops. Gates, not dates. A later phase is not authorised because its planned start date has arrived. Each project passes a readiness gate before scale-up (verified scope, owner, financing, safeguards, land access and offtake), consistent with Chapter 6. Phases therefore overlap in practice: a Phase 2 processing investment can proceed in 2027 if its power, land and market prerequisites are already verified. The budget-priority tension. Asked where budget should concentrate, respondents put Foundations first (29 of 71) and the operating systems second (15), with Enablers fifth (6), even though readiness data identify Enablers as the binding cluster. The two views are reconciled rather than overruled: Enablers investments are selected and justified by the Foundations pipelines they unlock, such as farm-to-market roads, cold chain and power for agro-processing (Chapter 7, B4).

passages.title: Financing logic and 2035 targets
passages.text: The ₱120–160 billion envelope is an indicative requirement for public and catalytic finance over the decade, not a single approved budget. Chapter 6 sets out an illustrative financing scenario of 35 percent from BARMM appropriations and other regional public resources, 25 percent from national government programmes, 30 percent from official development assistance and climate finance, and 10 percent from private capital, public–private partnerships and Islamic finance. Stakeholders broadly support blended finance (63 of 72 agree or strongly agree), but rated the fairness of the proposed mix more cautiously (3.68 of 5). Each share must be replaced by verified appropriations or signed commitments as they become available.

passages.title: Managing the risks of integration
passages.text:
Table 3-13. IEDS strategic targets for 2035 by BEIE cluster driver
Outcome area | 2035 strategic target | Principal cluster drivers
Macroeconomy and investment | GRDP of ₱550 billion or more; investment approvals of ₱15 billion or more a year; export growth | Transformers, Connectors, Financiers
Employment and poverty | At least 20,000 jobs; poverty incidence below 20 percent | Enablers, Foundations
Halal and green economy | Growth in halal-certified MSMEs and accepted export certificates; ₱500 million or more a year in verified green revenue | Transformers, Foundations, Connectors
Financial inclusion | Deeper Islamic banking assets and adult financial account ownership | Financiers, operating systems
Infrastructure and human capital | Household electrification of 90 percent (100 percent by 2040); higher functional literacy; broadband expansion | Enablers, Connectors
Governance | Budget execution of at least 90 percent; published service standards; one verified baseline register | Operating systems
Targets are strategic ambitions to be assessed against verified, five-province baselines; definitions, baselines and calibration are set in Chapter 4 and the BSC objectives in Chapter 5. Sources: Chapters 4–6; MENRE-BARMM (2024).

passages.title: Managing the risks of integration
passages.text:
The principal risk of IEDS is the one its feasibility score anticipates: coordination load. Integration multiplies interfaces between ministries, local governments, investors and development partners, and the weakest interface sets the pace. Table 3-14 lists the main risks and the mitigation built into the roadmap. Table 3-14. Principal risks of the integrated strategy and their mitigation
Risk | How it would show | Mitigation in the roadmap
Coordination overload | Projects wait for permits and decisions held by different agencies; issues escalate without resolution | One investment-facilitation network (BIF-Net) with an Orchestration Office in MTIT-BoI for case management, data and aftercare; five BEIE cluster councils (Chapter 7, A2–A3)
Resource dilution | Many small allocations, few completed assets | Readiness gates and a ranked, version-controlled project pipeline (Chapter 6)
Target drift | Targets lowered quietly when performance lags | Variance triggers and documented corrective plans; quarterly BSC review (Chapters 5–6)
Political transition | Reprioritisation after a change of administration | Anchoring in law and budget rules; policy review calendar to 2035 (Chapter 7, D1)
Territorial concentration | Investment clusters in the mainland corridor | Proposed allocation floor for lagging and island areas; provincial investment nodes (Chapter 7, B3)

passages.title: Managing the risks of integration
passages.text: Stakeholders favoured the same direction. Asked which mitigation mattered most, 45 of 61 chose a single coordination centre for investment delivery (presented in the survey as an investment command centre), ahead of trigger-based budgeting (9), climate finance for green sequencing (5) and a 20 percent contingency reserve (2). Chapter 7 gives this function its institutional form as the BIF-Net Orchestration Office: a coordinating and case-management function, not an additional approving body. On reform sequencing, 42 of 73 respondents preferred institutional, fiscal and regulatory reforms to proceed in parallel.

passages.title: Systems Archetype-Informed Strategic Leverage Points
passages.text:
Section A chose the strategy; Section B identifies where, within the system, that strategy should push. A leverage point is a place in a system where a small, well-placed change produces a large and lasting shift in behaviour (Meadows, 1999). Meadows ranked twelve such places from the least to the most powerful, and the hierarchy is used here as a practical diagnostic: for each archetype diagnosed in Chapter 2, it asks which level of intervention would weaken the structure that produces the problem. Table 3-15. Meadows' hierarchy of leverage points, grouped into four realms
Realm | Meadows levels | Typical BIRD intervention
Parameters (shallow; quick to change) | L12 constants and numbers; L11 buffers; L10 stock-and-flow structures | Incentive rates, budget amounts, reserve capacity, physical infrastructure
Feedbacks | L9 delays; L8 balancing loops; L7 reinforcing loops | Faster approvals and project delivery, rapid-response mechanisms, performance-linked funding
Design | L6 information flows; L5 rules; L4 self-organisation | Published delivery data, accreditation rules, co-management and cluster councils
Intent (deep; slow to change, most durable) | L3 goals; L2 paradigms; L1 transcending paradigms | Inclusive and stewardship-based goals, a shift from competition to collaboration
Sources: Meadows (1999); the four realms follow Abson et al. (2017).

passages.title: Systems Archetype-Informed Strategic Leverage Points
passages.text: Three numbering systems, kept distinct. In this report, L1–L12 refer to Meadows' levels; LP1–LP5 are the five Critical Leverage Points (identifiers, not Meadows levels); and the Balanced Scorecard's Learning and Growth objectives in Chapter 5 use separate codes.

passages.title: B.1 Identifying Leverage Points: A Three-Step Diagnostic Process
passages.text: Leverage points were identified through a three-step process from the Strat Planner Pro architecture, applied first in the regional and provincial workshops and then tested in the validation survey (Silva, 2026; BoI-MTIT, 2026). Step 1: Diagnostic synthesis. Recurring patterns are identified from the scored SWOT register and the workshops: production that cannot scale beyond local power and logistics limits; certification and processing capacity that lags demand; shared resources degraded by fragmented governance; investment concentrated in the mainland corridor; and short-term financing that delays durable institutions. Step 2: Loop mapping. Each pattern is traced to its feedback structure. Chapter 2 mapped the investment–development reinforcing loop and the governance–investor confidence loop (rated accurate by 97 and 91 percent of respondents) and the balancing loops that cap them. The question at this step is where a loop is delayed, broken or dominated by a balancing limit. Step 3: Tiered selection. Interventions are chosen across realms. Parameter changes are fast but shallow; design and intent changes are slow but durable. A credible portfolio uses both, with deeper interventions protecting the gains of shallower ones.

passages.title: B.1 Identifying Leverage Points: A Three-Step Diagnostic Process
passages.text: Respondents found the leverage points clear (mean 4.00 of 5; 76.7 percent agree) and agreed that activating them would accelerate the ecosystem (4.03; 79.5 percent).

passages.title: B.2 From Archetypes to Leverage Points
passages.text:
Table 3-16 maps each archetype to the levels at which it can be weakened, the Critical Leverage Point that carries the response and the TOWS strategies that deliver it. It is the bridge between the diagnosis of Chapter 2 and the objectives and actions of Chapters 5 and 6. Table 3-16. Archetype-to-leverage map
Archetype (cluster; rated accurate) | Structure that produces the problem | Leverage levels | CLP | TOWS response
Fixes that Fail (OS; 96%) | Quick fixes, such as incentives without capacity milestones, relieve pressure and then recreate the problem | L5 performance-linked rules; L6 published delivery data; L3 goals | LP3 | WT-1, ST-2, WO-2
Tragedy of the Commons (F; 99%) | Shared watersheds, forests and fishing grounds are over-used under fragmented governance | L5 Forestry Code and benefit sharing; L4 co-management; L6 resource monitoring | LP5 | SO-2, WT-3
Growth and Underinvestment (T; 95%) | Certification, testing and processing capacity lag demand, so performance erodes | L10 capacity ahead of demand; L9 shorter delays; L7 performance-linked funding | LP1 | SO-1, WO-3, ST-1
Limits to Growth (E; 99%) | Investment growth meets power, logistics and skills ceilings | L10 infrastructure and skills stock; L11 reserve capacity; L9 delivery delays | LP2 | WO-1, WO-2, WT-2

passages.title: B.2 From Archetypes to Leverage Points
passages.text:
Success to the Successful (C; 99%) | Early advantages draw more resources to the connected mainland | L5 allocation floor; L3 provincial equity goals; L10 island links | LP3, LP2 | SO-3, WT-4
Shifting the Burden (Fi; 96%) | Ad hoc or conventional finance meets immediate needs and delays Islamic finance capacity | L4 new providers and products; L5 enabling regulation | LP4 | WO-4
Drifting Goals (OS; 99%) | Persistent gaps create pressure to lower targets | L3 protected goals; L6 transparent variance reporting | LP3 | WT-1, WT-4
Escalation (OS; 96%) | Provinces, groups or agencies match each other's claims, draining resources | L2 shared superordinate goals; L5 formula-based allocation; L8 de-escalation | LP3 | ST-3, WT-4
Big Man (OS; 99%) | Reliance on individual authority makes delivery fragile when leaders change | L2 "power with" governance; L5 merit and transparent procurement; L6 open budget data | LP3 | WT-1, WT-4
Accuracy = share of respondents rating the archetype "very" or "somewhat" accurate; 63–74 valid answers per archetype. Big Man had the strongest endorsement of any archetype (62 percent "very accurately"). Sources: BIRD Validation Survey (2026); BIRD systems map (Silva, 2026).

passages.title: Activating leverage points
passages.text:
The archetype map shows a clear pattern. Four levels recur across almost every archetype: L10 (building the stock of physical and human capacity), L6 (making performance visible), L5 (changing the rules that shape behaviour) and L3 (protecting the goals). BARMM's past interventions have concentrated on L12 and L10, through budget amounts, incentive rates and infrastructure projects. These remain necessary, but without the design and intent levels they are vulnerable to Fixes that Fail and Drifting Goals. IEDS therefore pairs every major capital programme with a rule, an information flow and a goal that protect it.
Design principle. No major investment without its protecting rule. For example: a processing facility (L10) is paired with an accreditation pathway (L5) and published certification times (L6); an energy interconnection (L10) with a tariff and dispatch arrangement (L5) and a reliability dashboard (L6); a provincial allocation (L12) with an equity floor (L5) and a provincial disparity indicator (L3, L6).

passages.title: B.3 The Five Critical Leverage Points
passages.text:
The archetype map converges on five Critical Leverage Points (CLPs). They are the points where intervention changes the behaviour of the whole BEIE system, and they are used throughout Chapters 4 to 7: as badges on the headline KPIs, as anchors of the BSC causal pathways and as the organising logic for the policy recommendations. Table 3-17. Critical Leverage Points: definition, depth and links to later chapters
CLP | What changes | Dominant Meadows levels | Archetypes weakened | Links to Chapters 5–7
LP1 Halal certification integrity | Accepted, traceable certification that opens export markets; testing and certifier capacity built ahead of demand | L5, L6, L10 | Growth and Underinvestment | BSC Pathway 1 (halal value chain); Chapter 7, A4 and C2
LP2 Infrastructure, energy and human capital | Power, logistics, connectivity and skills that raise the growth ceiling | L10, L9, L11 | Limits to Growth | Pathway 2 (infrastructure-enabled growth); Chapter 7, B2–B3
LP3 Governance and investor confidence | One facilitation network, published service standards, protected goals and equitable allocation | L6, L5, L3, L2 | Fixes that Fail; Drifting Goals; Escalation; Big Man; Success to the Successful | Pathway 2; Chapter 7, A1–A3 and D1–D3

passages.title: B.3 The Five Critical Leverage Points
passages.text:
LP4 Islamic finance ecosystem | New Shariah-compliant providers, products and financial capability for MSMEs and projects | L4, L5 | Shifting the Burden | Pathways 4–5 (inclusive development; Islamic finance); Chapter 7, C3
LP5 Green economy revenue | Lawful, safeguarded revenue from PES, renewable energy and eligible carbon instruments | L5, L4, L6 | Tragedy of the Commons | Pathway 3 (green economy); Chapter 7, A1 and A4
Sources: BIRD systems map and CLP register (Silva, 2026); Chapter 5, Section F.2; Chapter 7. LP3 stands apart: it weakens five of the nine archetypes, and it is the leverage point on which the others depend, because certification, infrastructure delivery, finance and green revenue all require agencies to coordinate, publish and keep their commitments. This is consistent with what respondents said: asked who should lead stakeholder alignment, 40 of 65 named the Bangsamoro Government through BoI-MTIT and a further 18 named all stakeholders equally through BIF-Net. Stakeholders also identified inclusive development as the strongest causal pathway (25 of 69), ahead of infrastructure-enabled growth (16) and the halal economy (14).

passages.title: B.4 Prescription: Front-Loading the Ecosystem Enablers
passages.text:
The first prescription addresses the Limits to Growth and Growth and Underinvestment archetypes. BARMM's growth has repeatedly stalled not for want of opportunity or investor interest, but because power, logistics, certification and skills could not support production at scale. The prescription is to raise capacity ahead of demand, so that the ceiling moves before growth reaches it. Respondents agreed that capacity traps are a real constraint (mean 3.99 of 5; 74.0 percent agree). Table 3-18. Why the weakest link sets the pace: cluster readiness and system throughput
Stage in the value chain | Readiness (1–5) | As share of 5 | Cumulative throughput
C1 Foundations | 3.45 | 69.0% | 69.0%
C3 Enablers (binding) | 3.33 | 66.6% | 46.0%
C2 Transformers | 3.40 | 68.0% | 31.2%
C4 Connectors | 3.61 | 72.2% | 22.6%
C5 Financiers | 3.55 | 71.0% | 16.0%
Operating systems (applied to the chain) | 3.58 | 71.6% | 11.5%
Readiness is an indicative stakeholder rating, not an econometric estimate. Source: Chapter 2, Table 2-16; BIRD Validation Survey (2026). Two enabler tracks run in parallel from Phase 1.

passages.title: B.4 Prescription: Front-Loading the Ecosystem Enablers
passages.text: The hardware track (L10, L11) covers energy interconnection and renewable mini-grids, including completion of the Zamboanga–Basilan Interconnection Project; farm-to-market roads in the production corridors of Maguindanao del Sur, the SGA and Lanao del Sur; port and island logistics for Tawi-Tawi and Basilan; cold-chain nodes; and digital connectivity under the Bangsamoro e-Governance Master Plan (MICT, 2025). The software track (L9, L10) covers functional literacy and industry-aligned technical and vocational training; certifiers, laboratory analysts and investment-facilitation officers recruited and trained before demand peaks; and shorter preparation and approval times for priority projects. The test for every Phase 1 project is not only whether it is worthwhile in itself, but which downstream investment it unlocks. Basilan illustrates the point: improved power supply and the province's declaration as free of the Abu Sayyaf Group change what its 48,366 hectares of rubber can support, from raw cup-lump sales towards processing and rubber-wood products, but only if processing, logistics and skills follow in the same sequence.

passages.title: B.5 Prescription: Going Below the Waterline and Architecting Collaborative Governance
passages.text:
The second prescription works at the deeper levels of the hierarchy. The iceberg model distinguishes visible events from the patterns, structures and mental models beneath them; intervening only at the level of events produces short-term fixes (Senge, 1990). Respondents strongly endorsed this framing (mean 4.26 of 5; 85.1 percent agree), and agreed that collaborative governance is essential to the roadmap (4.08; 80.6 percent). Table 3-19. Interventions at each level of the iceberg
Level | What it looks like in BARMM | IEDS response
Events | Approvals announced; budget releases; individual projects launched or delayed | Track realised investment, not only approvals; report physical as well as financial progress (L12, L6)
Patterns | Approvals rising faster than realised investment; execution below target; recurring delays at the same agencies | Variance triggers and corrective plans; quarterly cluster reviews (L8, L6)
Structures | Overlapping mandates; fragmented data; ad hoc allocation; capacity gaps in new municipalities in the SGA | One facilitation network and register; cluster councils; formula-based allocation with an equity floor (L5, L4)

passages.title: B.5 Prescription: Going Below the Waterline and Architecting Collaborative Governance
passages.text:
Mental models | Zero-sum competition for resources; value seen in raw commodities rather than processing; development equated with external funding; authority vested in individuals rather than institutions | Shared regional goals through inter-provincial compacts; stewardship ( khalifa ) and moral governance as operating principles; "power with" rather than "power over" (L3, L2)
Collaborative governance resolves three governance traps together. Big Man dynamics are weakened by institutionalising decisions: merit-based appointments, transparent procurement and open budget data (L5, L6), and by a shift from authority exercised over others to authority exercised with them (L2). Escalation is weakened by shared superordinate goals, such as the halal hub and BIMP-EAGA integration, that make cooperation between provinces more valuable than competition (L2), and by transparent, formula-based allocation (L5). Success to the Successful is weakened by explicit equity goals and a proposed allocation floor for lagging and island areas, subject to legal design (L3, L5; Chapter 7, B3).

passages.text:
No single leverage point resolves every archetype, and no single province faces the same mix. Table 3-20 shows which CLP carries the primary and supporting response to each archetype; Table 3-21 translates the analysis into Phase 1 entry points by territory.

passages.text:
Table 3-21. Leverage-point priorities by territory: Phase 1 entry points
Territory | Dominant constraint (Chapter 2) | Priority archetype | Priority CLP | Phase 1 entry intervention
MDN Maguindanao del Norte | Largest economy; risk of drawing a disproportionate share of resources | Success to the Successful | LP3, LP1 | Halal Park and Polloc as regional platforms with supplier links to other provinces; publish provincial investment distribution

passages.title: Strategic Alignment with the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy
passages.text: The Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy (IEDS), recommended in Chapter 3, operationalizes a synchronized, cluster-integrated investment pathway that treats economic growth as a function of interdependent systems rather than isolated sectoral outputs. Consequently, the metrics and Key Performance Indicator (KPI) framework for the Bangsamoro Investment Roadmap Development (BIRD) 2026–2035 must transcend traditional siloed monitoring. It must measure cross-cluster synchronization , governance operating system health , and the conversion of foundational endowments into export-ready, culturally authentic, and environmentally sustainable value (Silva, 2026; Kaplan & Norton, 1992). This chapter establishes a calibrated, evidence-based benchmarking architecture anchored in BARMM's master plans, regulatory frameworks, and international standards. Each KPI is phased to align with the IEDS implementation timeline: Phase 1: Foundation Building (2026–2028) , Phase 2: Acceleration (2029–2031) , and Phase 3: Consolidation and Global Integration (2032–2035) . The framework ensures that progress is measurable, comparable, and adaptive, enabling policymakers, development planners, and investors to track systemic transformation rather than incremental activity.

passages.title: Strategic Alignment with the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy
passages.text: For continuity with the draft series, many tables retain 2030 as an interim checkpoint; the formal end-of-phase gates are 2028, 2031 and 2035. Where a 2031 value is not yet defined, it must be calibrated and approved rather than interpolated silently. The KPI framework is designed to feed directly into the Balanced Scorecard (Chapter 5), which organizes metrics across four causal perspectives: Financial, Stakeholder, Internal Process, and Learning & Growth. This chapter provides the what and how much of measurement; Chapter 5 provides the why and so what by linking each KPI to strategic objectives and causal pathways. Together, Chapters 4 and 5 form the measurement and management engine of the BIRD 2026–2035 (Kaplan & Norton, 1996; Silva, 2026). Measurement Integrity and Data Contract. The KPI layer should be read together with the consolidated Chapter 2 diagnostic and Chapter 3 strategy architecture. The latest linked validation snapshot contains 76 consented survey responses, while the live analytics contract is analyticsVersion 2 . Survey-derived SWOT diagnostics use the repository's canonical formulas: Strength RI = (Impact × Likelihood) / 5; Opportunity RI = √(Impact × Likelihood); Weakness Risk = Impact × Likelihood; and Threat VI = (Impact² × Likelihood) / 25. Missing SWOT families are treated as missing observations, not as zero scores.

passages.title: Strategic Alignment with the Integrated Ecosystem Development Strategy
passages.text: These diagnostics support prioritisation and learning; they do not, by themselves, constitute official administrative baselines or future targets. All numerical baselines, including values labelled “approximately”, “estimated”, “less than”, “not measured” or “baseline”, remain provisional until the named data owner confirms the source, reference period, method, geography and revisions. A target is a planning proposition until formally approved by the responsible authority. Beyond Checklists: The Capabilities-Based Approach. Conventional ESG and development monitoring relies on checklists — counting activities completed rather than capabilities built. The BIRD KPI framework, informed by capabilities-based thinking (Beyond ESG, 2025), measures not whether a training was conducted but whether functional literacy improved; not whether a road was built but whether logistics costs declined; not whether a halal certificate was issued but whether export revenue grew. This shift from output metrics to outcome metrics is essential for tracking genuine ecosystem transformation.

passages.title: KPI Architecture and Calibration Methodology
passages.text: The KPI register is calibrated against the IEDS sequence and organised by indicator definition, unit, source owner, reference period, disaggregation, reporting frequency, verification status and phase milestone. SMART criteria are applied alongside data-quality and feasibility tests. The source draft proposes three portfolio dimensions—cross-cutting operating-system metrics (30%), cluster-specific metrics (45%) and benchmark alignment (25%). These percentages are proposed management weights, not externally validated measures of causal contribution. They may be used for a composite only after each constituent indicator has a documented direction of improvement, normalisation rule, missing-data policy and approval record. Until then, dashboards should show raw indicators and their status separately.

passages.title: B.1 Four Calibration Tiers
passages.text:
KPI Calibration and Phasing Architecture
Calibration Tier | Time Horizon | Strategic Focus | Strategy Phase Alignment | Data Verification Mechanism

Phase 1 gate | 2028 | Baseline confirmation, governance foundations, enabler deployment and readiness review | Phase 1: Foundation Building (2026–2028) | Approved definitions; source-owner-verified administrative records; audit and project-readiness evidence
Phase 2 gate | 2031 (2030 retained as interim checkpoint) | Value-chain acceleration, scale-up, export readiness and financing mobilisation | Phase 2: Acceleration (2029–2031) | Source-owner-verified administrative, sector, finance and outcome series; project-readiness and safeguards review

passages.title: B.1a KPI Calculation and Dashboard Metric Dictionary
passages.text:
Every indicator displayed in a MEL dashboard or Balanced Scorecard (BSC) perspective must have a version-controlled metric specification. The table below defines the common calculations; indicator-specific numerator, denominator, unit, disaggregation and exclusions must be recorded in the KPI register before publication. Table 4-1a. Standard calculation rules for MEL dashboards and the BSC
Metric / BSC use | Calculation | Interpretation and control
Percentage / rate | (Eligible cases meeting the stated condition ÷ all eligible cases in the defined population and period) × 100 | Publish numerator, denominator, population, reference period and exclusions. Never treat missing records as zero. Annual investment approvals (₱) | Sum of the approved value of distinct projects formally approved during the reporting year | Separate approvals from commitments, actual capital expenditure, disbursements and operational projects. Deduplicate projects; disclose whether cancelled or amended approvals are netted off. GRDP and GRDP growth | GRDP is the official PSA series; annual growth = ((current-year GRDP ÷ previous-year GRDP) − 1) × 100 | Use the same price basis and published vintage across comparisons. Do not splice current-price and constant-price series or treat planning targets as observed data.

passages.title: B.1a KPI Calculation and Dashboard Metric Dictionary
passages.text: Exports / product or sector value | Sum the value of eligible exports within the defined product, origin, destination and reporting-period scope | Record currency, valuation basis, product classification, data owner and revision date. Avoid adding subcategories already included in total exports. Count / cumulative reach | Count unique eligible entities or people meeting the indicator definition by the cut-off date | Use persistent IDs and deduplication. Distinguish annual flow from active stock, cumulative reach and currently active entities. Completion / execution rate | For budget execution: eligible expenditure ÷ approved allotment or other explicitly chosen official denominator × 100. For physical completion: independently verified completed units ÷ planned units × 100. | Do not combine financial execution with physical delivery. Define denominator, cut-off date, treatment of variations and source system. Average processing time | Sum of elapsed calendar or working days for completed eligible cases ÷ number of completed eligible cases | State whether calendar or working days; publish median and percentile values where feasible; disclose open cases and paused-clock rules.

passages.title: B.1a KPI Calculation and Dashboard Metric Dictionary
passages.text: Survey / satisfaction score | Documented scoring rule applied to valid responses; publish valid n, scale, question wording, weighting and uncertainty where appropriate | Survey diagnostics are not administrative baselines. A consented sample of 76 responses does not automatically represent the whole investor or business population. Provincial disparity (percentage-point spread) | Maximum provincial value − minimum provincial value for the same indicator, year and method | Use a consistent geography and population. Show province-level values and missing geographies; do not use percentage change when the intended measure is a percentage-point spread. Composite BSC / portfolio score | Only after approval: weighted sum of directionally aligned, normalised and quality-checked indicator scores, using the approved weights and coverage rules | Publish normalisation method, bounds, weights, indicator coverage, treatment of missing values and sensitivity checks. Do not silently redistribute weights when data are missing. Target achievement / gap to target | For a higher-is-better indicator: actual ÷ target × 100. For a lower-is-better indicator: target ÷ actual × 100, where meaningful and actual is non-zero. | Use only for compatible units and periods. For zero, negative, bounded or non-ratio metrics, show the absolute gap or a purpose-designed rule instead. Measurement contract.

passages.title: B.1a KPI Calculation and Dashboard Metric Dictionary
passages.text: Each KPI record must include: unique ID; definition; formula; unit; direction of improvement; baseline value and year; source owner; source document or dataset; collection frequency; reporting cut-off; disaggregation; validation status; 2028, 2031 and 2035 phase-gate values where approved; data-quality flag; revision history; responsible officer; and approval authority. The 2030 value may be retained for comparison with the original planning series, but it does not replace the formal Phase 2 end-point of 2031. The calibration architecture ensures that KPIs remain responsive to IEDS synchronization requirements. Cross-cluster metrics are prioritized to prevent siloed progress from masking systemic bottlenecks. For example, tracking halal certification processing speed (Transformers cluster) in isolation would miss its direct influence on export volume (Connectors cluster) and investor retention (Stakeholder perspective). The framework explicitly maps these interdependencies, ensuring that lagging indicators in one cluster trigger diagnostic attention in connected clusters (Silva, 2026).

passages.title: B.2 The Six Pareto KPIs
passages.text:
For executive monitoring, the BIRD framework uses six Pareto-style headline KPIs as a compact management shortlist. They should not be interpreted as a statistically established claim that exactly 80% of IEDS impact is caused by six variables; they provide a high-signal navigation layer that complements the full KPI register. These KPIs are tracked in real-time through the BIF-Net/MEL dashboard (proposed operating model) and serve as the primary navigational instruments for strategy execution. Each Pareto KPI is linked to specific Leverage Points (LP1-LP5) and Systems Archetypes, enabling rapid identification of intervention points when deviations occur (Silva, 2026). Six Pareto KPIs — Strat Planner Pro MEL Dashboard Tracking
# | KPI | Baseline | 2028 Gate | 2030 Checkpoint | 2035 Target | Primary CLPs | Data Source
1 | Annual Investment Approvals (₱B) | ₱5.0B (2025) | ₱6.5B | ₱10B | ₱15B+ | LP1 + LP3 | MTIT–Bureau of Investments administrative investment-approval records (subject to source-owner verification)
2 | BARMM GRDP (₱B, five provinces) | ₱266.59B (2025) | ₱331B | ₱383B | ₱550B+ | LP1 + LP2 | PSA-BARMM quarterly
3 | Total Export Value (₱B) | <₱10B | ₱20B | ₱26B | ₱40B+ | LP1 | PSA-BARMM trade data
4 | Halal-Certified MSMEs | ~500 | 1,500 | 3,000 | 5,000+ | LP1 | BHB certification logs

passages.title: B.2 The Six Pareto KPIs
passages.text:
5 | Electrification Rate (%) | Baseline requires source-owner verification | Proposed milestone; confirm after baseline | Proposed milestone; confirm after baseline | Proposed milestone; confirm after baseline | LP2 | DOE/MPW field data
6 | Broadband Connectivity (%) | <30% | 58% | 70% | 85% | LP2 | DICT/MICT surveys
How the six headline KPIs are calculated. (1) Annual investment approvals = sum of the formally approved values of distinct projects recorded within the reporting year; not disbursement or realised investment. (2) GRDP = the published PSA series, with annual growth calculated as (current-year ÷ previous-year − 1) × 100 using the same price basis. (3) Total exports = sum of eligible export values for the defined regional/product scope and period, with the data owner and valuation basis recorded. (4) Halal-certified MSMEs = unique MSMEs holding a valid certificate on the cut-off date; distinguish active certificates from cumulative certifications. (5) Household electrification rate = households with electricity access ÷ total eligible households × 100, using the same household definition and geography. (6) Broadband connectivity = eligible households, premises or population with the defined quality threshold of broadband access ÷ the corresponding total eligible denominator × 100. The dashboard must not mix household, premises and population denominators.

passages.title: B.2 The Six Pareto KPIs
passages.text:
To prevent the "Fixes that Fail" systems archetype, the BIRD framework employs adaptive recalibration: incentives and resource releases are conditional on enabler capacity meeting production demand thresholds. If a KPI deviates >15% from its approved trajectory, the following protocol activates: Step 1: Alert through the dashboard only after the relevant data connector and notification rule have been tested. Step 2: Cross-cluster diagnostic — is the deviation caused by internal cluster failure or upstream/downstream dependency?
Step 3: Leverage-point diagnosis — which of the five CLPs and relevant BSC objectives addresses the root cause?
Step 4: Trigger-based intervention — recommend resequencing, corrective action or escalation to the legally responsible decision-maker; funding changes require the applicable approval process.

passages.title: Cross-Cutting Operating Systems Metrics
passages.text: The IEDS positions Moral Governance, Resilience, Inclusivity, and Peace as the operational backbone of economic transformation. KPIs in this dimension measure institutional health, adaptive capacity, equitable participation, and security-investment alignment. The draft assigns these cross-cutting metrics a proposed 30% portfolio weight because they function as systemic multipliers — improvements in governance transparency, climate resilience, social inclusion, and peace directly amplify performance across all five BEIE clusters (Silva, 2026; OCM-BARMM, 2020).

passages.title: C.1 Moral Governance
passages.text:
Moral Governance, anchored in the Bangsamoro Moral Governance Framework 2020-2035 (OCM-BARMM, 2020), is the operating system that determines whether all other clusters function effectively. The framework operationalizes Islamic ethics (khalifa stewardship), transparency, and accountability as foundational governance principles. KPIs in this dimension track the institutionalization of these principles across BARMM government operations (Silva, 2026). Moral Governance KPIs and Master Plan Anchors
KPI | Baseline (2024) | 2028 Gate | 2030 Checkpoint | 2035 Target | Lead Agency | Policy Anchor
Public financial disclosure compliance rate | ~65% (est.) | 80% | 95% | 100% | OCM-BARMM | BMGF 2020-2035
Investor ombudsman operationalisation | Not established | Established | Fully functional | 8.0+/10 satisfaction | MTIT–Bureau of Investments | BIC; BEGMP 2025–2030
Digital procurement and licensing adoption | <30% | 70% | 90% | 100% | MFBM / DICT | BEGMP 2025–2030
Budget execution rate | <80% | 85% | 88% | >90% | MFBM | BDP 2023–2028
Inter-agency coordination score | ~5.5/10 | 6.5/10 | 7.5/10 | 8/10 | BDP / Bangsamoro Corp | BDP / MOA framework
The budget execution rate KPI is particularly critical because it captures the absorptive capacity constraint that has historically undermined BARMM's development.

passages.title: C.1 Moral Governance
passages.text: At less than 80% execution, BARMM effectively leaves 20%+ of allocated funds unspent — a pattern that constitutes both fiscal waste and lost development opportunity. The 2035 target of >90% requires systematic reform of procurement processes, human resource deployment, and inter-agency coordination. Provincial variation is significant: Maguindanao del Norte (administrative centre) likely exceeds 85% execution, while the SGA (8 newly created municipalities) may execute below 60% due to capacity constraints. The BEGMP digital platform provides real-time tracking of budget execution at provincial and municipal levels, enabling targeted capacity-building interventions (MFBM, 2025; BDP, 2023).

passages.title: C.2 Resilience
passages.text:
Resilience metrics capture BARMM's capacity to absorb, adapt to, and recover from climate shocks, economic disruptions, and security incidents. The climate resilience dimension is particularly urgent: El Nino-induced crop losses of ₱346 million in Maguindanao del Sur (2024) and Pestalotiopsis disease infestation of 800+ hectares of rubber plantations demonstrate the vulnerability of the agricultural base that supports 32.4% of BARMM's GRDP (MENRE-BARMM, 2024; PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2025). Resilience KPIs and Policy Anchors
KPI | Baseline (2024) | 2028 Gate | 2030 Checkpoint | 2035 Target | Lead Agency | Policy Anchor
Climate-risk screening coverage for major projects | 0% | 60% | 85% | 100% | MENRE | Climate Resilience Master Plan 2024–2035
Regional resilience index operationalisation | Not developed | Pilot deployed | Fully integrated | standardised reporting | MENRE / BPDA | Food, Water & Energy Security Framework 2025–2035
Early warning system coverage (provinces) | 2 (est.) | 4 | 5 | Coverage of all currently applicable and formally recognised jurisdictions (verify denominator) | MENRE / OCD | Climate Resilience Master Plan
Climate-takaful products deployed | 0 | 2 | 5 | 10+ | MFBM / Al-Amanah | Climate Resilience Master Plan
Provincial Resilience Insight: The resilience KPIs must be disaggregated by province because climate vulnerability varies dramatically.

passages.title: C.2 Resilience
passages.text: Tawi-Tawi faces sea-level rise threatening 50,000+ seaweed livelihoods; Maguindanao del Sur faces El Nino crop losses (₱346M in 2024); Basilan faces rubber Pestalotiopsis disease (800+ ha); and Lanao del Sur faces Lake Lanao watershed degradation affecting 340 sq km of water resources. A single regional resilience score would mask these distinct vulnerability profiles. The MENRE-BARMM Climate Resilience Master Plan (2024–2035) provides province-specific risk assessments that should inform disaggregated KPI targets.

passages.title: C.3 Inclusivity
passages.text:
Inclusivity metrics ensure that economic growth translates into equitable benefit distribution across provinces, genders, age groups, and marginalized communities. With poverty incidence among families at 34.8% in the first semester of 2023 (23.5% on the full-year measure, still among the highest of all regions), the lowest basic literacy of any region (81.0%) and functional literacy of 64.7% against 70.8% nationally (PSA, 2025), and significant provincial disparities (Maguindanao del Sur at 53% vs. Lanao del Sur at 31.5%), inclusivity is not merely a social objective but an economic imperative — inclusive growth generates larger markets, more productive workforces, and more stable communities (PSA, 2024; PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2024). passages.title: C.3 Inclusivity
passages.text:

passages.title: C.4 Peace and Security
passages.text:
Peace and security metrics capture the intersection of conflict dynamics and investment climate. BARMM's post-conflict context — including Basilan's ASG-free declaration (June 2024), the Marawi rehabilitation (₱15B+), and ongoing normalization of former combatants — requires KPIs that track both security outcomes and their translation into investor confidence (OPAPRU, 2024; PIA, 2025). KPI | Baseline (2024) | 2028 Gate | 2030 Checkpoint | 2035 Target | Lead Agency | Policy Anchor

passages.title: C.4 Peace and Security
passages.text: Investor perception may be tested as a leading indicator of investment approvals, but a 6–12 month lag and any correlation coefficients must not be treated as established until the underlying dataset, sample, instrument, period and statistical method are documented and independently reproduced. The latest linked validation survey contains 76 consented responses under analyticsVersion 2; that diagnostic sample alone does not establish official investor satisfaction or validate causal effects. Chapter 5 therefore treats pathways from process quality and peace-and-security conditions to investment outcomes as hypotheses for repeated measurement, not as proven causal relationships.

passages.title: Cluster-Specific Performance Indicators
passages.text: Cluster KPIs are calibrated to measure throughput, value addition, market access, and financial channeling. Each indicator is explicitly linked to IEDS synchronization requirements and master plan milestones. The draft assigns these metrics a proposed 45% portfolio weight and are organized around the five BEIE clusters: Foundations (agriculture, fisheries, forestry, energy, environment), Transformers (industry, manufacturing, logistics, halal, tourism, MSMEs), Enablers (infrastructure, digital, health, education, human capital), Connectors (trade, exports, BIMP-EAGA, digital trade), and Financiers (Islamic banking, takaful, microfinance, waqf) (Silva, 2026).

passages.title: D.1 Foundations Cluster
passages.text:
The Foundations Cluster captures BARMM's natural resource endowments — agriculture (32.4% of GRDP), fisheries, forestry, and renewable energy (75.86% mix). KPIs in this cluster measure productivity gains, post-harvest loss reduction, cooperative strengthening, renewable energy expansion, and environmental conservation. Provincial data integration is essential because each province specializes in different commodities: Basilan (rubber, 48,366 ha, 69,392 MT), Tawi-Tawi (seaweed, 40% national output), Lanao del Sur (pineapple, corn, Lake Lanao fisheries), and Maguindanao del Sur (rice, corn, coconut) (PSA-RSSO BARMM, 2024; MAFAR, 2025). The post-harvest loss reduction KPI illustrates the cross-cluster dependency that the BIRD framework captures: reducing losses from 20-40% to 30%+ requires cold chain infrastructure (Enablers cluster), cooperative organisation (Foundations cluster), and market linkages (Connectors cluster). Basilan's 69,392 MT rubber production currently loses an estimated 25-30% value between harvest and export due to lack of processing facilities — a loss of approximately ₱400M annually that could be captured through halal-certified rubber goods manufacturing if the Transformers cluster develops concurrently (MAFAR, 2025; MTIT-BARMM, 2025).

passages.title: D.2 Transformers Cluster
passages.text:
The Transformers Cluster measures value addition, manufacturing, and market-readiness across halal industry, tourism, MSME development, and ecozone operations. This cluster is where BARMM's foundational endowments are converted into export-ready products and services. KPIs track halal certification expansion, export value growth, tourism development, MSME formalization, and industrial locator performance (MTIT-BARMM, 2025; BEZA, 2025). passages.title: D.2 Transformers Cluster
passages.text: The halal-certified MSME trajectory — from ~500 (2024) to 5,000+ (2035) — is the single highest-leverage Transformers KPI because each certified MSME represents: (a) a micro-enterprise with formal market access, (b) a household with increased income, (c) a node in the halal value chain, and (d) a data point in the BHB certification system. At scale, 5,000+ certified MSMEs create a self-reinforcing ecosystem where certification demand drives BHB capacity, BHB capacity drives certification quality, and certification quality drives export revenue. This is the Investment-Development Virtuous Cycle (R1) identified in Chapter 3-2 (Silva, 2026; BHIDP, 2025).

passages.title: D.3 Enablers Cluster and Human Capital
passages.text:
The Enablers Cluster captures the physical, digital, and human infrastructure that enables all other clusters to function. This is the highest-priority cluster in IEDS Sequence A (2026-2028) because, as the systems mapping in Chapter 3-2 demonstrated, infrastructure and human capital deficits constitute the binding "Limits to Growth" constraints that stall economic transformation. The Enablers KPIs are divided into two sub-dimensions: physical/digital infrastructure and human capital development (BEGMP, 2025; TESDA-BARMM, 2025). Enablers Cluster KPIs and Policy Anchors

passages.title: D.3 Enablers Cluster and Human Capital
passages.text:
The human capital development sub-dimension addresses BARMM's most persistent binding constraint: the lowest basic literacy rate of any region (81.0% against 90.0% nationally) and functional literacy of 64.7% against 70.8% nationally (PSA 2024 FLEMMS). In Tawi-Tawi, functional literacy is only 33.2%. Human capital is the "software" that determines whether physical infrastructure investments generate returns — a road without skilled drivers is underutilized, a processing facility without trained technicians is inefficient, and a digital platform without literate users is empty. The human capital KPIs span employment, education, skills alignment, health access, and digital literacy (PSA, 2024; TESDA-BARMM, 2025; MOLE, 2025). passages.title: D.3 Enablers Cluster and Human Capital
passages.text: At 64.7% functional literacy, and with the lowest basic literacy of any region, BARMM cannot fully utilize digital governance platforms (BEGMP), operate complex processing machinery (Transformers), or engage with Islamic financial products (Financiers). The 15.7 percentage point improvement target requires coordinated action across DepEd (basic education), TESDA (technical skills), and MICT (digital literacy) — a cross-agency coordination challenge that the inter-agency coordination score (5.5/10 → 8/10) directly measures.

passages.title: D.4 Connectors Cluster
passages.text:
The Connectors Cluster measures trade facilitation, export readiness, BIMP-EAGA integration, and digital trade infrastructure. This cluster becomes the priority in IEDS Sequence C (2032-2035) because market access is only valuable when production capacity (Transformers) and logistics infrastructure (Enablers) are already in place. Premature focus on Connectors without adequate Foundations, Transformers, and Enablers creates "empty corridors" — trade routes with insufficient volume to justify their cost (BIMP-EAGA, 2024; MTIT-BARMM, 2025).

passages.title: D.5 Financiers Cluster
passages.text:
The Financiers Cluster measures the depth and reach of Islamic banking, takaful, microfinance, and waqf instruments across BARMM. With Islamic banking assets below ₱2 billion and adult financial inclusion at approximately 38% (vs. national targets of 70%+), the Financiers cluster represents both a significant gap and a transformative opportunity. Islamic finance is uniquely aligned with BARMM's identity — Shariah-compliant instruments provide culturally appropriate financial access for Muslim communities that may avoid conventional banking for religious reasons (IsDB-ICD, 2025; BSP, 2024). General formal financial inclusion and penetration of Shariah-compliant products are distinct measures. Establish and publish separate definitions and source-owner-confirmed baselines before setting numerical targets. Institutions may then report account ownership, active-use rates, geographic access and Shariah-compliant product uptake as separate indicators, avoiding denominator drift.

passages.title: International, National and Regional Benchmark Alignment
passages.text:
To ensure global competitiveness and policy coherence, BIRD KPIs are explicitly calibrated against four external benchmarking frameworks: OIC/SMIIC halal standards, ESG disclosure criteria, the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023–2028, and the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This multi-layer alignment ensures that BARMM's metrics remain investable, auditable, and comparable to ASEAN and OIC member economies — critical for attracting foreign direct investment, accessing ODA and climate finance, and securing halal market recognition (SMIIC, 2021; NEDA, 2023; UNDP, 2023).
