Complete a legally harmonised Investment Code before enactment. Direct MTIT, BBOI, BEZA, BPDA, MFBM and the Office of the Chief Minister to prepare a clean legislative master with one numbering system, consistent definitions, reconciled institutional mandates, and a provision-by-provision legal review. The uploaded draft dated 22 April 2026 contains duplicated or conflicting section numbering, overlapping alternative clauses and incomplete text; these are substantive risks to interpretation, not editorial issues.

passages.title: A.1 Legislative agenda for the first elected Parliament
passages.text: Harmonise the Code with the Bangsamoro Organic Law, Administrative Code and applicable national rules, including RA 12066 (CREATE MORE), without restating or expanding national incentives beyond BARMM’s lawful authority. Specify the RIPP process and how it uses BIRD evidence, while preserving the relevant national SIPP and statutory approval routes. For incentives, define jurisdiction and approval thresholds, eligibility, monitoring of actual performance, fiscal cost-benefit review, due process and legally available suspension/recovery remedies. Owner: MTIT and BBOI with BEZA, BPDA, MFBM and OCM; Parliament to determine the legislative route. Horizon: clean master and legal concordance before refiling; target enactment during the first legislative year, subject to legislative process. Evidence: Chapters 1 and 3 identify the legal anchors and investment-priority logic; Chapter 2 identifies institutional and capacity constraints; Chapter 4 requires measurable results; Chapter 6 requires funded and accountable implementation. The survey’s 44.9% regulatory-priority response is a stakeholder signal, not legal proof.

passages.title: A.2 Resolve council overlap and harmonise the institutional model
passages.text: The draft Investment Code proposes a Bangsamoro Investment Development Council (BIDC), the proposed BIF-Net Executive Order establishes a BIF-Net Council, and Chapter 6 describes a Bangsamoro Investment Command Center (BICC) as an implementation and performance-management hub. Their functions and reporting relationships overlap in the current drafts, creating a risk of duplicate approvals, unclear accountability and competing data systems. The evidence from Chapters 2–3 on institutional bottlenecks and escalation supports resolving this overlap before operationalisation. The final design must be settled through legal review against the Bangsamoro Organic Law, Administrative Code and other applicable laws; an Executive Order must not displace powers that require legislation or are assigned by statute. Resolve institutional overlap and adopt one coordinated operating model. Subject to legal review, use one policy council for cross-government investment coordination, one BIF-Net network for inter-agency facilitation, and one designated Secretariat/operating office within MTIT–BOI for case management, data and aftercare. Determine whether BIDC and the BIF-Net Council should be merged, reconstituted or assigned distinct non-duplicative functions in the Code and EO.

passages.title: A.2 Resolve council overlap and harmonise the institutional model
passages.text: Define the BICC's status as a function or operating unit—not an additional approval body—unless a separate legal basis is established. Preserve BBOI, BEZA, ministry, national-agency and LGU statutory decision rights. Add private-sector and LGU participation with conflict-of-interest, confidentiality and recusal rules. Owner: OCM and MTIT, with legislative counsel and relevant agencies. Horizon: reconcile in the amended EO and Code package before final issuance/enactment.

passages.title: A.3 BIF-Net as ecosystem orchestrator
passages.text:
BIF-Net should act as the facilitation and orchestration layer for the IEDS, not as a new licensing or incentive-granting authority. Consistent with the proposed EO, its core functions are to provide a “No Wrong Door” entry point, maintain a central case registry, assign a lead investment officer, coordinate referrals and parallel processing where lawful, monitor agreed service standards, escalate unresolved inter-agency bottlenecks, and provide investor aftercare. Chapters 5–6 require the same operating system to connect the investment pipeline with the Balanced Scorecard (BSC), Programs–Activities–Projects (PAPs), budgets and MEL. Any cluster councils or coordination forums should be subordinate coordination mechanisms, not additional statutory approval gates. Table 7.5. BEIE cluster councils
Cluster council | Public lead (co-leads) | Agenda focus
Foundations | MAFAR (MENRE, SPDA, MIPA) | Feedstock, land tenure and FPIC, seaweed, rubber, fisheries, renewable supply

Enablers | MPW (MOTC, MENRE-Energy, MHSD, MBHTE, BPDA) | Roads, ports, power, digital, skills; PPP sequencing
Connectors | MTIT and BEZA (MOTC; BIMP-EAGA desk) | Trade facilitation, Polloc Freeport, corridors, tourism circuits
Financiers | MFBM (Darul-Ifta advisory; CSEA;

passages.text:

Operationalise BIF-Net through enforceable coordination protocols and a traceable case-management service. Specify case stages from inquiry and completeness review through agency referrals, registration/incentive decisions by the legally mandated authority, permitting, implementation, closure and aftercare. Give each case a unique reference, named lead officer, participating-agency list, next action, responsible office, applicable statutory timeline and escalation route. Publish service standards for BIF-Net actions—such as acknowledgement, assignment, status updates and escalation—separately from statutory approval periods. The Green Lane may coordinate and expedite processing where permitted by law; it must not waive required permits, consultations, environmental and labour safeguards, taxes, or other legal obligations. Establish privacy, access control, audit-trail, data-sharing, complaints and continuity rules for the digital system. Owner: MTIT–BOI Secretariat with member agencies and LGUs. Horizon: IRR, Rules of Procedure and Green Lane Guidelines before full operation.

passages.title: A.4 Standards, finance and energy institutions
passages.text: Halal assurance (LP1). International buyers do not buy a label; they buy the credibility of the body behind it. Halal certification weakness is rated a 15.65 of 25 risk and standards recognition a 2.77 of 5 threat. The policy priority is institutional: a certification authority (the Bangsamoro Halal Board referred to in Chapter 6) with a statutory basis, an accreditation path aligned with OIC/SMIIC requirements for halal certification bodies, laboratory capacity in Cotabato City and Marawi, and a mutual-recognition sequence that starts with BIMP-EAGA partners and extends to GCC markets as accreditation matures. Put halal assurance on a statutory and accredited footing. Owner: halal certification authority with MTIT and MOST. Horizon: statutory basis and accreditation plan in Phase 1; first mutual-recognition arrangement in Phase 2; SMIIC-aligned recognition by 2035. Islamic finance (LP4). Banking regulation is a national function: the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas licenses and supervises Islamic banks under RA 11439. The Bangsamoro role is to build demand, pipeline, Shariah governance capacity and public-sector use of Islamic instruments. Among respondents, 72.3% consider a coordinating Islamic finance authority essential and a further 18.5% support one once basic banking is strengthened.

passages.title: A.4 Standards, finance and energy institutions
passages.text: Their top actions are financial literacy (29.4%), human capital (23.5%) and regulatory clarity, including tax neutrality (22.1%). Establish a Bangsamoro Islamic finance coordination council. Located in MFBM, with Bangsamoro Darul-Ifta advisory and a working protocol with BSP. Mandate: literacy and talent programmes, a sukuk-ready project pipeline, takaful for climate and agricultural risk, and advocacy on national tax-neutrality rules. It does not license or supervise institutions. Owner: MFBM. Horizon: Phase 1. Energy (LP2). The DOE and MENRE signed a transition agreement in 2026 to devolve power-sector regulation and development functions to MENRE in phases. Devolution creates an opportunity and a capacity risk. Reported electrification also depends heavily on definition: about 40% of potential household connections in BARMM electric cooperative areas (NEA, 2023), against 67.52% of households region-wide at end-2025 in the devolution announcement. Transmission links such as the Zamboanga–Basilan interconnection fall under the grid operator's franchise and ERC regulation, so they require a national interface rather than regional procurement alone. Make energy devolution investable.

passages.title: A.4 Standards, finance and energy institutions
passages.text: Adopt one household-electrification metric for all BIRD reporting; build MENRE's regulatory and planning capacity on a published schedule; prioritise electric cooperative turnaround and island mini-grids; and coordinate transmission projects with NGCP, ERC and DOE through the national interface. Owner: MENRE. Horizon: Phase 1, reviewed annually. Why these are institutional recommendations. Each of A4–A6 strengthens a body that must exist and perform before incentives can work. Granting incentives to halal exporters without a recognised certifier, or to agro-processors without reliable power, would reproduce the Fixes that Fail pattern documented in Chapter 2.

Several official series in circulation still describe the region as it was before that decision, and different documents use different definitions for the same indicator. passages.title: B.1 One set of baselines
passages.text: BPDA, with PSA-RSSO BARMM and each official data owner, should maintain one controlled register with each KPI’s definition, unit, geographic coverage, reference period, price basis where relevant, disaggregation, baseline, target path, source, validation method, update frequency and accountable data owner. Reconcile the five-province geography and include the SGA and Cotabato City where the indicator’s definition supports it. Resolve the GRDP, poverty, population and electrification discrepancies listed in Table 7.6; do not select a value solely because it yields a preferred target. Use Chapter 6’s phase boundaries—2026–2028, 2029–2031 and 2032–2035—consistently across the narrative, dashboard and annual plans. Changes must be versioned with a dated rationale and approved through the legally designated process. Owner: BPDA with PSA-RSSO BARMM, MTIT–BOI and relevant ministries. Horizon: register approved before formal BSC scoring; continue revisions through controlled releases.

passages.title: B.2 Budgeting for delivery, not intention
passages.text: A plan's value is the portion of it that becomes output. Underspending is one of the highest-rated weaknesses in the survey (16.85 of 25), and infrastructure cost overruns are among the highest-rated threats (3.07 of 5). Two budgeting reforms address both. First, tag every budget line that funds a BIRD programme to its BEIE cluster and leverage point, so that the Parliament can see the investment logic in the appropriations. Second, align later-phase releases with verified project readiness, procurement and delivery gates, as Chapter 6 proposes. Any central contingency reserve should be separately justified, costed and authorised through the budget process. The first-year action plan illustrates concentration risk: the chapter’s illustrative budget table assigns ₱2.0 billion of ₱2.063 billion to one transmission project, while the remaining institutional actions are much smaller. These are planning figures that should be reconciled to approved appropriations and current project estimates before execution. Protect critical institutional and project-preparation activities from routine reallocation through lawful budget tagging, readiness gates and transparent variance reporting; do not imply that this chapter can ring-fence funds outside the appropriations process. Link expenditure to readiness, delivery and results.

passages.title: B.2 Budgeting for delivery, not intention
passages.text: Tag BIRD-related budget items by PAP, BEIE cluster and leverage point; connect release decisions to approved appropriations, project readiness, procurement milestones and verified outputs; and report quarterly on obligations, disbursements, physical progress, cost variance and delays. Protect essential institutional and project-preparation work through the formal budget process. Treat the BSC’s >90% execution target as a management target, not a substitute for output verification: high expenditure without output should trigger review. Any 20% contingency reserve or other funding rule must be separately costed, authorised and reflected in the budget. Owner: MFBM with BPDA and implementing agencies. Horizon: 2027 budget cycle onward. Sequence Enablers by the Foundations pipeline they unlock. Prioritise farm-to-market roads, cold chain, port upgrades and power for named agro-processing and fisheries projects, rather than infrastructure in the abstract. Stakeholders favour physical connectivity (58.9%) and market-access assets (32.9%) over digital backbones (8.2%) as the first priority. Owner: MPW and MAFAR through the Enablers council. Horizon: Phase 1 project list by Q3 2027. Close the skills gap with an industry compact. Functional literacy (18.19 of 25) and skills mismatch (16.96) are the top-rated human-capital weaknesses.

passages.title: B.2 Budgeting for delivery, not intention
passages.text: MBHTE's technical-education arm, MOLE and cluster councils agree occupational skills plans tied to the investment pipeline, with employer co-design and placement targets. Owner: MBHTE and MOLE. Horizon: first plans in 2027; annual update. A note on the target. Holding ₱550B as the 2035 GRDP goal is a strategic ambition, but the implied annual growth rate depends on whether the target and base use comparable current-price or constant-price series, geography and rebasing. The current illustrative calculation uses the cited ₱266.59B five-province 2025 base and produces approximately 7.5% annual growth under the stated assumptions; it should not be treated as a verified real-growth requirement until the price basis and official series are confirmed. The register (B1) should publish the reproducible calculation and annual path so that slippage is visible early.

passages.title: B.3 Territorial delivery across the Bangsamoro
passages.text:
One model will not serve a mainland agro-industrial basin, a lake-and-highland province, a freshly organised Special Geographic Area, an administrative city and two island provinces. The territorial units for BIRD are the five provinces of Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Maguindanao del Sur, Basilan (excluding Isabela City) and Tawi-Tawi, together with the Special Geographic Area and Cotabato City. Two boundary facts matter for delivery. Basilan's provincial seat, Isabela City, lies outside BARMM, so BARMM-side delivery in Basilan should run through Lamitan and municipal centres, with a cross-boundary arrangement for port and logistics links through Isabela City and Zamboanga City. Sulu is now outside the region; it is a neighbour and corridor partner, not a delivery territory. Table 7.7. Territorial delivery typology
Unit | Primary role | Binding constraints to address | Delivery node and instrument
Maguindanao del Norte | Halal hub and freeport gateway | Industrial land, power reliability, logistics to Polloc | Polloc Freeport; Matanog Halal Park; BEZA
Maguindanao del Sur | Agro-industrial basin | Flooding, farm-to-market roads, tenure | Provincial node in Buluan; agri-processing clusters
Lanao del Sur | Energy, highland agriculture, Marawi services | Rehabilitation completion, watershed protection | Marawi node; Wao–Amai Manabilang corridor

passages.title: B.3 Territorial delivery across the Bangsamoro
passages.text:
Basilan | Rubber and aquaculture; peace-dividend province | Power interconnection, processing, cross-boundary logistics | Lamitan node; Region IX coordination
Tawi-Tawi | Maritime gateway; seaweed; BIMP-EAGA | Shipping, cold chain, connectivity, island power | Bongao node; seaweed processing; BIMP-EAGA trade facilitation
Special Geographic Area | Mindanao land bridge; new municipalities | Basic services, LGU capacity, tenure | SGA node; LGU investment-readiness support
Cotabato City | Administrative and commercial capital | Urban services, port, flood risk | BIF-Net head office; services and logistics
The survey shows why an explicit rule is needed. Respondents name Maguindanao del Norte as the priority node (53.4%) but judge Tawi-Tawi to hold the most trapped value (61.1%), and 56.2% say Basilan and Tawi-Tawi serve different corridors and deserve equal weight. Left to habit, resources follow existing capacity; that is the Success to the Successful archetype. Implement a transparent, place-based delivery approach. Use provincial diagnostics and documented project readiness to allocate technical assistance, project preparation and enabling infrastructure.

passages.title: B.3 Territorial delivery across the Bangsamoro
passages.text: Prioritise appropriate delivery nodes for Bongao, Lamitan and the SGA, and establish lawful cross-boundary arrangements with Region IX for Basilan’s logistics links, noting that Isabela City is outside BARMM and Sulu is a corridor partner rather than a delivery territory. Chapter 6 proposes a 30% minimum allocation for lagging and island areas; validate the rationale, eligible expenditure base, territorial criteria and fiscal implications before adoption, and implement only through authorised plans and appropriations. Island-province preferences come from the Basilan and Tawi-Tawi provincial workshops rather than the online survey; keep consulting the island provinces in person as delivery nodes are designed. Owner: MTIT–BOI with MILG, BPDA and LGUs. Horizon: Phase 1 framework and pilot nodes, subject to local readiness and funding.

passages.title: C.1 From incentives to investability
passages.text: Incentives alone do not establish investability. A project also needs lawful registration and eligibility, secure site and tenure arrangements, predictable permitting, available infrastructure and power, credible market/offtake, appropriate safeguards, and risks that can be priced. The Code must align any regional incentive provisions with applicable national law and the jurisdiction of the relevant investment promotion agency; the Guidebook must explain actual eligibility rather than advertise incentives as automatic. BARMM's comparative advantages are its halal credibility, its Islamic finance potential and its BIMP-EAGA position. Investment mobilisation should convert these into a pipeline of prepared projects. Establish a project-preparation function and quality-controlled pipeline. Prepare priority projects through pre-feasibility, land/tenure and site due diligence, environmental and social safeguards, climate and conflict sensitivity, market/offtake testing, cost estimates and transaction advice. For every entry, record the sponsor, location, stage, dependencies, approvals required, capital need, financing status, risks and next decision. Use clear statuses—concept, under preparation, feasibility-complete, approval-ready, financing-committed, under construction and operating.

passages.title: C.1 From incentives to investability
passages.text: Do not describe an opportunity as bankable or investment-ready until the evidence and responsible sponsor support that designation. Owner: MTIT–BOI with BPDA, sector agencies, LGUs and development partners. Horizon: facility design by Q4 2027 and an initial prepared-project cohort in 2028, subject to funding and readiness.

passages.title: C.2 Market corridors and standards
passages.text:
Asked where to point the export effort, 52.1% of respondents chose BIMP-EAGA and UAE/GCC markets together, 35.6% BIMP-EAGA first and 12.3% UAE/GCC first. The two corridors have different entry conditions. BIMP-EAGA markets are near, culturally close and reachable with existing products; GCC markets pay more but require recognised standards and reliable logistics. The policy implication is a sequence within a parallel strategy: build volume and traceability in BIMP-EAGA now, while the standards work in A4 opens GCC access.
Run a two-corridor market strategy. Prioritise BIMP-EAGA trade facilitation, Tawi-Tawi and Polloc logistics and buyer-supplier matching in Phase 1; develop GCC access through accredited halal certification and traceability as recognition is secured. Owner: MTIT with BEZA and the Connectors council. Horizon: Phase 1 for BIMP-EAGA; Phase 2 for GCC scale-up.

passages.title: C.3 The capital stack
passages.text: The Roadmap models a ₱120–160 billion public catalytic envelope against a total investment requirement of about ₱0.99–1.13 trillion (ICOR 3.5–4.0 on the five-province gap to ₱550B; Table 7.6), an indicative leverage of about 6–9× each peso of public capital. These figures should be treated as planning assumptions until a costed financing plan and commitments are verified; they are not evidence that funds have been appropriated or that private capital is secured. The Validation Survey indicates stakeholder support for blended finance (87.5%), with preferences for infrastructure-scale instruments (56.3%), MSME access (25.0%) and risk mitigation (18.8%). These are preferences, not proof of bankability. The financing architecture should combine project preparation, clearly allocated public and private risks, development-finance guarantees where available, Shariah-compatible financing, MSME capital and climate/agricultural risk coverage, subject to mandates and market testing. Develop an auditable, blended and Shariah-compatible financing plan. For each priority programme/project, disclose the capital source, instrument, expected timing, financing gap, risk allocation, readiness status and responsible sponsor.

passages.title: C.3 The capital stack
passages.text: Report public appropriations, signed commitments, indicative interest and aspirational mobilisation separately; define how the 6–9× leverage assumption is calculated and avoid counting the same capital twice. Establish first-loss, guarantee, sukuk, MSME-finance or takaful proposals only where a qualified financier and lawful operating arrangement are identified. Owner: MFBM with MTIT–BOI, project sponsors and prospective financing partners. Horizon: financing plan in Phase 1, updated quarterly as commitments change.

passages.title: C.4 Aftercare, retention and reinvestment
passages.text: The cheapest investment to attract is the next one from a firm already operating in the region. Reinvestment depends on how existing investors are treated: whether problems are solved, whether rules are stable and whether the government listens. The Balanced Scorecard target of investor satisfaction at 8.0 of 10 by 2035 has no baseline yet, and the investor information that exists is spread across separate documents and systems. Institutionalise investor aftercare and grievance resolution. Assign a case/account officer for facilitated and registered investors according to risk and service capacity; maintain a confidential channel for complaints and a de-identified systemic-issue log; track response, resolution and recurrence; and record actual versus pledged investment, employment and reinvestment using the proper agency data owner. Establish an investor-satisfaction baseline before claiming progress against the Chapter 5 target of 8.0/10 by 2035. Owner: designated BIF-Net Secretariat with BBOI, BEZA and relevant agencies. Horizon: phased start from 2027, with annual reporting. Rebuild the Investors’ Guidebook as a controlled, investor-facing service product. Publish a version date, content owner, change log and correction channel.

passages.title: C.4 Aftercare, retention and reinvestment
passages.text:
For each investor pathway, state the responsible office, legal basis, eligibility, documents, fees where applicable, official processing time, sequence, referral route and escalation channel. Clearly distinguish statutory processing periods from BIF-Net service standards; explain Green Lane eligibility and the fact that facilitation does not waive legal requirements. Use the canonical baseline register (B1) and label opportunities as concepts, under preparation, finance-ready, approved, under construction or operational—never describe an unverified concept as an approved or bankable project. Owner: MTIT–BOI with BBOI, BEZA and member agencies. Horizon: first controlled digital edition in 2027 and updates when rules or agency procedures change, with a full annual review. Table 7.8. Investment mobilisation measures and the leverage points they serve
Measure | Leverage point | Primary cluster | Headline KPI affected
C1 Project preparation facility | LP2, LP3 | Enablers, Transformers | Annual investment approvals; realised investment
C2 Two-corridor market strategy | LP1 | Connectors | Total exports
C3 Blended capital stack | LP4, LP5 | Financiers | Islamic banking assets; leverage ratio
C4 Aftercare and grievance channel | LP3 | Cross-cutting | Investor satisfaction; reinvestment

passages.title: C.4 Aftercare, retention and reinvestment
passages.text:
C5 Verified investment information | LP3 | Cross-cutting | Investor inquiries converted to registrations
Green economy revenue (LP5). Stakeholders favour pursuing payments for ecosystem services, carbon credits and eco-tourism fees together (53.5%). The binding conditions are legal: the Forestry Code, the JMC and community benefit-sharing rules (A1). Carbon transactions should not proceed ahead of those safeguards, whatever the market timing.

passages.title: D.1 Transition-proofing the roadmap
passages.text:
The first regular Bangsamoro Parliament was elected on 14 September 2026. No party won a majority: the Bangsamoro Federalist Party and the United Bangsamoro Justice Party lead with close seat counts, so the Chief Minister will be elected through coalition (Reuters, 2026). A ten-year roadmap that belongs to one administration will not survive its successor. BIRD's continuity therefore depends on being adopted as a shared framework rather than a partisan programme.
Adopt BIRD as a shared, cross-party investment framework. Present BIRD to the first session for endorsement by resolution; feed it into the next Bangsamoro Development Plan as the investment chapter; and require any change to headline targets to pass through the baseline register and the agreed governance body with a published rationale. Owner: OCM, MTIT and BPDA. Horizon: endorsement within the first parliamentary year.

passages.title: D.2 Learning, evidence and review
passages.text: Respondents prefer quarterly adaptive review (51.4%) over annual review (31.4%). The current evidence base also has known limits. About three-quarters of respondents are government-affiliated, only 11 of 76 (14.5%) are from the private sector, and Cotabato City (27) and Maguindanao del Norte (22) supply most responses. The online survey drew none from Basilan or Tawi-Tawi; island-province findings therefore rest on their provincial workshops (Basilan, 20 June 2026; Tawi-Tawi, 28 October 2026). Run a second validation wave with quotas. In 2027, repeat validation with minimum quotas for the SGA and the private sector, the two groups thinnest in the 2026 evidence, using province-based workshops where online access is weak. Remove response options that refer to territory outside BARMM. Owner: MTIT-BoI with BPDA. Horizon: before the first annual BSC assessment. Apply one evidence and reporting contract across the Roadmap, BIF-Net and investor information. Keep (1) official statistics and administrative records, (2) stakeholder-validation survey results, and (3) management targets, forecasts and financing assumptions visibly separate. Every published indicator should show source, date, geography, definition and status; survey measures should be labelled as perceptions and not administrative baselines.

passages.title: D.2 Learning, evidence and review
passages.text: Link BIF-Net case data and Guidebook content to the controlled register where appropriate, while protecting confidential business information and personal data. Report the conversion chain separately: inquiry → qualified pipeline → registration/approval → permits/facilitation → realised investment → jobs, exports and wider outcomes. Owner: BPDA and MTIT–BOI with official data owners. Horizon: immediate design rule; continuous application.

passages.title: D.3 Systemic risk triggers
passages.text:
Table 7.9. Highest-rated threats and their policy triggers
Threat (VI, 0–5) | Early-warning indicator | Pre-agreed response
Security incidents (3.20) | Incidents in investment zones; investor withdrawals | Activate MPOS investor-security protocol; targeted risk cover through C3
Climate change (3.14) | Flood and drought losses to agriculture and infrastructure | Climate screening for all projects; takaful and contingency release
Infrastructure cost overruns (3.07) | Cost variance >15% on priority projects | Independent review before additional release (B2)
Drifting goals (3.03) | Unlogged target changes; KPI variance >15% for two quarters | Escalation to the agreed governance body; public variance note (B1)
National coordination (2.91) | Pending national permits beyond service standards | Escalation through the national interface and IGRB
Political transition (2.85) | Leadership change; budget reallocation away from tagged lines | Cross-party endorsement (D1); ring-fenced institutional actions (B2)
Trigger governance rule. Thresholds in Table 7.9 are proposed management triggers for review, not automatic legal sanctions or evidence of causation. Each trigger should name the validating data source, accountable reviewer, response authority, review deadline and closure evidence.

passages.title: D.3 Systemic risk triggers
passages.text: For example, a cost variance should first be reconciled to approved scope, inflation, procurement and engineering data before any funding decision; a permit delay should be escalated through the lawful inter-agency route. Adopt the trigger table as part of the MEL protocol , reviewed quarterly by the designated investment coordination body. For each trigger, document the evidence source, validation step, responsible agency, response authority and closure criteria. Owner: BIF-Net Secretariat with BPDA and relevant agencies. Horizon: after adoption of the operating protocol. Publish an annual, evidence-checked BIRD performance report and dashboard. Report KPI baselines and targets, PAP status, budget and physical progress, investment pipeline stages, processing performance, realised investment, outcome indicators and recurring systemic issues. Publish aggregate information only where disclosure is lawful; protect commercially confidential applications, personal data and security-sensitive information. Explain revisions and missed milestones rather than silently changing target paths. Owner: MTIT–BOI and BPDA with data owners. Horizon: first consolidated report in 2027, then annually; quarterly operational updates where data are validated. Survey support for transparency (57.5%) is a stakeholder signal, not a substitute for privacy and disclosure rules.

LP1: standards and certification integrity; LP2: infrastructure, energy and connectivity; LP3: governance, information and investor confidence; LP4: Islamic finance ecosystem; LP5: green-economy revenue and safeguards. LP3 is prominent because Chapters 2–3 identify institutional throughput as a binding constraint. This is a prioritisation judgement supported by the roadmap’s diagnostics, not a claim that other leverage points are dispensable.

passages.title: The first 180 days
passages.text:
The period from the new Parliament's first session to mid-2027 decides whether BIRD becomes the region's investment framework or one document among many. The sequence below asks for decisions, not large budgets.
Table 7.11. Decisions for the first 180 days (November 2026 – April 2027)
Window | Decision | Recommendations
Days 1–30 | Brief the Chief Minister and cabinet; designate the proposed BIF-Net Secretariat/operating office subject to the final EO; agree the legal design for the policy council and operating network. | A2, D1
Days 31–60 | Complete legal review and issue the amended BIF-Net EO if within executive authority; finalise/refile the Investment Code and Forestry Code through the lawful legislative process; execute JMC No. 2026-01 only after required approvals. | A1, A3
Days 61–90 | Start the baseline register with PSA-RSSO; tag the 2027 budget; adopt the trigger table. | B1, B2, D4
Days 91–120 | Stand up the Transformers, Enablers and Financiers councils; open the Bongao and Lamitan nodes; set up aftercare. | A3, B3, C4
Days 121–180 | Launch the second validation wave; scope the project preparation facility; publish the first quarterly dashboard. | C1, D2, D5

passages.title: Policy review calendar to 2035
passages.text:
2027 — Foundation year. Complete legal harmonisation of the Code and BIF-Net instruments; establish the agreed governance arrangement; approve the baseline register; conduct the first annual BSC assessment and publish a validated performance report, subject to legislative and budget processes.
2028 — End of Phase 1. Gate review of Phase 1 deliverables before Phase 2 releases; first prepared projects reach financing; halal accreditation plan in execution.
2030 — Mid-term review. External evaluation; recalibration of targets on rebased data; decision on whether BIF-Net remains a network or becomes an attached agency.
2031 — Second regular Parliament. Renewed cross-party endorsement; SIPP submission for an expanded BARMM list; review of incentive effectiveness.
2035 — Terminal assessment. Evaluation against the Balanced Scorecard; design of the successor roadmap.

passages.title: Closing statement
passages.text:
Rules Institutions Information Delivery capacity Investable projects Capital Jobs and resilience
BIRD 2026–2035 does not ask BARMM to rely on a single sector, one incentive or one administrative body. It recommends a coherent sequence: use the evidence in Chapters 1–2 to identify constraints; apply the IEDS and leverage points in Chapter 3; maintain the calibrated KPIs and baseline discipline in Chapter 4; manage the causal pathways and Balanced Scorecard in Chapter 5; and implement the budgeted PAPs and MEL cycle in Chapter 6. The Investment Code should provide lawful and durable authority; the BIF-Net EO and rules should organise lawful inter-agency facilitation; the Investors’ Guidebook should explain verified requirements and opportunities; and the Roadmap should align all three with territorial priorities, financing and measurable results. This architecture will build investor confidence only if responsibilities are clear, commitments are funded, legal safeguards are respected and performance is reported against verifiable evidence.

passages.title: Basilan Economic and Investment Outlook 2026-2035
passages.text:
Transforming the post-conflict recovery economy into a resilient, export-linked, and inclusive economic hub within BARMM through integrated ecosystem-based development.
Explore the Outlook Investment Opportunities
Overview Macroeconomic BEIE Framework Performance Challenges Recommendations

passages.title: Provincial Overview
passages.text:
Understanding the geographical, demographic, and post-conflict context of Basilan, a province of strategic importance in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.
Evidence status: this outlook was validated in person at the Basilan provincial workshop on 20 June 2026 in Isabela City, part of the BIRD 2026–2035 provincial consultations (Report, Chapter 1, F.4).

passages.title: Geographic Profile
passages.text: Basilan is the largest and northernmost of the major islands in the Sulu Archipelago, with a total land area of approximately 1,134 square kilometers. The province is strategically located just off the southern coast of Zamboanga Peninsula, separated by the Basilan Strait, positioning it as a potential economic spillover zone and logistics gateway between Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago.

passages.title: Demographic Profile
passages.text: The 2024 Census recorded Basilan's population at 541,947, representing a significant increase from previous years. The province's population growth rate has been among the highest in the country, indicating a youthful demographic profile. Basilan is characterized by a diverse ethno-linguistic composition including Yakan, Tausug, Samal, Bajau, and Iranon communities.

passages.title: Post-Conflict Context
passages.text: Basilan was officially declared Abu Sayyaf Group (ASG)-free in June 2024, marking a historic milestone in the peace process. The remaining ASG members surrendered on December 26, 2024. This security improvement has created favorable conditions for economic recovery and development, enabling the normalization of economic activities and the return of displaced families.

passages.title: Macroeconomic Performance
passages.text: Analysis of GDP growth, sectoral composition, and price stability dynamics from 2018 to 2023, highlighting the province's economic resilience and post-conflict recovery.

passages.title: GDP Growth Trajectory (2018-2023)
passages.text:
Basilan's GDP expanded from ₱19.04 billion in 2018 to ₱23.15 billion in 2023 at constant prices, representing a cumulative real increase of approximately 21.6 percent over the five-year period. The province recorded a GDP growth rate of 2.9 percent in 2023, demonstrating economic resilience despite post-conflict challenges and climate-related disruptions.

passages.title: Sectoral Composition & Structural Shift
passages.text: Basilan's economy is structured around three broad sectors: Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries (41%), Services (36%), and Industry (23%). The AFF sector maintains dominance reflecting the province's strong agricultural base, while showing gradual diversification toward services. The Services sector emerged as a key growth driver, expanding from ₱6.41 billion (2018) to ₱8.32 billion (2023).

passages.title: Price Stability & Inflation Dynamics
passages.text: Basilan posted a year-to-date inflation rate that remained well-controlled in 2024–2025. The province recorded an inflation rate of 0.4 percent in December 2025, significantly lower than the 1.2 percent recorded in December 2024. In February 2025, Basilan's inflation rate was at -0.9 percent, the second lowest in BARMM. This low inflation trajectory provides a stable macroeconomic backdrop for investment planning.

passages.title: BARMM Regional Growth (2025)
passages.text: The Bangsamoro regional economy reached ₱266.59 billion in 2025 at constant 2018 prices, recording a 5.0% growth rate—ranking sixth fastest among the Philippines' 18 regions. Health and social services led sectoral growth at 13.9%, followed by education at 12.0% and public administration at 9.6%. Agriculture, forestry, and fishing expanded by 4.9%, reinforcing the region's food security foundations.

passages.title: Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework
passages.text:
Applying the integrated systems model to analyze sectoral interlinkages and identify priority investment corridors in Basilan.
How the BEIE Framework works: The BEIE Framework organizes economic activity into five functional clusters—Foundations, Transformers, Enablers, Connectors, and Financiers—anchored by Moral Governance and driven by four cross-cutting enablers: Tourism and Culture, Peace and Security, Human Capital, and Environmental Sustainability. This systems lens reveals investment opportunities that a conventional sectoral analysis would miss.

passages.title: Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework
passages.text: The BEIE Framework visualizes the interconnected nature of economic clusters in BARMM. Each cluster supports and reinforces the others, creating a holistic ecosystem for sustainable development.

passages.title: Foundations — Agriculture, Fisheries, Forestry & Energy
passages.text:
The resource base on which Basilan's entire economic ecosystem depends. As the largest rubber-producing province in the Philippines, Basilan's AFF sector contributes 41% of GDP.
• Agriculture & Fisheries: Basilan is historically known as the largest rubber-producing province with approximately 48,366 hectares planted to rubber trees. The province produced 69,392 metric tons of rubber in 2024. Coconut/copra and seaweed farming are also major agricultural outputs.
• Energy: The utilities sector has been the most consistent growth driver, expanding 37.8% from 2018 to 2023. The ₱6.67 billion Zamboanga-Basilan Interconnection Project (ZBIP) will connect Basilan to the Mindanao grid.
Investment Opportunities: Rubber plantation rehabilitation and modernization, coconut value chain development, seaweed farming and processing, organic and halal-certified agriculture, solar and biomass energy installations.

passages.title: Transformers — Industrial Development & Agro-Processing
passages.text:
If Foundations provide the raw material, Transformers create the value. Basilan's manufacturing subsector is dominated by agro-processing, particularly rubber and copra processing.
• Rubber Processing: Establishing modern rubber processing plants capable of producing technically specified rubber (TSR), crepe rubber, and latex-based products would capture more value within the province.
• Coconut Processing: Opportunities for integrated processing facilities producing virgin coconut oil (VCO), desiccated coconut, coconut milk/cream, and activated carbon.
Investment Opportunities: Modern rubber processing plants, integrated coconut processing complexes, cold chain and food processing facilities, feed milling and livestock integration.

passages.title: Enablers — Infrastructure, Logistics & Connectivity
passages.text:
No production capability can generate export value without physical infrastructure to move goods. Infrastructure gaps remain among the most cited constraints on investment in Basilan.
• Transport Infrastructure: The Ministry of Public Works readied ₱627 million for Basilan infrastructure projects in 2025. The proposed Basilan-Zamboanga Bridge, projected for completion by 2030, will be transformative.
• Connectivity: A 2.24-kilometer bridge linking Malamawi Island to mainland Isabela City is set to be constructed, enhancing intra-provincial connectivity.
Investment Opportunities: Farm-to-market roads, port and wharf development, warehousing and cold storage, digital infrastructure expansion, water and sanitation systems.

passages.title: Connectors — Trade, Exports & BIMP-EAGA Integration
passages.text:
This cluster links Basilan's production to regional and global markets. Basilan's strategic location positions it as a potential gateway for trade within the BIMP-EAGA corridor.
• Regional Trade: Basilan's proximity to Sabah, Malaysia, and location along maritime trade routes provide opportunities for cross-border trade and investment within the BIMP-EAGA network.
• Domestic Markets: Isabela City contributed 62% of the district's total tax collection in 2024 and ranked 14th among the most competitive component cities in Mindanao in 2024.
Investment Opportunities: Export-oriented agro-processing, halal certification and production, trade facilitation infrastructure, domestic market integration through improved logistics.

passages.title: Financiers — Islamic Banking & Ethical Finance
passages.text:
The Financiers cluster is particularly strategic for Basilan given the province's significant Muslim population and cultural alignment with Islamic finance principles.
• Financial Inclusion: Basilan's financial and insurance subsector grew from ₱50.49 million in 2018 to ₱77.10 million in 2023, but remains significantly underpenetrated relative to the province's economic size.
• Islamic Finance: The expansion of Islamic banking would reduce the barrier to capital access for MSMEs, farmers, and fisherfolk, amplifying the impact of investments across all clusters.
Investment Opportunities: Islamic banking branches, microfinance and cooperative development, agricultural credit and insurance, digital financial services deployment.

passages.title: Cross-Cutting Drivers — Moral Governance, Tourism & Peace
passages.text:
These drivers operate across all clusters and determine the effectiveness of the entire ecosystem.
• Peace and Security: Basilan's declaration as ASG-free in June 2024 marked a historic milestone, creating a favorable environment for investment and development.
• Tourism: The province has significant tourism potential including uncharted forest wilderness, marine sanctuaries, cultural heritage sites, and historical landmarks. Isabela City won the 2024 Tourism Champions Challenge Mindanao Category.
Investment Opportunities: Eco-tourism and adventure tourism, cultural and heritage tourism, halal tourism infrastructure, tourism support services.

passages.title: Investment Climate and Recent Performance
passages.text: Tracking BARMM's investment momentum and highlighting significant projects in Basilan that demonstrate the province's growing attractiveness to investors.

passages.title: BARMM Investment Momentum
passages.text:
BARMM's investment climate has undergone a structural upswing. The Bangsamoro Board of Investments (BBOI) approved ₱5.1 billion worth of investments as of April 2026, creating over 750 jobs in the first quarter alone. This strong performance reflects growing investor confidence in the region's stability and potential.
In 2025, BARMM hit ₱5 billion in investment approvals, surpassing its full-year target in the first quarter, driven by new projects across the region. The BBOI approved ₱1.6 billion worth of investments during its 1st Board Meeting of 2026, creating over 750 jobs. This momentum demonstrates the region's emergence as a viable investment destination.
Philippine Statistics Authority data confirmed that BARMM ranked second in Mindanao in approved investments, behind only the Davao Region, and placed within the top 10 regions nationally for Q2 2025. This regional ranking reflects a structural shift in investor perception—from BARMM as a conflict-affected risk zone to an emerging destination with governance credibility and strong growth fundamentals.

passages.title: Strategic Investment Priority Areas
passages.text: Based on the BEIE Framework analysis, existing investment momentum, and the province's structural endowments, the following priority investment corridors are identified for Basilan through 2035:

passages.title: Priority Investment Corridors
passages.text:
• Rubber Value Chain Development Zone (Mainland Municipalities): Integrated rubber plantation rehabilitation, modern processing facilities, and value-added product manufacturing.
• Coconut Agro-Industrial Corridor (Coastal and Island Municipalities): Coconut processing complexes producing VCO, desiccated coconut, and coir products.
• Seaweed Farming and Processing Belt (Coastal Areas): Expansion of seaweed cultivation and establishment of carrageenan processing facilities.
• Isabela City Commercial and Tourism Hub: Mixed-use commercial development, halal tourism infrastructure, and MSME support facilities.
• Renewable Energy Development Zone: Solar farms, biomass power plants, and mini-grid systems for remote areas.
• Basilan-Zamboanga Bridge Economic Corridor: Logistics hubs, warehousing, and industrial parks along the bridge route.
• Fisheries and Marine Resources Development Zone: Cold chain facilities, fish ports, and marine aquaculture development.

passages.title: Challenges, Risks, and Structural Constraints
passages.text: Identifying the key obstacles and vulnerabilities that must be addressed to realize the investment outlook and ensure sustainable development.

passages.title: Poverty and Human Development
passages.text: Despite significant improvements, poverty remains a defining structural challenge. Basilan recorded a poverty incidence of 33.7 percent in 2023, though this represents improvement from 73.5 percent in 2018 and 53.5 percent in 2021. The province has the highest poverty incidence in BARMM, reflecting the lingering impacts of conflict and limited economic opportunities.

passages.title: Infrastructure Gaps
passages.text: While infrastructure investment is improving, significant gaps remain. Road networks in interior municipalities limit market access for farmers, increase logistics costs, and constrain the viability of agro-industrial investment. Water supply systems in many municipalities remain inadequate. Digital connectivity is uneven, with broadband penetration in rural areas remaining limited.

passages.title: Peace and Security Dynamics
passages.text: Although Basilan has been declared ASG-free, localized armed incidents, clan conflicts (rido), and the residual presence of lawless elements in some municipalities create security risks that investors must assess. The peace dividend is real and measurable, but its sustainability depends on continued progress in the peace process and effective governance.

passages.title: Governance and Institutional Capacity
passages.text: Coordination capacity remains a constraint. The BEIE Framework identifies this as the central challenge: "It's not about launching more programs—it's about aligning existing ones into a coherent system." Inter-agency coordination between MAFAR, SPDA, MPW, MTIT, BBOI, and local governments is essential for synchronized development.

passages.title: Climate Vulnerability
passages.text: El Niño-induced drought and flooding have caused significant agricultural losses in Basilan. In 2023, the province faced flooding that impacted agricultural production, while rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns pose long-term risks to rubber and coconut production. Climate adaptation measures are critical.

passages.title: Investment Perception Risks
passages.text: The historical conflict legacy may deter cautious investors despite significant recent improvements in stability and governance. Residual negative reputation can activate the Security-Investment Tensions balancing loop, requiring proactive efforts to communicate the province's new reality and investment potential.

passages.title: Strategic Outlook and Investment Recommendations
passages.text:
Defining the ten-year economic vision and prioritizing ecosystem-based investments to transform Basilan into a self-sustaining, export-linked, and inclusive economic hub.
Vision Statement: Transform Basilan from a post-conflict recovery economy into a self-sustaining, export-linked, and inclusive economic hub within BARMM and the BIMP-EAGA corridor, grounded in its comparative advantages—strategic location, abundant agricultural resources, cultural heritage, youthful population, and alignment with the global halal economy.

passages.title: Policy Recommendations for Policymakers
passages.text:
Strategic actions to create an enabling environment for investment and sustainable development.
• Establish a dedicated Basilan Investment Facilitation Office within the BBOI to serve as a one-stop shop for investors, reducing transaction costs and coordination delays.
• Fast-track the completion of the Zamboanga-Basilan Interconnection Project (ZBIP) to provide reliable and affordable electricity, critical for industrial development.
• Prioritize the Basilan-Zamboanga Bridge project and ensure its completion by the target date of 2030, as this will be transformative for the province's economic integration.
• Develop a Basilan Rubber Industry Roadmap integrating the ₱195 million BARMM investment with provincial programs, focusing on plantation rehabilitation and modern processing.
• Accelerate Islamic banking licensing and expand the Al-Amanah Islamic Investment Bank network in Basilan municipalities to improve capital access for MSMEs.
• Strengthen climate adaptation programs for the agriculture sector, including drought-resistant crop varieties and irrigation systems.
• Enhance tourism development by implementing tourism plans, developing eco-tourism sites, and promoting halal tourism infrastructure.

passages.title: Investment Recommendations for Investors
passages.text:
Strategic opportunities and priority zones for private sector investment.
• Agro-industrial investors: Look at the rubber and coconut value chains as priority sectors, where BARMM support programs, existing production base, and government investment create a favorable ecosystem.
• The halal food and consumer goods sector: Isabela City presents a first-mover advantage. The city's cultural diversity and strategic location create opportunities for halal-certified products targeting BIMP-EAGA and Middle Eastern markets.
• Infrastructure investors: Assess the farm-to-market road and cold chain gap between Basilan's agricultural interior and export nodes as a high-priority, high-return infrastructure corridor.
• Renewable energy investors: Recognize Basilan as a significant underserved market with growing electricity demand, high power costs, and abundant solar and biomass resources.
• Tourism investors: Conduct feasibility studies for eco-tourism, cultural heritage circuits, and halal hospitality in anticipation of the peace dividend's continued maturation.
• Islamic finance and fintech investors: Recognize Basilan as a significant underserved market: a province of 541,947 primarily Muslim residents with a growing economy but minimal formal financial service penetration.

passages.title: Ecosystem-Based Investment Priorities (2026–2035)
passages.text:
Integrated investment matrix aligned with the BEIE Framework clusters.
• Foundations: Rubber plantation rehabilitation, seaweed farming expansion, renewable energy (Target: 2026–2030) - Expanded AFF output, reliable power supply.
• Transformers: Modern rubber processing plants, coconut processing complexes (Target: 2026–2032) - Value-added exports, MSME employment.
• Enablers: Basilan-Zamboanga Bridge, farm-to-market roads, digital infrastructure (Target: 2026–2030) - Reduced logistics costs, market access.
• Connectors: BIMP-EAGA trade linkages, halal export certification (Target: 2026–2035) - Export revenue, regional market integration.
• Financiers: Islamic banking expansion, microfinance, agricultural credit (Target: 2026–2030) - Inclusive capital access, MSME financing.
• Cross-Cutting: Eco-tourism, cultural heritage, human capital development (Target: 2026–2035) - Diversified income, skilled workforce.

passages.title: Provincial Overview
passages.text: Understanding the geographical, demographic, and post-conflict context of Lanao del Sur, the second-largest provincial economy in BARMM.

passages.title: Geographic Profile
passages.text: Lanao del Sur occupies the highland interior and lake basin of central Mindanao with a total land area of approximately 15,055 sq km. It borders Lanao del Norte to the north, Bukidnon to the east, Cotabato to the south, Maguindanao to the southwest, and Illana Bay to the west. The province is home to Lake Lanao, one of the largest and deepest lakes in Southeast Asia.

passages.title: Demographic Profile
passages.text: The 2020 Census recorded Lanao del Sur's population at 1,195,518, representing 27.14% of BARMM's total population. The province has an annual population growth rate of 2.86%, indicating a youthful demographic profile. The Maranao people form the dominant cultural community, known for their rich traditions in weaving, metalwork, and Islamic scholarship.

passages.title: Post-Conflict Context
passages.text: The 2017 Marawi siege displaced approximately 369,196 individuals and inflicted severe damage on the city's commercial district and infrastructure. Significant rehabilitation efforts have been underway, though recovery remains ongoing as of 2026. Despite the challenges, economic data suggests recovery is generating new momentum.

passages.title: Macroeconomic Performance
passages.text: Analysis of GDP growth, sectoral composition, and price stability dynamics from 2018 to 2023, highlighting the province's robust economic trajectory.

passages.title: GDP Growth Trajectory (2018-2023)
passages.text:
Lanao del Sur's GDP expanded from ₱58.53 billion in 2018 to ₱75.38 billion in 2023, representing a cumulative real increase of approximately 28.8%. The province recorded its highest growth rate in 2023 at 5.02%, surpassing BARMM's regional growth rate and outpacing all other provinces in the region.

passages.title: Sectoral Composition & Structural Shift
passages.text: The province's economic structure underwent notable transformation. The Services sector contributed 38% of GDP in 2023, followed by Industry at 33% and Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries (AFF) at 29%. The Industry sector grew significantly, consolidating its position with utilities subsector expansion. The AFF sector showed impressive 8.7% growth in 2023.

passages.title: Price Stability & Inflation Dynamics
passages.text: Lanao del Sur maintained macroeconomic stability with a year-to-date inflation rate of 3.4% in 2024 and a December 2024 monthly rate at 2.5%. This trajectory provides a stable backdrop for investment planning. Housing and utilities saw modest price increases of 1.8%, while transport prices declined 0.8%, indicating improving logistics cost competitiveness.

passages.title: BARMM Regional Growth (2025)
passages.text: The Bangsamoro regional economy reached ₱266.59 billion in 2025 at constant 2018 prices, recording a 5.0% growth rate—ranking sixth fastest among the Philippines' 18 regions and improving markedly from 3.4% in 2024. Health and social services led sectoral growth at 13.9%, followed by education at 12.0% and public administration at 9.6%. Agriculture, forestry, and fishing expanded by 4.9%, reinforcing the region's food security foundations.

passages.title: Bangsamoro Economic and Investment Ecosystem (BEIE) Framework
passages.text:
Applying the integrated systems model to analyze sectoral interlinkages and identify priority investment corridors in Lanao del Sur.
How the BEIE Framework works: The BEIE Framework organizes economic activity into five functional clusters—Foundations, Transformers, Enablers, Connectors, and Financiers—anchored by Moral Governance and driven by four cross-cutting enablers: Tourism and Culture, Peace and Security, Human Capital, and Environmental Sustainability. This systems lens reveals investment opportunities that a conventional sectoral analysis would miss.

passages.title: Foundations — Agriculture, Fisheries, Forestry & Energy
passages.text:
The resource base on which Lanao del Sur's entire economic ecosystem depends. This cluster feeds raw materials into Transformers and commodities into Connectors.
• Agriculture & Fisheries: The AFF sector's 8.7% growth in 2023 signals renewed momentum. The SPDA's Agro-Industrial Development Program in Wao and Amai Manabilang is beginning to yield results, attracting foreign investment.
• Energy: Lake Lanao hosts the Agus hydroelectric power cascade. Utilities subsector grew 37% from 2018-2023, positioning Lanao del Sur as a potential clean energy hub.
Investment Opportunities: Organic and halal-certified rice and corn production, freshwater fisheries development, bamboo and abaca fiber plantation, agro-processing facilities, hydropower rehabilitation, and solar energy installations.

passages.title: Transformers — Industrial Development & Halal Manufacturing
passages.text:
If Foundations provide the raw material, Transformers create the value. This cluster includes manufacturing and the strategically significant halal industry.
• Halal Industry: The province's Muslim majority population, cultural authority in Islamic practice, and access to raw agricultural inputs create a natural ecosystem for halal food production and certification.
• Agro-Industrial Processing: The Dole Philippines pineapple packing facility in Wao exemplifies the transformative potential of anchor agro-industrial investment.
Investment Opportunities: Halal slaughterhouses, cold chain facilities, halal food processing plants, halal cosmetics and pharmaceuticals, Islamic fashion manufacturing leveraging Maranao textile traditions.

passages.title: Enablers — Infrastructure, Logistics & Connectivity
passages.text:
No production capability can generate export value without physical infrastructure to move goods. Infrastructure gaps remain key investment constraints.
• Infrastructure: The MPW has initiated major infrastructure projects in Lanao del Sur's 2nd District, targeting road network rehabilitation and water supply improvements.
• Logistics: Within BARMM's broader logistics vision, Lanao del Sur stands to benefit from the planned Polloc Freeport development.
Investment Opportunities: Farm-to-market road construction, cold chain and warehouse facilities, digital logistics platforms, renewable energy infrastructure for agro-processing.

passages.title: Connectors — Trade, Exports & BIMP-EAGA Integration
passages.text:
This cluster links Lanao del Sur's production to regional and global markets through BIMP-EAGA integration.
• Trade Corridors: Lanao del Sur's geographical location connects it to regional trade arteries that link to BIMP-EAGA partners.
• Export Markets: BARMM is pursuing the UAE as a major export destination for halal agriculture and fisheries products.
Investment Opportunities: Establishing trade links with UAE and GCC markets, developing export-ready supply chains, BIMP-EAGA trade corridors.

passages.title: Financiers — Islamic Banking & Ethical Finance
passages.text:
The Financiers cluster is strategically important given the province's Muslim majority and alignment with Islamic finance principles.
• Islamic Banking: The approval of CARD Islamic Bank operations in Marawi City marks a pivotal step in building culturally appropriate financial infrastructure.
• Microfinance: The financial and insurance subsector remains significantly underpenetrated, indicating a large addressable market.
Investment Opportunities: Expansion of Islamic banking, takaful (Islamic insurance), waqf instruments, and microfinance to reduce barriers to capital access for MSMEs.

passages.title: Cross-Cutting Drivers — Moral Governance, Tourism & Peace
passages.text:
These drivers operate across all clusters and determine the effectiveness of the entire ecosystem.
• Moral Governance: The operating system determining whether all other clusters function effectively.
• Tourism: Underdeveloped potential in Lake Lanao, Maranao cultural heritage, and post-conflict regeneration narrative.
• Peace & Security: Foundational requirement for investor confidence and sustainable development.
Investment Opportunities: Cultural tourism, Lake Lanao eco-tourism, post-conflict urban regeneration in Marawi City.

passages.title: Investment Climate and Recent Performance
passages.text: Tracking BARMM's investment momentum and highlighting significant projects in Lanao del Sur that demonstrate the province's growing attractiveness to investors.

passages.title: BARMM Investment Momentum
passages.text: BARMM's investment climate has undergone a structural upswing. The Bangsamoro Board of Investments (BBOI) had set a 2025 target of ₱3 billion in new investment approvals. This target was breached in April 2025, with ₱3.2 billion in registered investments by mid-year, focusing on healthcare, agriculture, and agribusiness. By October 2025, total 2025 investments had reached ₱5 billion, generating 2,029 jobs across BARMM. The momentum accelerated dramatically into 2026. In the first quarter of 2026 alone, BARMM registered ₱2.4 billion in investments, projected to generate 930 jobs. By April 2026, the region had already surpassed its entire 2025 full-year record, with total approved investments reaching ₱5.1 billion—exceeding the ₱3.2 billion annual target in just four months. These investments are expected to create 2,583 jobs for Bangsamoro constituents. On April 30, 2026, the BBOI approved six new projects worth ₱2.6 billion during its 3rd Regular Board Meeting, projected to generate 1,657 jobs. Philippine Statistics Authority data confirmed that BARMM ranked second in Mindanao in approved investments, behind only the Davao Region, and placed within the top 10 regions nationally for Q2 2025.

passages.title: BARMM Investment Momentum
passages.text: BBOI Chairperson Mohamad Omar Pasigan attributed the achievement to growing investor confidence in BARMM "as a rising hub for sustainable, inclusive, and high-impact investments," reflecting the business community's trust in the Bangsamoro government's commitment to transparency, ease of doing business, and investor protection under Chief Minister Abdulraof Macacua's Mas Matatag na Bangsamoro agenda and the Economic Jihad campaign anchored on moral governance.

passages.title: 2025 Investment Sectoral Composition
passages.text: The ₱5 billion in registered investments for 2025 was distributed across priority sectors aligned with the Bangsamoro development agenda. Agriculture and agribusiness dominated with ₱4.51 billion in approved investments, creating 1,861 jobs. Other significant sectors included mass housing (₱221.87 million, 35 jobs), health and education services (₱169.63 million, 33 jobs), Islamic finance (₱85.93 million, 44 jobs), and aquaculture and fishery (₱15 million, 56 jobs). This sectoral distribution underscores BARMM's strategic focus on food security, shelter, and culturally aligned financial services.

passages.title: Strategic Investment Priority Areas
passages.text: Based on the BEIE Framework analysis, existing investment momentum, and the province's structural endowments, the following priority investment corridors are identified for Lanao del Sur through 2036:

passages.title: April 2026 BBOI Approved Projects
passages.text:
The April 30, 2026 BBOI approvals demonstrate the breadth of emerging opportunities across BARMM:
• Health and Wellness + Tourism Facilities (Cotabato City): ₱177 million investment generating 69 jobs in the region capital.
• Agriculture and Agribusiness Project 1 (Mainland Province): ₱167 million investment projected to create 113 jobs.
• Agriculture and Agribusiness Project 2 (Mainland Province): ₱58 million investment expected to employ 143 workers.
• Major Island Province Investment (Basilan or Tawi-Tawi): ₱2.2 billion flagship project projected to generate 1,330 jobs.

passages.title: Priority Investment Corridors
passages.text:
• Halal Food Manufacturing and Export Hub (Marawi City, Wao, Balabagan): Leveraging existing Maranao food traditions, MAFAR support infrastructure, and BARMM-UAE halal market linkages.
• Freshwater and Coastal Fisheries Value Chain (Lake Lanao, Balabagan, Malabang): Development of processing, cold chain, and aquaculture facilities along the province's extensive water resources.
• Agro-Industrial Corridor (Wao–Amai Manabilang–Madalum): Building on SPDA programs and the Dole Philippines anchor investment to develop an integrated plantation-processing-export zone.
• Islamic Finance and MSME Ecosystem (Marawi City): Expansion of Islamic banking, takaful, and microfinance to channel capital to post-conflict reconstruction enterprises.
• Cultural Tourism and Heritage Circuit : Development of Maranao cultural sites, torogan conservation, Lake Lanao eco-tourism, and halal-certified hospitality infrastructure.
• Renewable Energy Development : Hydropower rehabilitation along the Agus cascade and solar-powered agro-industrial facilities in upland municipalities.
• Marawi City Post-Conflict Urban Regeneration : Mixed-use commercial, industrial, and residential development in the rehabilitated Most Affected Area (MAA).

passages.title: Poverty and Human Development
passages.text: Despite improvements, poverty remains a defining structural challenge. BARMM recorded a poverty incidence of 34.8% in the first semester of 2023. The Bangsamoro's functional literacy rate is 64.7% (PSA 2024 FLEMMS, against 70.8% nationally), and its basic literacy rate (81.0%) is the lowest of any region, and 45% of children under five are affected by stunting. These human capital deficits constrain the province's capacity to supply skilled labor for modern agro-industrial and services investment.

passages.title: Peace and Security Dynamics
passages.text: Although BARMM's peace framework has broadly held since 2019, localized armed incidents, clan conflicts (rido), and the residual presence of non-MILF armed groups in some municipalities create security risks that investors must assess. The peace dividend is real and measurable, but its sustainability depends on continued progress in the Bangsamoro peace process.

passages.title: Governance and Institutional Capacity
passages.text: The Bangsamoro Government acknowledges that coordination capacity remains a constraint. The BEIE Framework identifies this as the central challenge: "It's not about launching more programs—it's about aligning existing ones into a coherent system." Inter-agency coordination between various government units is essential for synchronized development.

passages.title: Climate Vulnerability
passages.text: El Niño-induced drought caused significant agricultural losses across BARMM in 2024, prompting a state of calamity in Maguindanao del Sur. Climate-related agricultural risks, including drought, flooding, and changing rainfall patterns, require investment in climate-resilient crop varieties, irrigation systems, and adaptation planning.

passages.title: Provincial Overview
passages.text: Understanding the geographical, demographic, and strategic context of Maguindanao del Norte, BARMM's fastest-growing province and administrative center.

passages.title: Geographic Profile
passages.text: Maguindanao del Norte occupies the northern portion of the former Maguindanao province, encompassing the BARMM administrative center (Cotabato City area) and extending to the coastal municipalities. The province features fertile river basins, coastal areas along Illana Bay, and strategic access to the Polloc Freeport. The terrain is predominantly flat agricultural land with river systems supporting rice and corn production.

passages.title: Demographic Profile
passages.text: The 2020 Census recorded Maguindanao del Norte's population at over 1.2 million, representing a significant portion of BARMM's total population. The province has the highest annual population growth rate in BARMM at 4.3%, indicating a youthful and expanding demographic profile. The population is predominantly Muslim, creating a natural ecosystem for halal industries and Islamic finance. The Maguindanao people form the dominant cultural community.

passages.title: Strategic Location
passages.text: Maguindanao del Norte occupies a strategic position as the BARMM administrative center and gateway to the Polloc Freeport, the region's primary logistics and trade hub. The province's river basins support extensive rice and corn production, while its coastal location provides access to Illana Bay and BIMP-EAGA trade corridors. The Parang East Diversion Road project enhances connectivity between production areas and the freeport.

passages.title: Macroeconomic Performance
passages.text: Analysis of GDP growth, sectoral composition, and economic dynamics highlighting the province's status as BARMM's fastest-growing economy.

passages.title: GDP Growth Trajectory (2018-2024)
passages.text: Maguindanao del Norte has emerged as BARMM's fastest-growing province, recording an impressive 4.1% growth rate in 2024. This growth outpaces the BARMM regional average of 2.7% and reflects the province's strategic advantages as the administrative center, agricultural productivity, and emerging industrial base. The province's economy is driven by agriculture, services, and growing industrial activity.

passages.title: Sectoral Composition & Structural Shift
passages.text: The province's economic structure reflects its role as both an agricultural producer and administrative center. Agriculture, Forestry, and Fisheries (AFF) remains the dominant sector, with rice, corn, and coconut as key crops. The Services sector is growing rapidly, driven by government administration, education, healthcare, and emerging commercial activities in Cotabato City. The Industry sector includes agro-processing, construction, and utilities.
